inputs.description: Template text; each {placeholder} becomes an input port, and a placeholder used twice fills only the first time

outputs.name: formatted
outputs.description: Format with every placeholder substituted, and an unset placeholder replaced by nothing

dynamicPorts.description: Input ports are created for each "{tag}" appearing in the "format" parameter string.

enrichment.summary: Builds a string from a template: each {tag} in the Format text becomes an input port whose value is spliced in.
enrichment.description: String Format takes a template on its `format` (Format) parameter and outputs the filled-in text on `formatted` (Formatted), a string value. Every {tag} in the template (tag characters: letters, digits, underscore) becomes a string input port named exactly like the tag, and each occurrence is replaced by that input's current value — or by nothing while the input is still undefined. The same tag may appear multiple times; every occurrence is filled. The output recomputes after any input or the template changes, once per update cycle. The node displays its format text as its label in the editor.
enrichment.whenToUse: The idiomatic way to put values inside text: 'Saved at {time}', '{count} items', building URLs or messages from parts. For two fixed alternatives use Boolean To String; for value-keyed lookup use String Mapper; for transformations of the values themselves (padding, casing, math) do that upstream in an Expression or Function.

ports.format: String parameter with {tag} placeholders; changing it re-registers the input ports and reformats.
ports.formatted: String value output: the template with every {tag} replaced by its input's value (empty where an input is still undefined).

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Input ports are created from the `format` parameter: each unique {tag} yields one string input named exactly <tag> (no braces). The editor updates the port list live as the format is edited. An authoring tool must first set `format`, then may connect to or set parameters for each tag name it wrote; no other inputs exist.
patterns: Counter `currentCount` → the {n} input of format "{n} pcs" → a Text's `text`: numbers cast to string on connection, so no converter node is needed.
antiPatterns: Tags with spaces or dashes ({item-count}) — tag names are limited to [A-Za-z0-9_]; anything else stays literal text.

inputs.name: defaultMapping
inputs.description: Published when Input String matches none of the numbered inputs

inputs.name: inputString
inputs.description: The string to look up among the numbered inputs

outputs.name: mappedString
outputs.description: The mapping paired with the input that matched, or Default when none did

dynamicPorts.description: Accepts an unbounded numbered series of inputs (see numberedInputs); ports are named "<base> <N>" counting from 0.

parameterEncoding.reason: The port helper needs project context this generator cannot supply headlessly — a live component, a connected node, or a backend schema.

enrichment.summary: Looks a string up in a configured key list and outputs the matching mapping — a wirable lookup table with a default.
enrichment.description: String Mapper compares `inputString` (Input String) against its numbered "input N" entries (displayed Input 0, Input 1, …) using exact string equality. On a match, the `mappedString` (Mapped String) output takes the value of the "output N" entry with the same N (displayed Mapping 0, Mapping 1, … — these mappings are themselves inputs, despite the port name); with no match it takes `defaultMapping` (Default). All values are coerced to strings before comparison, and the mapping re-runs once per update cycle after any of its inputs change. Keys and mappings are usually typed in as parameters but can also be connected.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it to translate machine values into display text: status codes to labels, option keys to descriptions, locale keys to phrases. For just true/false use Boolean To String; for composing text with variables inside use String Format; for mappings that live in data rather than in the graph, use an Object or a Function.

ports.inputString: String value to look up; compared with strict equality after toString coercion.
ports.defaultMapping: String value used whenever no key matches — also the output before `inputString` first matches anything.
ports.mappedString: String value output: the mapping paired with the matched key, or `defaultMapping`.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Two numbered port series, both inputs, indexed from 0: keys are named "input 0", "input 1", … (group Inputs) and their mapped values are named "output 0", "output 1", … (group Mappings) — pair N maps key N to value N. The editor always offers the next unused index. An authoring tool typically writes both series as parameters (e.g. "input 0": "S", "output 0": "Small"), and may connect any of them.
patterns: A Radio Button Group's `value` → `inputString`, mappings to human copy → a Text's `text`: option keys stay short and stable while the UI text stays editable in one place.
antiPatterns: Using it for numeric ranges ('0-9' → 'low') — matching is exact equality only; use Expression or Condition chains for ranges.

inputs.name: index
inputs.description: Which of the numbered strings to publish, counting from zero and truncated to a whole number

outputs.name: currentValue
outputs.description: The numbered string sitting at Index, or nothing when there is none

outputs.name: indexChanged
outputs.description: Fires when Index changes, after Current Value has been updated

dynamicPorts.description: Accepts an unbounded numbered series of inputs (see numberedInputs); ports are named "<base> <N>" counting from 0.

parameterEncoding.reason: The port helper needs project context this generator cannot supply headlessly — a live component, a connected node, or a backend schema.

enrichment.summary: Deprecated 'Index To String' lookup: outputs one of a numbered list of author-defined strings selected by a number index.
enrichment.description: String Selector (shown as 'Index To String') holds a numbered series of author-entered strings and outputs the one at the current `index` on `currentValue`, firing `indexChanged` when the index changes. It is deprecated; a States node (mapping each state to arbitrary values) or an Expression covers the same need with more flexibility.
enrichment.whenToUse: Do not use in new graphs — use States or an Expression instead.
enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Inputs are a numbered series: ports named 'input 0', 'input 1', … (displayed 'String for N') are added by the editor as each is used; there is no static bound on the count.

ssr.note: A realtime subscription cannot be opened during a server render and would hold one connection per request; the node subscribes in the browser after hydration.

inputs.name: enabled
inputs.description: Hold the subscription open. Turn it off to stop receiving changes without deleting the node — the connection is closed and Subscribed goes false. On by default: this node has nothing else to do

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Any of the three, and also the backend saying the view may be stale after a reconnect — the one to react to if you do not care which happened

outputs.name: changedEvent
outputs.description: create, update, delete, init or resync

outputs.name: changedRecord
outputs.description: The record the change was about. ⚠️ Null on a delete against Directus, which sends only the key — use Changed Record Id, which every backend fills

outputs.name: changedRecordId
outputs.description: The id of the changed record, always a string — even where the backend's primary key is an integer

outputs.name: changedRecords
outputs.description: Every record in the change frame; some backends batch

outputs.name: created
outputs.description: Another client created a record in this collection

outputs.name: deleted
outputs.description: Another client deleted a record from this collection

outputs.name: realtimeError
outputs.description: The last realtime failure, with a code and whether retrying can help; null until one happens

outputs.name: realtimeFailure
outputs.description: Fires when a subscription cannot connect, is rejected, or has been given up on

outputs.name: realtimeStatus
outputs.description: connecting, subscribed, interrupted or stopped. Four states rather than a boolean, because "connecting for the first time" and "dropped and retrying" want different things on screen

outputs.name: subscribed
outputs.description: True while the backend has confirmed the subscription and is delivering changes

outputs.name: updated
outputs.description: Another client updated a record in this collection

dynamicPorts.description: Every input but "enabled" is discovered at runtime. "backendId" is a dropdown of the project's backends, defaulting to "_active_" and omitted entirely when the project has only one; "collectionName" is a dropdown of the selected backend's introspected classes; "visualFilter" is a query-filter editor built from that class's schema, and each filter value bound to a port mints one "qp-<name>" input. An authoring tool should set "collectionName" (and "backendId" only when the project has more than one backend); the outputs are all static.

parameterEncoding.reason: No parameter on this node carries the list its ports are generated from, so the port set could not be observed headlessly.

enrichment.summary: Fires signals when another client creates, updates or deletes a record in a backend class.
enrichment.description: Subscribe To Changes holds a live connection to the selected backend and reports what changes in one class. It does not query and it holds no list: when the server pushes a change it publishes the row on `changedRecord`, its key on `changedRecordId` and the kind on `changedEvent`, then fires `created`, `updated` or `deleted` and always `changed`. The transport is chosen from the backend's type and hidden — Server-Sent Events on the built-in NodeGX backend and on PocketBase, a WebSocket on Directus, Parse LiveQuery where one is running — so the ports mean the same thing whichever backend the project uses. It is on as soon as you pick a class: `enabled` defaults to true and the Backend picker defaults to the project's active backend (and is hidden entirely when there is only one). When a backend cannot push at all, the node does not go quiet — `realtimeError` carries a sentence saying why and `realtimeFailure` fires.
enrichment.whenToUse: When something in the app should react to a change another user made, without owning a query — 'any change to orders, refresh the badge', 'a new message arrived, play a sound'. If you already have a Query Records node and want its `items` to stay current, turn on that node's own Subscribe To Changes checkbox instead of adding this one: it re-runs the query, which this node deliberately does not. For a socket you control yourself — a third-party feed, device telemetry, an LLM stream from someone else's API — use the WebSocket or SSE node; those are raw transports with no backend awareness. This node is client-only: it is inert during server-side rendering and subscribes in the browser after hydration, and it is not available in cloud functions at all (a function is one request and is torn down when it answers).

ports.enabled: On by default. Turning it off closes the connection and sets `subscribed` false; turning it back on opens a new one. There is no `Do` — the node has nothing to trigger.
ports.backendId: Runtime-discovered dropdown. Defaults to the project's active backend and is not shown at all in a single-backend project, which is why the node needs no configuration there.
ports.collectionName: The class to watch, from the selected backend's introspected schema. Nothing happens until it is set.
ports.visualFilter: ⚠️ Server-side on the built-in NodeGX backend ONLY. PocketBase, Directus and Parse accept no filter on a subscription, so on those backends every change in the class arrives and this setting is ignored. It is never applied on the client: events that were never delivered are not events a filter excluded, and quietly filtering locally would make one setting mean two different things.
ports.subscribed: True only while the backend has confirmed the subscription — false while connecting, during a reconnect, and after a failure it will not retry. Wire it to a 'live' indicator so people can see when updates are actually flowing.
ports.realtimeStatus: connecting, subscribed, interrupted or stopped. `subscribed` alone cannot tell 'reconnecting' from 'never started'.
ports.realtimeError: The last failure, with a code and whether retrying can help; null until one happens. This is where an unsupported backend explains itself — Supabase has no transport built at all, and Parse LiveQuery usually is not running.
ports.realtimeFailure: Fires when a subscription cannot connect, is rejected, or has been given up on. A capability that fails silently is the defect this signal exists to prevent.
ports.created: Another client created a record. Fires after the Changed outputs have been updated.
ports.updated: Another client updated a record. Fires after the Changed outputs have been updated.
ports.deleted: Another client deleted a record. ⚠️ On Directus the frame carries the key only, so `changedRecord` is null here and `changedRecordId` is the output that works.
ports.changed: Fires alongside every created/updated/deleted, and also on a `resync` — the backend saying your view may be stale after a reconnect. The one to react to when you do not care which happened.
ports.changedEvent: create, update, delete, init or resync. `init` is the confirmation snapshot and fires no create/update/delete signal — a subscription must not look like a burst of writes the moment it connects.
ports.changedRecord: The record the change was about, or null when the backend sent only a key.
ports.changedRecords: Every record in the change frame; some backends batch. Empty when the frame carried keys only.
ports.changedRecordId: The key of the changed record, always a string — even where the backend's primary key is an integer. Every backend fills this, which is why it is the one to reach for on a delete.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Only `enabled` is a static input. `backendId`, `collectionName`, `visualFilter` and one `qp-<name>` port per filter value bound to a port are all generated from the project's backend metadata and the selected class's schema, and are pushed to the editor per instance. An authoring tool should set `collectionName`, and `backendId` only when the project has more than one backend. Every output is static and always present — the Realtime ports are never gated on whether the selected backend can push, because a capability that disappears from the panel when the picker moves is worse than one that says why it cannot connect.
patterns: `changed` → a Query Records node's `Do`: the same live-list effect as that node's own checkbox, but with the subscription visible on the canvas as a thing that exists.
`created` → a notification or a sound, without re-fetching anything — this node publishes the new row on `changedRecord` already.
`changedRecordId` → a Delete Record or a Set Variable: the one output that is filled on every backend and every event type.
`subscribed` → an indicator's visibility, and `realtimeError` → an error Text: an outage becomes something a user can see rather than a screen that has quietly stopped updating.
antiPatterns: Adding this beside a Query Records node whose `items` you want kept current. Turn on that node's Subscribe To Changes instead — it re-runs the query, which this node does not.
Reading `changedRecord` on a delete. Directus sends the key only, so it is null there; use `changedRecordId`.
Expecting the Filter to narrow anything on PocketBase, Directus or Parse. It reaches a server on the built-in NodeGX backend only, and is deliberately not applied on the client.
Polling with a Timer on a backend that can push. Subscribe and react to `changed`.
Assuming silence means 'no changes'. Read `realtimeStatus` and `realtimeError` — Supabase has no transport at all and says so.

inputs.name: end
inputs.description: Position to stop before; leave it unset to run to the end of the string, since setting it to 0 yields nothing

inputs.name: start
inputs.description: Position of the first character to keep, counting from zero; a negative value counts back from the end

inputs.name: string
inputs.description: Text to take the substring from; it must not be cleared to null, which raises an error rather than yielding an empty result

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: The section of String between Start and End

enrichment.summary: Extracts part of a string between a start index (inclusive) and end index (exclusive).
enrichment.description: Substring takes a `string` (String) input and outputs the characters from index `start` (Start, 0-based, inclusive) up to but not including index `end` (End) on the `result` (Result) string value output. While `end` has never been set, the substring runs from `start` to the end of the string — so a node with only `start` configured behaves like 'drop the first N characters'. Setting `end` to -1 also means 'to the end of the string'. Non-string inputs are converted with toString() first, and any input change updates the result immediately.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for simple positional trims: a short prefix of an id, truncating a preview, slicing fixed-width data. For pattern-based extraction, case changes or search-and-replace, use Expression or a Function; for assembling text from parts, use String Format.

ports.end: Number value, exclusive end index. Left unset (or set to -1) the substring extends to the end of the string; note that an explicit 0 means an empty result, not 'to the end'.
ports.result: String value with the extracted range.

patterns: Unique Id `guid` → `string` with `start` 0 / `end` 4: a short human-readable tag from a longer id.
antiPatterns: Setting `end` to 0 expecting 'until the end' — 0 is a real exclusive index and yields an empty string; leave `end` unset or use -1 instead.

inputs.name: flip
inputs.description: Switches to whichever state it is not currently in

inputs.name: off
inputs.description: Switches off, or fires Unchanged if it is already off

inputs.name: on
inputs.description: Switches on, or fires Unchanged if it is already on

inputs.name: onFromStart
inputs.description: State to start in, and setting it announces a switch on Switched even though nothing switched

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the switch actually changed state

outputs.name: state
outputs.description: True while the switch is on — wire it into a mounted or visible port for a gate that turns on AND off

outputs.name: switched
outputs.description: Fires on every state change, alongside whichever of Switched To On and Switched To Off applies

outputs.name: switchedToOff
outputs.description: Fires when the switch becomes off

outputs.name: switchedToOn
outputs.description: Fires when the switch becomes on

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when it was already in that state, so none of the Switched signals fired

enrichment.summary: A remembered on/off boolean, driven by On / Off / Flip signals — the graph's toggle and one-bit memory.
enrichment.description: Switch stores a single boolean state. The `on` (On), `off` (Off) and `flip` (Flip) signal inputs change it; `onFromStart` (State) is a boolean value input that sets the state directly and provides its initial value (default false). The current state is always readable on the `state` (Current State) boolean value output, and every state change also fires signals: `switched` (Switched) on any change, plus `switchedToOn` or `switchedToOff` matching the new state. `on` and `off` are ignored when the state already matches, so they never re-fire the signals; `flip` always changes state.
enrichment.whenToUse: The idiomatic node for anything a user toggles: expand/collapse, mute, edit mode. Use `state` (a level) to drive `visible`/`enabled`-style inputs, and the switched signals only when something must happen at the moment of change. For more than two states use States; for deriving a boolean from data rather than events, use Condition or Expression.

ports.flip: Signal; inverts the state and always fires the switched signals.
ports.on: Signal; sets the state to true. Does nothing (and fires nothing) if it is already true.
ports.off: Signal; sets the state to false. Does nothing (and fires nothing) if it is already false.
ports.onFromStart: Boolean value (displayed as State); sets the state directly and defines the initial state. Changing it also fires the switched signals.
ports.state: Boolean value that always reflects the current state — wire this to `visible`/`enabled` style inputs.
ports.switched: Signal; fires on every state change, after `state` has been updated.
ports.switchedToOn: Signal; fires when a change leaves the state true.
ports.switchedToOff: Signal; fires when a change leaves the state false.

patterns: Button `onClick` → `flip`, `state` → a Group's `visible`: the standard show/hide toggle.
`state` → Boolean To String `input` → the toggling button's `label`: the button describes what it will do next.
antiPatterns: Wiring `switchedToOn` (a momentary signal) to a boolean input like `visible` — it delivers only a pulse; use `state` for anything that must stay on.

dynamicPorts.description: Declares conditional/expandable port groups whose visibility depends on parameter values (see declaredPortGroups).

declaredPortGroups.condition: sizeMode = explicit OR sizeMode = contentHeight OR sizeMode NOT SET

parameterEncoding.notes: This node computes no port names. Its dynamic behaviour is visibility only: every port it can ever have is listed in `inputs`/`outputs` above, and `dynamicPorts.declaredPortGroups` says which parameter values reveal which of them.

enrichment.summary: Renders a piece of text with typography controlled by a text style or explicit font parameters.
enrichment.description: Text displays the string on its `text` input. Typography comes either from a project-wide `textStyle` (preferred, keeps the app consistent) or from explicit `fontFamily`/`fontSize`/`color` parameters that override it. Like all visual nodes it sits in the children hierarchy, has size/margin/alignment parameters, and reports basic interaction signals (`onClick`, hover) and geometry. Text has no box of its own: it takes margins, but padding, background colour, border and corner radius are not ports on it — a padded, filled or rounded label is a Text inside a Group carrying those, which is what the design system's own components do.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any static or data-bound text: headings, labels, list-item fields, error messages. Not for user-editable text (use net.noodl.controls.textinput) and not for button captions (the Button control has its own label). For anything with an inset, a fill or a rounded edge, wrap the Text in a Group and set padding, backgroundColor and borderRadius on the Group.

ports.text: The string to render; bind data here (e.g. a Component Inputs property or a String variable).
ports.textStyle: Named project text style supplying font, size and color; explicit font parameters on this node override individual fields of it.
ports.sizeMode: How the node takes its size: content-driven by default, or explicit width/height.
ports.visible: Boolean level; hides/shows without removing layout logic elsewhere.

outputs.name: done

outputs.name: timerStarted

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires on a Start while one is already running, or a Stop with nothing running

enrichment.summary: Delay: fires a Finished signal a set number of milliseconds after being started; restartable for debouncing.
enrichment.description: Timer (displayed as Delay) turns one signal into a later signal. Triggering `start` (Start) begins a countdown of `duration` milliseconds (after an optional `startDelay`, also milliseconds); when it completes, `timerFinished` (Finished) fires. `timerStarted` (Started) fires at the moment the countdown actually begins. `start` does nothing while the timer is already running, whereas `restart` (Restart) always begins the countdown again from zero — that difference is what makes `restart` the debounce input. `stop` (Stop) cancels a running countdown without firing `timerFinished`. With the default `duration` of 0 the finish fires on the next tick, which still defers the signal until after the current update.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it to defer an action (auto-dismiss a toast, poll once after mount) or, via `restart`, to debounce a noisy source such as typing. For repeating ticks, loop `timerFinished` back into `restart`. For animating a value over time use Animation instead — Timer carries no value, only timing.

ports.start: Signal; starts the countdown only if the timer is not already running.
ports.restart: Signal; starts the countdown unconditionally, restarting from zero if already running — use for debouncing.
ports.stop: Signal; cancels the countdown; `timerFinished` will not fire.
ports.startDelay: Number value in milliseconds added before the countdown begins (default 0).
ports.timerStarted: Signal; fires when the countdown actually starts (also on each restart).
ports.timerFinished: Signal; fires once when the countdown completes; suppressed by `stop`.

patterns: Value Changed `valueChanged` → `restart`, act on `timerFinished`: debounce — the action runs only after the input has been quiet for `duration` ms.
`timerFinished` → its own `restart`: a simple repeating tick.
antiPatterns: Using `start` for debouncing — while running it ignores triggers, so the action fires on the first quiet gap after the *first* event, not the last. Use `restart`.
Treating `duration` as seconds — it is milliseconds.

ssr.note: The scheduler clock is frozen during server render; the transition does not animate or complete there.

enrichment.summary: Provides a random 10-character alphanumeric id, with a signal to generate a fresh one on demand.
enrichment.description: Unique Id holds a randomly generated id string — 10 characters of A–Z, a–z, 0–9, the same generator the runtime uses for model ids — on its `guid` (Id) string value output. One id is generated when the node initializes, so `guid` is usable immediately; triggering the `new` (New) signal input replaces it with a fresh id and pushes the change downstream. patterns: The signal that creates a local item also triggers `new`, and `guid` is stored with the item: every item gets its own key.

enrichment.summary: Uploads a browser file to cloud storage when triggered, reporting progress and yielding a cloudfile handle.
enrichment.description: Upload File takes a browser File (typically from Open File Picker) on its untyped `file` input and, when `upload` fires, stores it in the cloud backend's file storage. Progress streams out (`progressLoadedPercent`, byte counts, `progressChanged`), and on `done` the stored file is available as `cloudFile` — the handle to attach to a record's file property or unwrap with Cloud File. `failure` carries `error` and `errorStatus`.
enrichment.whenToUse: Attachments, avatars, imports — any user-picked file that must persist server-side. The upload stores the file only; associating it with a record is a separate write (Create/Set Record).

ports.file: The browser file to upload; untyped so any file source connects.
ports.private: Boolean, default false. When true the backend ACLs the upload to its uploader instead of leaving it public — the resulting cloudfile's plain `url` then only works for the uploader (or an admin); use Sign File URL to get a usable link back out.
ports.cloudFile: The stored file's handle, valid from `done` onward.
ports.progressLoadedPercent: Number level 0–100 while uploading; drive progress UI from here.
ports.bucket: Supabase Storage bucket to upload into. Supabase only, and there is no default.
ports.path: Object path inside the bucket, e.g. avatars/me.png. Supabase only; blank uses the file's own name.
ports.collection: PocketBase collection holding the record the file attaches to. PocketBase only.
ports.recordId: The record the file attaches to. PocketBase only.
ports.field: The file-typed field on that record. PocketBase only.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: A `backendId` (Backend) input is registered at runtime rather than declared, so it appears only once a project has more than one backend — the node then uploads through whichever backend the picker names instead of the project's `cloudservices` endpoint (BCN-007 step 6). A backend id naming nothing is an error, never a silent fallback. The static inputs are also **per backend, not universal**: `bucket` and `path` are Supabase Storage only, and `collection`/`recordId`/`field` are PocketBase only, because PocketBase stores a file as a field on a record rather than as an object of its own. Leave them unset on the built-in, Parse and Directus backends. BCN-010 gates the node on `files.upload`, so a backend that cannot accept an upload marks the node with the reason before it is triggered.
patterns: Picker `done` → `upload`, upload `done` → record write: three nodes, each owning one step.
`private: true` uploads pair with Sign File URL: wire the same `done` signal to both the record write and the signer.
antiPatterns: Treating `cloudFile` as set before `done` fired — sequence record writes on the Done signal.
Setting `private: true` and then binding `cloudFile.url` straight to an Image/link — a private file's plain url 403s for anyone but the uploader; sign it first.

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: Value to watch; changes are detected by identity, so editing an Object or Array in place is not a change here

outputs.name: valueChanged
outputs.description: Fires when Input becomes a different value, including the first time it arrives

enrichment.summary: Turns value changes into events: fires a signal every time its input receives a different value.
enrichment.description: Value Changed watches one input of any type (`value`, displayed as Input) and fires the `valueChanged` (Value Changed) signal each time the incoming value differs from the last one it saw — including the very first value it receives. Comparison uses strict equality, so for objects and arrays a change means a different reference, not a mutation of the same object. It is the bridge from the value world (levels) to the signal world (events).
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it when something must happen at the moment data changes: restart a debounce Timer while the user types, re-run a Function when a selection changes, or trigger a save when a field updates. If you only need the value itself downstream, connect the value directly — no node needed. If you care about a boolean becoming true specifically, connect the boolean straight to a signal input (rising-edge trigger) instead.

ports.value: Value input of any type; each strictly-unequal new value fires the output. Object/array mutations without a new reference do not count as changes.
ports.valueChanged: Signal; fires once per detected change, including the first value ever received.

patterns: A text input's `text` → `value`, `valueChanged` → a Timer's `restart`: debounce — the Timer only finishes once typing pauses.
`valueChanged` → an Event Sender's `sendEvent`: broadcast that a piece of state changed.
antiPatterns: Using it to detect a boolean turning true — it also fires on true→false. Connect the boolean directly to the target signal input (edge-triggered) or use Condition.

enrichment.summary: Deprecated first-generation named app-wide variable node; superseded by Variable2 and Set Variable.
enrichment.description: The original read/write node for the named app-wide variable store, with an explicit `store` (Set) signal to commit its `value` input. It is superseded by Variable2 (shown as 'Variable' in the picker), which writes whenever its value input receives data, together with Set Variable for explicit signal-driven writes with type control. Both read and write the same underlying store as this node.
enrichment.whenToUse: Do not use in new graphs — use Variable2 to read and write a named variable, and Set Variable for explicit signal-driven writes.

outputs.name: name
outputs.description: The variable name this node is currently bound to

outputs.name: value

enrichment.summary: Reads and writes one named app-wide variable; every node bound to the same name sees the same value.
enrichment.description: Variable2 (shown as 'Variable' in the editor) binds to one entry in the app-wide variable store — a single shared, untyped key/value map for the running session (in memory only, not persisted across reloads). `name` selects the variable; the `value` output reads it, and the `value` *input* writes it: sending a value in stores it under the current name for every other Variable node to see. When the variable is written anywhere else in the app, `changed` fires and the `value` output updates automatically. Connecting the `fetch` signal input changes this to pull mode: external changes and name changes no longer propagate on their own, and the node only re-reads when `fetch` fires, after which `fetched` fires. This is the shared counterpart of the per-instance Boolean/Number/String/Color holders, which each keep a private value.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for state shared across components — the logged-in user's name, a selected id, a UI mode — reading it where needed and writing via its `value` input or, for explicit signal-driven writes with type control, a Set Variable node. For a value used only inside one component prefer a per-instance holder (Boolean/Number/String/Color); for structured data use Model2.

ports.name: String value input naming the variable; all Variable/Set Variable nodes with the same name share one value. With `fetch` unconnected, changing the name immediately re-reads and fires `fetched`.
ports.value: As an input: writes — the received value is stored into the named variable. As an output: the variable's current value (untyped).
ports.fetch: Signal; re-reads the named variable on demand. Connecting it disables automatic updates — external changes then reach the outputs only when Fetch fires.
ports.changed: Signal; fires when the variable is changed from anywhere in the app (suppressed while `fetch` is connected).
ports.fetched: Signal; fires after each read triggered by `fetch` or by a name change.
ports.done: Signal; the outcome of a Fetch. A name change fires `fetched` without one, because a value setter is not an invocation.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every Fetch whatever the outcome — wire it to carry on regardless.
ports.failure: Signal; a value arrived on the `value` input with no `name` set, so it was refused rather than stored where nothing can read it. ⚠️ This belongs to the `value` input, not to `fetch`: it reports no outcome and does not fire `completed`.

patterns: Set Variable writes on a user action; Variable2 nodes with the same name anywhere in the app update reactively — the idiomatic shared-state shape.
`value` output → an Expression → visual inputs: derive display text or booleans from shared state where it is consumed.
antiPatterns: Expecting each Variable2 instance to hold its own value — the name is the identity, all instances with one name share one value. For private per-node state use Boolean/Number/String/Color.
Using variables as persistent storage — the store is in-memory and resets on page reload; persist important data in the cloud database or browser storage nodes.

enrichment.summary: Plays video from a URL or MediaStream, with play/pause/restart/reset signals and playback-position output.
enrichment.description: Video renders an HTML `video` element. `src` (a string URL or project asset path) or `srcObject` (a MediaStream, e.g. a camera feed) supplies the media; `poster` shows an image before playback; `autoplay`, `loop`, `muted`, `controls` and `volume` map directly onto the element. Playback is driven by four signal inputs: `play` resumes, `pause` pauses, `restart` seeks to the start and plays, `reset` seeks to the start and pauses. Outputs report state: `onPlay`/`onPause`/`onCanPlay` are signals from the element's events, `onTimeUpdate` (Playback Position) is a number holding the current time in seconds, and `videoWidth`/`videoHeight` give the intrinsic size once known.
enrichment.whenToUse: Embedded video content, background/hero loops, and camera previews (wire a media stream to `srcObject`). For still pictures use Image. Browsers block unmuted autoplay — combine `autoplay` with `muted` for background video, or start playback from a user action via `play`.

ports.src: String value: URL or project asset path of the video file.
ports.srcObject: MediaStream value; when set, the element plays the stream instead of `src` — used for camera/microphone previews.
ports.play: Signal; resumes playback of the current source.
ports.restart: Signal; seeks to time 0 and plays.
ports.reset: Signal; seeks to time 0 and pauses — 'stop'.
ports.onTimeUpdate: Number value (Playback Position): current playback time in seconds, updated as the video plays.
ports.onCanPlay: Signal; fires when enough data is buffered to start playing — a good moment to reveal the player.
ports.onVideoElementCreated: DOM-element reference to the underlying `video` element, for custom JavaScript integration.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: `width`/`height` appear based on `sizeMode`, per-side border width/color ports appear once a border style is chosen, and `pointerEventsEnabled` appears when `pointerEventsMode` is 'explicit'. The playback and event ports are always present.
patterns: Button `onClick` → `play`: user-initiated playback that satisfies browser autoplay policies.
Background hero: `autoplay` + `muted` + `loop` true, `controls` false, `objectFit` 'cover'.
antiPatterns: Expecting `autoplay` alone to start sound-on playback — browsers refuse; either set `muted` or trigger `play` from a user gesture.

enrichment.summary: Action Dispatcher: executes actions a backend sent, restricted to a vocabulary this graph explicitly registered.
enrichment.description: Turns messages like `{ "type": "OPEN_SESSION", "sessionId": "123" }` into things that actually happen in the app, so a server-side agent can drive the UI instead of only sending data to display. The vocabulary is **closed**: an action runs only if an Action Handler node registered its type, or it is one of the four built-in store actions (`SET_STORE`, `MERGE_STORE`, `DELETE_STORE_KEY`, `CLEAR_STORE`) and the author listed that name in `builtIns`, which is empty by default. Everything else is refused with a reason on `refusalReason` and a `refused` signal — never silently ignored, and never executed. Actions run strictly one at a time in arrival order, so an array of actions is a multi-step flow; the queue is bounded and overflow refuses the newest rather than reordering what was accepted. An action whose handler has not mounted yet waits up to `waitForHandler` milliseconds rather than losing a mount race, and `waitingFor` names it while it waits.
enrichment.whenToUse: Whenever a backend needs to cause something rather than just report something: an AI agent that says "let me open that for you", a guided tour driven from the server, a workflow whose steps arrive over a stream. Wire a Server-Sent Events or WebSocket node's `data` to `action` and its `onMessage` to `dispatch`. Do not use it as a general message router for data you are simply going to display — wire that straight to its consumer.

ports.channel: Names the handler registry this dispatcher draws on. Only handlers on the same channel are reachable. Leave as `default` unless two independent flows must not see each other.
ports.action: One action object, an array of them to run in order, or JSON text holding either. A frame's raw text works as well as its parsed value.
ports.dispatch: Admits the current action. Acts immediately rather than at end of frame, so several actions arriving in one frame all run instead of coalescing to the last.
ports.cancel: Discards everything queued and abandons anything in flight, reporting the count on `cancelledCount`.
ports.builtIns: Comma-separated built-in action names this dispatcher may execute. Empty — the default — means a server cannot write the store at all. A name that is not a built-in is reported on `lastError` and grants nothing.
ports.storeName: The only store the built-in actions can write. A `storeName` inside an incoming action is ignored: the graph chooses the store, not the server.
ports.allowedKeys: Comma-separated keys the built-in store actions may write. Blank means any key of the configured store. Setting any key also refuses `CLEAR_STORE`, which would remove keys outside the list.
ports.handlerTimeout: How long a handler has to signal Complete or Fail before the action fails and the queue moves on. 0 waits forever.
ports.waitForHandler: How long an action waits for its handler to appear before being refused as unknown. Everything behind it waits too, because order is preserved. 0 refuses immediately.
ports.maxQueueSize: Bound on queued actions; overflow refuses the newest. 0 is unbounded, which a hostile or looping server can grow without limit.
ports.rateLimit: Max actions executed per window; excess is refused, not delayed. 0 is unlimited.
ports.actionType: Type of the action currently executing, or the last one that did.
ports.actionId: The action's `id` if it carried one, else a generated one. Useful for acknowledging back to the server.
ports.payload: The action's `payload`, else its `data`, else the whole action object.
ports.result: What the completing handler or built-in returned.
ports.dispatched: Fires when an action starts executing — after it passed every check.
ports.actionCompleted: Fires when one action's handlers have all completed. Per *action*: one Dispatch of an array fires this once per member.
ports.done: Fires once per invocation: a Dispatch that admitted at least one action, or a Cancel All that dropped at least one.
ports.unchanged: Fires once per invocation when there was nothing to do — a Cancel All with an empty queue.
ports.failure: Fires once per invocation when a Dispatch admitted nothing at all, because every action in it was refused.
ports.completed: Fires after `done`, `unchanged` or `failure`, once per invocation of Dispatch or Cancel All. Not to be confused with `actionCompleted`, which counts actions rather than invocations.
ports.failed: Fires when a handler failed, threw, or timed out. The action was allowed; it just did not work.
ports.idle: Fires when the queue drains. This is how a multi-step flow knows it finished.
ports.refused: Fires when an action was **not** executed. Wire this — it is the only way an author sees that a server asked for something disallowed.
ports.refusedType: The type that was refused, or empty when the message was too malformed to have one.
ports.refusalMessage: The human-readable reason, safe to show in a debug panel.
ports.lastError: The most recent failure or refusal message.
ports.queueSize: Actions waiting behind the one in flight.
ports.isExecuting: Whether an action is running right now.
ports.waitingFor: The action type held at the head of the queue because no handler has registered for it yet.
ports.completedCount: Actions completed since the node was created.
ports.failedCount: Actions that were allowed but did not work.
ports.refusedCount: Actions refused. A number that climbs unexpectedly means the server and the graph disagree about the vocabulary.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `data` → `action`, `onMessage` → `dispatch`: an agent stream that drives the UI.
One Action Handler per thing the server may do, each wired to the nodes that do it — that set of handlers *is* the permission list, visible on the canvas.
`refusalReason` and `refusalMessage` → a Text node in a debug group: the fastest way to find out that the server is sending `OPEN_VIEW` while the graph registered `OPEN_SESSION`.
Send an array of actions for a guided tour; set `autoComplete` off on the handlers that must finish before the next step starts, and wire `idle` to whatever runs at the end.
Enable `SET_STORE` with `allowedKeys` naming just the view keys the agent may steer, so a store write cannot reach an auth token that happens to live in the same store.

A built-in's own fields may sit on the envelope (`{type:'SET_STORE', key, value}`) or inside `payload` (`{type:'SET_STORE', payload:{key, value}}`) — the same resolution a handler's `payload` output uses, envelope first on a collision. `MERGE_STORE` wants `values` either way. A `storeName` in the message is always ignored in favour of the node's own.
antiPatterns: Enabling built-ins with `allowedKeys` blank on a store that also holds credentials or ids — a server can then overwrite any key in it.
Registering a catch-all handler that reads `payload.command` and switches on it: that re-opens the open vocabulary this node exists to close. One handler per action type.
Leaving `refused` unwired. A dispatcher that refuses everything looks identical to a dead stream if nothing shows the refusals.
Wiring `dispatch` from a signal that fires before `action` is set — the previous action runs again.
Setting `maxQueueSize` to 0 on a stream you do not control.

inputs.name: result

outputs.name: completed

enrichment.summary: Action Handler: declares one action type a backend is allowed to trigger, and what happens when it does.
enrichment.description: Registers a single action type with the Action Dispatcher's registry, and fires `trigger` with the action's `payload` whenever a matching action is dispatched. That registration is what makes the action executable at all — there is no separate permission list to keep in step, so an action a graph does not handle simply cannot happen. Registration follows the inputs automatically: no Register signal to remember, and an action that arrives just before the component mounts waits for it rather than being refused. By default the action is reported complete as soon as `trigger` has been sent and everything wired to it has run; turn `autoComplete` off and wire `complete` or `fail` yourself when a later step must wait for this one, or when the step can genuinely fail. Built-in action names (`SET_STORE`, `MERGE_STORE`, `DELETE_STORE_KEY`, `CLEAR_STORE`) are reserved and cannot be claimed here — attempting it reports on `error` and registers nothing.
enrichment.whenToUse: For every action a backend should be able to trigger, one node each. This is also the only way to grant capabilities the dispatcher has no built-in for — navigation, opening a panel, scrolling, showing a toast, refreshing a query — by wiring `trigger` to the nodes that already do those jobs. Be deliberate: whatever is downstream of `trigger` is something a remote server can cause.

ports.channel: Must match the Channel on the Action Dispatcher that should be able to reach this handler.
ports.actionType: The exact type this handler accepts, e.g. `OPEN_SESSION`. Case- and spelling-sensitive; a mismatch shows up as a refusal on the dispatcher, not here.
ports.enabled: Turning this off unregisters the handler, so the action is refused as unknown rather than quietly ignored. Useful for gating an action behind a signed-in state.
ports.autoComplete: Report the action complete as soon as Trigger has been sent. Turn off when a later step must wait for this one, and wire Complete or Fail.
ports.result: Handed back to the dispatcher as its `result` when this action completes.
ports.errorMessage: Handed back to the dispatcher as its `lastError` when Fail is signalled.
ports.complete: Marks the in-flight action done so the next queued action can start. Signalling it with nothing in flight reports on `error`.
ports.fail: Marks the in-flight action failed. The dispatcher fires `failed` and moves on — and this node reports `done`, because reporting the failure is what it was asked to do.
ports.done: Fires when Complete or Fail acted on the action in flight. `failure` means the opposite: there was nothing in flight to act on.
ports.trigger: Fires when a matching action is dispatched. The payload is already set when it fires.
ports.payload: The action's `payload`, else its `data`, else the whole action object — so `{type, sessionId}` gives you an object with `sessionId` on it.
ports.actionId: The dispatched action's id, for correlating an acknowledgement back to the server.
ports.registered: Whether this handler is currently in the registry. False means the action cannot run at all.
ports.triggeredCount: How many times this handler has run.
ports.error: Why registration failed, or that Complete/Fail was signalled with nothing in flight.

patterns: `trigger` → Navigate, `payload` → Set Variable: the server can open a screen. A real capability, granted visibly by this one wire.

`autoComplete` off, `trigger` → a cloud function call, its Success → `complete` and Failure → `fail`: the dispatcher then holds the rest of the flow until the call returns, and reports the failure if it does not.
`enabled` driven from a signed-in flag, so an action becomes reachable only once the user is authenticated.
Two handlers with the same `actionType` both run, in registration order — useful for a shared side effect such as logging every occurrence of one action.
antiPatterns: One handler with a generic type such as `RUN`, switching on a field of the payload. That rebuilds the open vocabulary the dispatcher closed; the refusal path then never fires for anything.
Leaving `autoComplete` on for a step a later step depends on — the flow moves to the next action while this one is still working.
Turning `autoComplete` off and forgetting to wire `complete`: the action sits until the dispatcher's `handlerTimeout` and fails.
Wiring `trigger` to something destructive without any confirmation in between.

inputs.name: array
inputs.description: The Array to watch. Items arriving and leaving are reported as they happen, and edits to the Objects inside it are reported as Item Changed; sending a different Array reports Array Replaced

outputs.name: arrayReplaced
outputs.description: Fires when a different Array arrives on the input, including the first one and including an explicit clear; Index, Item and Key are empty and Count is the new length

outputs.name: count
outputs.description: How many items the watched Array holds now. Kept accurate through reordering and length changes, which send no signal because they add and remove nothing

outputs.name: index
outputs.description: The position the last signal was about; empty after Array Replaced, which is about no single item

outputs.name: item
outputs.description: The item the last signal was about; empty after Array Replaced

outputs.name: itemAdded
outputs.description: Fires when an item is added to the watched Array; Index and Item describe it

outputs.name: itemChanged
outputs.description: Fires when one of the Objects inside the watched Array is edited in place; Key names the property that changed. Items that are not Noodl Objects cannot be watched

outputs.name: itemRemoved
outputs.description: Fires when an item is removed from the watched Array; Index is the position it occupied

outputs.name: key
outputs.description: The property of Item that changed, after Item Changed; empty after the other signals, which are about the item as a whole

enrichment.summary: Reports what changed inside an Array: items arriving and leaving with their index, and edits to the Objects within it.
enrichment.description: Array Changed watches one Array and reports its changes as they happen. `itemAdded` (Item Added) and `itemRemoved` (Item Removed) fire per item with `index` (Index) and `item` (Item); `itemChanged` (Item Changed) fires when one of the Objects *inside* the Array is edited in place, with `key` (Key) naming the property that changed; `arrayReplaced` (Array Replaced) fires when a different Array arrives, including the first one. `count` (Count) always holds the current length. Every value port is written before its signal is sent. A wholesale replacement of an Array's contents is reported item by item, not as one opaque event, because the runtime emits the individual arrivals and departures. A pure reorder — sort, reverse, or writing `length` — sends no signal, because nothing was added or removed; Count is still kept accurate through it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it when a graph must react to *what* moved in an Array rather than that it changed — animating a row as it arrives, saving a record the moment a field inside it is edited, or keeping a running total. Value Changed is the right node when only the fact of a change matters: it compares identity, so an Array mutated in place is not a change there. Use Object Changed when the input is a single Object.

ports.array: Accepts an Array or a Noodl Array. An empty (`undefined`) input abstains and leaves the current Array watched; `null` clears it, which reports Array Replaced and releases every subscription.
ports.index: Empty after Array Replaced, which is about no single item.
ports.key: Set only by Item Changed; the other signals are about the item as a whole and leave it empty.
ports.count: Kept accurate through reordering and length changes even though those send no signal.

patterns: `itemAdded` → a Function's `do` with `item` wired in: run per-item work as rows arrive, without re-walking the whole Array.
`itemChanged` with `item` and `key` → Set Record Properties: persist exactly the field an author edited.
`count` → a Text node: a live item count that survives reordering.
antiPatterns: Expecting Item Changed for members that are not Noodl Objects. A plain object in the Array broadcasts nothing, so only its arrival and departure can be reported.
Expecting a signal from sorting or reversing. Nothing was added or removed, so only Count is refreshed — watch the Array's own order downstream instead.
Mutating a raw array with `push` and expecting a report. Use the Array node's own actions, or `items`, so the mutation goes through the reactive path.

inputs.name: fetch

inputs.name: properties

inputs.name: runOnChange-object
inputs.description: Whether a new value on Object properties re-runs this node. On by default; untick to make this input passive so only the control signal runs it

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires when any property is written, unless Object properties is unticked under Run On Value Change

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation. This node has no other outcome — no Unchanged and no Failure — so it always fires together with Done, and wiring either one does the same thing. It is here on every action so that reaching for it is never a per-node decision

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once Fetch has republished every property, after Fetched

outputs.name: fetched
outputs.description: Fires once Fetch has republished every property

dynamicPorts.description: Property ports are created from the "properties" parameter (the schema of the component object).

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Component Object: per-component-instance shared state — every node in the same instance reads and writes the same object, no wires needed.
enrichment.description: Component Object exposes an object that belongs to the component *instance* it sits in: each instance of the component gets its own backing object, created on first use, and all Component Object nodes inside that instance — plus Parent Component Object nodes in child components — see the same data. Property names are declared in the `properties` parameter; each becomes a connection-only port that is both readable and writable, together with a per-property changed signal. Outputs are push-style: whenever the object changes (from this node, another Component Object node, a Set Component Object Properties node, or a child's Parent Component Object), the value outputs update and the changed signals fire. `fetch` is additive — it republishes every property now, then fires `fetched` and `done` — and untick Object properties under Run On Value Change to stop the push half.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for state shared across nodes within one component — form drafts, wizard step, selection — especially state a child component must also see via Parent Component Object. It is per-instance by design: two instances of the component never share data. For app-global state use a Variable (Variable2) or Object (Model2); for a fixed set of visual modes prefer States.

ports.fetch: Signal input; republishes every property output now, firing the per-property changed signals, `fetched` and then `done`. Additive: it does not stop the node pushing on change — untick Object properties under Run On Value Change for that.
ports.changed: Signal; fires whenever any property of the instance's object changes (push mode).
ports.fetched: Signal; fires whenever every property is republished, whether by `fetch` or by the node re-binding.
ports.properties: Edit-only stringlist declaring the object's property names; each becomes a `value-<name>` port and a `changed-<name>` signal.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior:
Ports are runtime-discovered from the `properties` parameter: each declared name p produces `value-

` — a connection-only, any-type port usable both as input (writing stores the value into the instance's object) and as output (reading the current value) — and a `changed-

` signal output that fires when that property changes. The ports do not exist until `properties` is set; an authoring tool must write the `properties` stringlist and may then connect `value-

`/`changed-

` by those exact names.
patterns: Component Object in the parent + Parent Component Object in children: parent↔child shared state without threading Component Inputs/Outputs through every level.
Inside a Repeater item component: per-row UI state (expanded, editing) — each item instance automatically gets its own object.
antiPatterns: Using it as global app state — every instance has a separate object, so two sibling components' Component Objects never see each other. Use Variables or Objects instead.
Writing a property and expecting the paired output on the same node to be a different value — input and output are two faces of the same stored property.

inputs.name: amount
inputs.description: How much to add. Negative subtracts. Months and years use whole steps

inputs.name: input
inputs.description: The instant to shift. A string or a millisecond timestamp arriving here is read as a date

inputs.name: unit
inputs.description: What Amount counts. Months and years are calendar steps and CLAMP: 31 January plus one month is 28 (or 29) February, never 2 March

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires after Result has been recomputed, whichever input caused it

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when Date could not be read, leaving Result unset

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Date shifted by Amount of Unit, or unset when Date could not be read

enrichment.summary: A date shifted by an amount of a unit. Months and years CLAMP: 31 January plus one month is 28 February.
enrichment.description: Date Add takes a date and produces the date that many units later, recomputing whenever Date, Amount or Unit changes. A negative amount subtracts. Milliseconds through weeks are fixed durations and are exact. Months and years are calendar steps and CLAMP to the end of the target month: 31 January plus one month is 28 February (29 in a leap year), never 2 or 3 March, and 29 February plus one year is 28 February. Both answers are defensible; the classic date bug is not knowing which one you have, so this one is written down. Date accepts a Date, an ISO string or a millisecond timestamp, because a JSON round trip through a Request or Response node turns a date into one of the latter two.
enrichment.whenToUse: Deadlines, trial expiry, renewal dates, 'thirty days from now', 'the same day next month'.

ports.input: The instant to shift. A string or a millisecond timestamp here is read as a date.
ports.amount: How much to add; negative subtracts. Whole steps for months and years.
ports.unit: Milliseconds, Seconds, Minutes, Hours, Days (default), Weeks, Months or Years.
ports.result: The shifted date, or unset when Date could not be read.
ports.changed: Fires after Result has been recomputed, whichever input caused it.
ports.failure: Invalid Date — fires when a date arrived that could not be read. It does not fire while Date is simply unset.

patterns: Now Date → Date Add (+14 days) → Create Record: a trial end date computed on the server.
antiPatterns: Using Days where Months was meant, to avoid thinking about clamping. 30 days and 1 month are different dates in eleven months of the year.

inputs.name: a
inputs.description: The instant being asked about

inputs.name: b
inputs.description: The instant it is compared against

inputs.name: granularity
inputs.description: How coarsely to compare. Day answers "is this the same day", which is almost always the question — two instants are hardly ever the same millisecond

outputs.name: after
outputs.description: True when Date is later than Compare To, at this Granularity

outputs.name: before
outputs.description: True when Date is earlier than Compare To, at this Granularity

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when a date arrived that could not be read, leaving all three answers unset

outputs.name: isAfter
outputs.description: Fires after a comparison that came out After

outputs.name: isBefore
outputs.description: Fires after a comparison that came out Before

outputs.name: isSame
outputs.description: Fires after a comparison that came out Same

outputs.name: same
outputs.description: True when the two land in the same Granularity bucket — the same day, month or year

enrichment.summary: Is this date before, after or the same as that one — at a granularity you choose, including 'the same day'.
enrichment.description: Date Compare answers all three questions at once, as booleans and as signals, and fires exactly one signal per comparison. Granularity is the point: two instants are almost never the same millisecond, so comparing raw dates answers 'no' to the question people are actually asking. Set Granularity to Day and 09:00 and 17:00 on the same date are Same. Truncation happens in the host's local zone, because 'the same day' is a question about a calendar somebody is looking at — on a server that calendar is whatever the container says, which is worth knowing before you rely on it.
enrichment.whenToUse: 'Is this overdue', 'is this today', 'did these two things happen in the same month'. Wire the booleans into a Condition or the signals into a flow.

ports.b: The instant it is compared against.
ports.granularity: Millisecond (default, exact), Second, Minute, Hour, Day, Month or Year.
ports.before: True when Date is earlier than Compare To, at this granularity.
ports.same: True when the two land in the same granularity bucket.
ports.isBefore: Fires after a comparison that came out Before.
ports.isAfter: Fires after a comparison that came out After.
ports.isSame: Fires after a comparison that came out Same.
ports.failure: Invalid Date — fires when a date arrived that could not be read.

patterns: Due date → Date, Now Date → Compare To, then On Before → the overdue branch.
antiPatterns: Leaving Granularity at Millisecond and expecting Is Same to mean 'the same day'. It will essentially never be true.

inputs.name: absolute
inputs.description: Drop the sign, so the output is a distance rather than a direction

inputs.name: from
inputs.description: The earlier instant, in the reading that makes Difference positive

inputs.name: to
inputs.description: The later instant. Difference is negative when this is actually earlier than From

inputs.name: unit
inputs.description: What Difference counts. Fixed units are exact and fractional (36 hours is 1.5 days); months and years are whole calendar steps

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires after Difference has been recomputed

outputs.name: difference
outputs.description: To minus From, counted in Unit. Unset while either date is missing or unreadable

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when a date arrived that could not be read, leaving Difference unset

enrichment.summary: How far apart two dates are, in a unit you choose. Signed, and unrounded for fixed units.
enrichment.description: Date Difference answers To minus From, counted in the chosen unit. It is signed — positive when To is later — so 'days until' and 'days since' are the same node read two ways, and Absolute drops the sign when only the distance matters. Fixed units divide exactly and are NOT rounded: 36 hours is 1.5 days. Months and years are counted in whole calendar steps, because a fractional month is not a quantity anyone can check; the answer is how many whole steps Date Add could take without overshooting, so 31 January to 28 February is 1 month and 31 January to 27 February is 0.
enrichment.whenToUse: Age, elapsed time, 'days remaining', SLA windows, deciding whether something is stale.

ports.from: The earlier instant, in the reading that makes Difference positive.
ports.to: The later instant. Difference is negative when this is actually earlier.
ports.unit: What Difference counts. Days by default.
ports.absolute: Drop the sign, so the output is a distance rather than a direction.
ports.difference: To minus From, in Unit. Unset while either date is missing or unreadable.
ports.changed: Fires after Difference has been recomputed.
ports.failure: Invalid Date — fires when a date arrived that could not be read.

patterns: Record date → From, Now Date → To, unit Days: how old this record is.
antiPatterns: Assuming the result is a whole number. Fixed units are deliberately fractional; round it downstream if you need to.
