inputs.description: The instant to take apart. A string or a millisecond timestamp here is read as a date

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires after a new Date has been taken apart and every part output is up to date

outputs.name: date
outputs.description: Day of the month, 1-31

outputs.name: dayName
outputs.description: The English name of the weekday. For a localised name, format through Date To String

outputs.name: dayOfWeek
outputs.description: Day of the week as 0-6, Sunday first — JavaScript s own numbering

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when a date arrived that could not be read, leaving every part unset

outputs.name: hours
outputs.description: Hour of the day, 0-23

outputs.name: isoWeek
outputs.description: ISO-8601 week number, 1-53: weeks start on Monday and week 1 holds the first Thursday

outputs.name: milliseconds
outputs.description: Milliseconds past the second, 0-999

outputs.name: minutes
outputs.description: Minutes past the hour, 0-59

outputs.name: month
outputs.description: Month as 1-12 — January is 1, not 0

outputs.name: seconds
outputs.description: Seconds past the minute, 0-59

outputs.name: timestamp
outputs.description: The instant as milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC

outputs.name: year
outputs.description: Four-digit year, in the host s local zone

enrichment.summary: The fields of a date — year, month, day, time, weekday and ISO week — as outputs off one node.
enrichment.description: Date Parts takes a date apart into eleven outputs. Month is 1-12, not JavaScript's 0-11: nobody reading a port called Month expects January to be 0. Day of Week keeps JavaScript's numbering (0 is Sunday) and Day Name gives the English name beside it. ISO Week is ISO-8601 — weeks start Monday and week 1 is the one holding the first Thursday, so 1 January 2027 is week 53 of 2026. All fields are read in the host's local zone, which on a server is whatever the container's TZ says; when the zone matters, format through Date To String's Timezone input instead of reading parts here.
enrichment.whenToUse: Grouping by month or year, branching on the weekday, building a custom label from pieces, or feeding a chart axis. One node rather than seven, so every field comes from the same instant.

ports.input: The instant to take apart. A string or a millisecond timestamp here is read as a date.
ports.dayName: English weekday name. For a localised one, use Date To String.
ports.timestamp: The instant as milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC.
ports.changed: Fires after a new Date has been taken apart.
ports.failure: Invalid Date — fires when a date arrived that could not be read, leaving every part unset.

patterns: Date Parts Month → String Mapper: a month name in your own wording, without a formatter.
antiPatterns: Reading parts here to render a date for a user in another timezone. Use Date To String with a Timezone; these fields are always local.

inputs.name: initialState
inputs.description: Keys to fill in on stores that do not already have them, as an object or as JSON text; live values are never overwritten

inputs.name: persist
inputs.description: Keeps the store in browser storage so it survives a reload; under SSR and cloud functions there is no storage and Error says so

inputs.name: storageKey
inputs.description: Name to store the persisted copy under, defaulting to Store Name; ignored unless Persist is on

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store this node reads; several nodes may share a name and every one of them sees the same state

outputs.name: changedKeys
outputs.description: Comma-separated keys that changed in the notification that fired State Changed

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: What the store could not do, prefixed by the phase it happened in: persist, load, clone or subscriber

outputs.name: ready
outputs.description: Fires once the store has been created and configured, so a graph can sequence its first read

outputs.name: state
outputs.description: The whole store as a live object; write through Set Global Store rather than mutating it

outputs.name: stateChanged
outputs.description: Fires once per commit to the store, however many keys that commit touched

outputs.name: storeId
outputs.description: The id of the Model backing this store, so a Function node can reach the same state through Noodl.Object

enrichment.summary: Declares a named observable store and outputs its state, so any component can read shared state without prop drilling.
enrichment.description: Creates (or attaches to) a named store and keeps `state` in step with it. A store is backed by the runtime's own Model, keyed `--ndl--global-store--<name>`, which is the same mechanism Variables already use — so a store is visible to Function nodes and `Noodl.Object`, and a write made directly to the backing Model notifies store subscribers exactly as Set Global Store does. Any number of Global Store nodes may name the same store; they all observe one shared object rather than each holding a copy. Notifications fire once per commit, not once per key: writes inside a batch collapse into a single `stateChanged`, and `changedKeys` lists only keys whose value actually differs — setting a key to the value it already held reports nothing. Re-entrant writes made from a subscriber are queued and applied rather than recursed, so a subscriber that writes cannot deepen the stack. Deleting the node releases its subscription.
enrichment.whenToUse: State more than one component needs: the signed-in user, a theme, a cart, an agent conversation, the open panel. Reach for it instead of threading Component Inputs down a tree or wiring a Send Event to every interested component. For state that belongs to one component, Variables and Component Object are simpler and stay local. For a value that must survive a reload, turn on Persist rather than writing your own storage step.

ports.storeName: Names the store. Two nodes with the same name share one object; change the name and the node moves to a different store rather than renaming the old one.
ports.initialState: Fills in keys the store does not yet have. It never overwrites live state, so a component that remounts cannot reset a store other components are using.
ports.persist: Saves the store and restores it on the next load. Persistence goes through an injected storage seam, and an unavailable or full store is reported on Error rather than silently skipped.
ports.storageKey: Where a persisted store is written. Defaults to a key derived from Store Name; set it explicitly when two projects share an origin.
ports.state: The whole store object. Updates once per commit.
ports.changedKeys: The keys that actually changed in the commit that just fired — the cheap way to react to one key without comparing whole objects.
ports.stateChanged: Fires once per commit, after State has updated.
ports.ready: True once the store exists and any persisted state has been read back, so a graph can wait rather than reading an empty store on the first frame.
ports.error: Carries persistence and subscriber failures. A subscriber that throws is isolated and reported here rather than taking down the other subscribers.
ports.storeId: The id of the backing Model, for wiring the store into nodes that take a Model reference.

patterns: One Global Store node per component that needs to read shared state; there is no 'owner' node to place first, because naming the store creates it.
`changedKeys` → a condition, rather than watching `state` and diffing by hand, when only one key matters.
Set Global Store with Batch With Others turned on for several related writes, so the UI updates once rather than flickering through intermediate states.
Wait on `ready` before reading a persisted store, instead of reading on the first frame and getting a store that has not loaded yet.
antiPatterns: Using a store for state only one component reads — Variables and Component Object are simpler and do not outlive the component.
Setting Initial State from several components expecting the last one to win: it fills gaps only and never overwrites, by design.
Treating `state` as a snapshot to hold on to. It is the live object; use the State History node if you need to keep earlier values.

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: Key to write; a Set with no key is refused rather than dropped

inputs.name: merge
inputs.description: Shallow-merges into the existing value when both the old and the new value are plain objects, instead of replacing it

inputs.name: set
inputs.description: Writes Value at Key, reading both as of the end of the current frame

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store to write; must match the Store Name of the Global Store node that owns it

inputs.name: transaction
inputs.description: Holds the notification until the end of the current microtask so several writers in one turn produce a single change

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: Value to write, of any type; null is stored as null and is not coerced to a blank string

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the write has been applied and every subscriber has been told

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last write failed; blank once a write succeeds

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the write could not be made, most often because Key is empty

enrichment.summary: Writes a key into a named global store, optionally merging an object and optionally batching with other writes in the same frame.
enrichment.description: Sets one key in the store named by Store Name. The write is deferred until every input on the node has landed, because Key, Value and the Set signal can arrive in one frame in no guaranteed order — so wiring Value and pulsing Set together behaves the way it reads. Setting a key to the value it already holds is not a change and notifies nobody. Writing `undefined` to a key that does not exist still registers as setting it, so absence and 'set to nothing' stay distinguishable to anything watching. Batch With Others coalesces this write with the other batched writes of the same frame into a single commit — subscribers see one notification with all the changed keys, instead of one per write.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any write to shared state: recording a sign-in, appending a streamed message, flipping a panel open. Use one Set per key; for several keys that belong together, turn on Batch With Others so the UI moves once. Use Merge Object to update part of an object without reading it first.

ports.storeName: Which store to write to. Writing to a name no Global Store node declares still creates the store — the store exists because it is named, not because a node owns it.
ports.key: The key to write. Required; an empty key reports on Error rather than writing something unnamed.
ports.value: The value to write. Any type, including objects, arrays, Models and Collections.
ports.merge: Merges Value into the existing object at Key instead of replacing it. With no existing object it behaves as a plain set.
ports.transaction: Batches this write with the other batched writes of the same frame into one commit, so subscribers get a single notification. It does not skip or suppress the notification — the change is always delivered.
ports.done: Fires after the write has been committed, so a chained action runs against the new state rather than the old.
ports.completed: Fires after `done` or `failure`, on every invocation. Wire it to carry on regardless; `failure` still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error.
ports.error: Carries a refused write — a missing key, or a store that could not be persisted — instead of failing quietly.

patterns: Several Set Global Store nodes with Batch With Others turned on, pulsed in the same frame, so a multi-field update renders as one change.
Merge Object to update one field of a settings object without reading, spreading and writing it back.
`done` → the next action, rather than assuming the write has landed by the time the next node runs. Use `completed` instead when the chain should continue even if the write was refused.
antiPatterns: Expecting Batch With Others to hide a change. It groups notifications; it never drops the write.
Setting the same key from several nodes each frame and relying on order — batched writes commit together, and last-write-wins within the batch.
Writing a whole rebuilt object every keystroke where Merge Object would change one field.

inputs.name: keys
inputs.description: Comma-separated keys to watch; leave blank to react to every change in the store

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store to watch; must match the Store Name of the Global Store node that owns it

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires when one of the watched keys changed, and not for a commit that touched only other keys

outputs.name: changedKeys
outputs.description: Comma-separated keys that changed in the notification that fired Changed

outputs.name: previousValue
outputs.description: The same projection as Value, as it was immediately before the change that fired Changed

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: The watched value: one key gives that key, several give an object of just those keys, none gives the whole store

enrichment.summary: Watches specific keys in a named global store and signals when they change, with the previous value alongside the new one.
enrichment.description: Subscribes to a store and fires only for the keys named in Keys, so a component that cares about one field is not woken by every unrelated write. Leaving Keys empty watches the whole store. Both Value and Previous Value update before `changed` fires, so a handler can compare them. Notifications arrive once per commit in subscriber registration order; a write that sets a key to the value it already held is not a change and fires nothing. Changing Store Name or Keys moves the subscription rather than adding a second one, and deleting the node removes it — a disposed node leaves no subscriber behind, which matters because a store outlives the components that read it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Reacting to shared state changing, rather than rendering it. To display a value, wire Global Store's `state` straight into the UI; use Subscribe when something must *happen* on a change — refetch, animate, navigate, log. Prefer naming Keys over watching everything, so unrelated writes do not trigger work.

ports.storeName: Which store to watch. The store need not exist yet; the subscription attaches when it appears.
ports.keys: Comma-separated keys to watch. Empty watches every key in the store.
ports.value: The current value of the changed key, or the whole store object when Keys is empty.
ports.previousValue: What that key held immediately before this change — the two are updated together so they can be compared in a handler.
ports.changedKeys: Which of the watched keys changed in this commit. A batched write can change several at once, and they arrive in one notification.
ports.changed: Fires once per commit that touched a watched key, after Value and Previous Value have updated.

patterns: Name the keys you care about instead of leaving Keys empty, so a busy store does not wake every component on every write.
Compare `previousValue` with `value` to react to a specific transition — signed-out to signed-in — rather than to any change at all.
Global Store `state` for rendering; Subscribe `changed` for side effects. Using Subscribe to drive display work is usually a sign the state should simply be wired in.
antiPatterns: Watching the whole store to react to one key: every unrelated write then does that component's work again.
Expecting one notification per key when several were written in a batch — a batch is one commit, and `changedKeys` names all of them.
Holding `previousValue` as a history. It is only the value immediately before this change; the State History node keeps a real history.

inputs.name: cancel
inputs.description: Abandons a request that is still in flight, which answers on Canceled rather than Failure; reports Unchanged when there is nothing to cancel

inputs.name: fetch
inputs.description: Sends the request using the values currently on the inputs

inputs.name: url
inputs.description: Address the request is sent to; any {name} in it becomes a Path Parameter input, and leaving it blank fails the request rather than sending one

outputs.name: canceled
outputs.description: Fires only when Cancel abandoned a request in flight; a timeout answers on Failure instead

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the server has answered with a 2xx status and Response is up to date

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: What went wrong with the last request, in one sentence; unchanged when a request succeeds

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the request could not be completed — no URL, a network error, a timeout, an unparseable body, or a non-2xx status — after the reason has been put on Error

outputs.name: response
outputs.description: Body the server sent, parsed as JSON when it said so and as text otherwise; it keeps the previous body when a request never reached the server

outputs.name: responseHeaders
outputs.description: Every header the server returned, keyed by lower-cased header name

outputs.name: statusCode
outputs.description: HTTP status the server answered with; it keeps the previous status when a request timed out or never reached the server

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when nothing was fetched and nothing changed: a Cancel that abandoned a request in flight, or a Cancel with no request to abandon. Canceled tells those two apart

dynamicPorts.description: Input and output ports derive from node parameters: configured headers and query parameters become inputs; response mappings become outputs.

parameterEncoding.reason: Ports are parsed from the configured headers, query parameters and response mappings in the node parameters.

enrichment.summary: HTTP Request: fetches a URL on demand, delivering the parsed response, status code and an outcome signal.
enrichment.description: The straightforward HTTP client: set `url` (plus method/headers/body via its configuration), fire `fetch`, and read `response` (parsed body, untyped), `responseHeaders`, and `statusCode`. `done`/`failure` split the outcome, with `error` describing failures, and `completed` fires after either so a chain can carry on regardless. `cancel` aborts an in-flight request: the abandoned request reports `unchanged` beside `canceled`, because nothing arrived and nothing changed, and the `cancel` itself reports `done` when it had something to abandon and `unchanged` when it did not.
enrichment.whenToUse: One-off or simple API calls where the response can be consumed directly or handed to a Function/Script for shaping. Prefer the REST node when an endpoint is reused enough to deserve declared ports; prefer a cloud function when credentials must stay off the client.

ports.response: Untyped output with the parsed body — being '*', it connects anywhere; downstream correctness is on the author.
ports.statusCode: Number level with the HTTP status of the last response.
ports.failure: Signal; wire error display/retry here, with `error` carrying the message.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Header and body inputs are runtime-registered from the node's method/headers configuration; only the core trigger/result surface is static. Dynamic outputs minted from Response Mapping are all prefixed `out-`, so an author's mapping name can never collide with the node's own ports. NDA-012: exceeding `timeout` fires `failure` with a message naming the timeout — `canceled` fires only for an explicit `cancel`. ERG-001: failures now also reach the runtime error channel, so `On App Error` sees them in a deployed build — codes are `http/no-url`, `http/error-status`, `http/timeout` and `http/network-error`. Requests genuinely overlap: a second `fetch` while one is in flight starts a second request, and each invocation carries its own outcome. `statusCode` and `response` keep the *previous* request's answer when a request never reached the server, because a value output cannot be cleared. Deleting the node does not abandon a request already in flight.
patterns: `failure` → Condition `eval` with `result` → error text `visible`: errors as levels, not pulses.

inputs.name: algorithm
inputs.description: Which SHA-2 digest to compute. MD5 and SHA-1 are not offered — WebCrypto has neither

inputs.name: encoding
inputs.description: How the digest bytes are rendered as text

inputs.name: hash
inputs.description: Computes the digest of Value

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: The text to hash, as UTF-8 bytes

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: digest
outputs.description: The hash of Value, rendered in Encoding. Available once Done has fired

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the digest has been computed and is available on Digest

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the digest could not be computed

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the digest could not be computed, most often because WebCrypto is not available here

enrichment.summary: SHA-256/384/512 digest of a string, rendered as hex, base64 or base64url. Works in the browser and in a cloud function.
enrichment.description: Hash takes the text on Value, hashes it with the chosen SHA-2 algorithm and puts the digest on Digest. It runs on WebCrypto, which both runtimes already have — there is no dependency behind it. The digest is computed asynchronously, so Done fires from a later turn than the Do that started it: wire Done, never assume Digest is fresh in the same frame. MD5 and SHA-1 are deliberately not offered; WebCrypto implements neither for digesting, and hand-rolling one would be shipping a broken hash. If you need a keyed digest, that is the HMAC node, which is cloud-only because it takes a secret.
enrichment.whenToUse: Content addressing, a cache key, an integrity check, or comparing a value against a digest somebody else published. Not for storing passwords — a plain SHA-2 is the wrong tool for that, whichever runtime you are in.

ports.value: The text to hash, encoded as UTF-8 bytes.
ports.encoding: hex (default), base64 or base64url — how the digest bytes are rendered as text.
ports.hash: Signal (Do); computes the digest. Nothing happens until this fires.
ports.digest: The digest, valid once Done has fired.
ports.done: Fires when Digest holds the finished digest.
ports.failure: Fires when WebCrypto is unavailable — in a browser that means the page is not in a secure context.
ports.error: Why the digest could not be computed.

patterns: Do → Done → the node that consumes Digest. The digest is asynchronous, so a wire off Done is the only way to sequence it correctly.
antiPatterns: Reading Digest immediately after pulsing Do, in the same frame. It is still the previous value.
Hashing a password with this node. Use your backend's password flow; a bare SHA-2 is not a password hash.

inputs.name: chunk
inputs.description: The next fragment of the stream; boundaries may fall anywhere, including inside a string

inputs.name: clear
inputs.description: Discards the pending text, the parsed values and the error counter

inputs.name: format
inputs.description: How values are framed on this stream: one per line, any concatenation of complete values, or one whole document

inputs.name: maxLength
inputs.description: Cap on unparsed text held while a value completes; exceeding it clears the buffer and reports an error rather than growing forever

inputs.name: parse
inputs.description: Appends the current Chunk and emits every value that is now complete; the chunk is retained between pulses

outputs.name: cleared
outputs.description: Fires once the pending text and the values have been discarded

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when a Parse consumed text or a Clear discarded something; Success is narrower and fires only when values came out

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last value or line would not parse; kept until the next failure or a Clear

outputs.name: errorCount
outputs.description: How many values have failed to parse since the last Clear

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires once when a Parse could not read part of its input, or when the pending text exceeded Max Pending; Error Count says how many

outputs.name: isComplete
outputs.description: True when the last Parse left nothing pending, so every value so far was whole

outputs.name: parsed
outputs.description: The last complete value the most recent Parse produced

outputs.name: pendingCharacters
outputs.description: Text held back because a value is not complete yet; persistently non-zero means Format does not match the stream

outputs.name: success
outputs.description: Fires when a Parse yielded at least one value, so a chunk that merely advanced an incomplete value stays quiet

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when there was nothing pending to parse, or nothing to clear — a valid action with nothing to do

outputs.name: valueCount
outputs.description: How many values have been parsed since the last Clear, across every Parse

outputs.name: values
outputs.description: Every value completed by the most recent Parse, in order

enrichment.summary: JSON Stream Parser: turns stream fragments into JSON values as NDJSON, concatenated values, or one whole document.
enrichment.description: Each `parse` appends the current `chunk` to a buffer and extracts whatever is now complete. 'NDJSON' takes one value per line and reports a line that does not parse rather than skipping it silently. 'Stream' accepts any concatenation of complete top-level values — whitespace-separated objects, or a JSON array whose elements are emitted as they close — and is safe at every chunk boundary, including one that falls inside a string. 'Single document' holds everything back until the whole buffer is one complete value, then emits it. Text that is not yet a complete value stays in the buffer and shows on `pendingCharacters`; `maxLength` stops a malformed stream from growing without bound by clearing the buffer and reporting it. `values` carries everything the last parse completed, `parsed` the last of them.
enrichment.whenToUse: A stream whose payloads are JSON but do not arrive one-per-event: NDJSON logs, a chunked HTTP body, an array streamed element by element. Not needed for Server-Sent Events with one JSON object per event — that node already parses each payload onto its Data output.

ports.chunk: The fragment to append. Empty chunks are ignored, so a Parse with nothing new re-tries the existing buffer.
ports.format: 'NDJSON' for line-delimited, 'Stream' for concatenated values and streamed arrays, 'Single document' to wait for one whole value.
ports.maxLength: Cap on unparsed text. Exceeding it clears the buffer and reports an error, which almost always means the wrong Format.
ports.parsed: The last value completed by the most recent Parse.
ports.values: Every value completed by the most recent Parse, in order. Wire this to For Each when a chunk can complete several.
ports.valueCount: Running total across all parses, not the size of the last batch.
ports.pendingCharacters: Text held back because a value is incomplete. Persistently non-zero means the Format does not match the stream.
ports.isComplete: True when the last Parse left nothing buffered.
ports.success: Fires only when the Parse produced at least one value, so an advancing-but-incomplete chunk stays quiet.
ports.failure: Fires once per Parse that could not read part of its input — not once per bad record; `errorCount` says how many. The stream keeps going rather than stalling.
ports.unchanged: Fires when a Parse had nothing pending, or a Clear had nothing to discard — a valid action with nothing to do.
ports.done: Fires when a Parse consumed text or a Clear discarded something. Wider than `success`, which needs a value to have come out.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `data` → `chunk`, `onMessage` → `parse`, format NDJSON: a log stream that arrives several lines per event.
`values` → For Each `items` renders everything a chunk completed, instead of only the last value.
`pendingCharacters` on a debug Text output makes a format mismatch obvious instead of looking like a dead stream.
antiPatterns: Using 'Single document' on a never-ending stream — the buffer grows until Max Pending trips.
Reading only `parsed` when a chunk can complete several values; the earlier ones are then silently ignored.
Adding this after Server-Sent Events when each event is already one JSON object — the SSE node's Data output has parsed it.

inputs.name: data
inputs.description: An optional object written alongside the message as structured fields. In a cloud function every property whose NAME says it holds a credential is redacted on the way out

inputs.name: level
inputs.description: How loud this line is. In a cloud function the backend drops anything below its configured level, so Debug lines cost nothing in production unless someone turns them on

inputs.name: log
inputs.description: Writes the line. Nothing is written until this fires

inputs.name: message
inputs.description: The line to write. Free text, so keep credentials out of it by habit — the backend does scrub the values of its own stored secrets out of this before it is written, but that cannot cover a credential it never issued

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: Passed straight through to the Value output, so this node can sit inline on a wire

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation. This node has no other outcome — no Unchanged and no Failure — so it always fires together with Done, and wiring either one does the same thing. It is here on every action so that reaching for it is never a per-node decision

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the line has been written

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: Whatever arrived on the Value input, unchanged — this node never alters what passes through it

enrichment.summary: Writes a line to the log — the structured backend log inside a cloud function, the browser console in an app.
enrichment.description: Log writes a message, at a level, when its Log signal fires. Where the line goes is chosen by the runtime, not by you: inside a cloud function it goes to the backend's structured log — one JSON line per event on stdout, carrying the run's request id and the id of this node — and a copy is recorded as a step in the run's execution record, so the History panel shows it beside the rest of the run. In a browser app the same node writes to the console at the matching level. Value passes straight through, so the node can sit inline on a wire without breaking the chain. The important difference from a Function node's console.log is redaction: in a cloud function every property of Data whose name says it holds a credential is replaced before the line is written, and the values of the backend's own stored secrets are scrubbed out of the message text as well — so wiring a Secret node's Value into a Log message writes [REDACTED], not the credential.
enrichment.whenToUse: Tracing what a cloud function actually did with a real request, and leaving a breadcrumb for the next person who has to answer 'what happened at 3am'. Use the Data object for anything you might want to filter on later: the backend's log is JSON, so `jq 'select(.orderId==7)'` works on structured fields and does not work on a sentence.

ports.message: The line to write. Free text.
ports.level: Debug, Info, Warning or Error. A cloud function's backend drops anything below its configured level, so Debug costs nothing in production until someone turns it on.
ports.data: An optional object written alongside the message as structured fields. Credential-named properties are redacted in a cloud function.
ports.value: Passed straight through to the Value output so this node can sit inline on a wire.
ports.log: Signal; writes the line. Nothing is written until this fires.
ports.done: Fires once the line has been written.
ports.completed: Fires after every write. This node has no other outcome.

patterns: Splice it onto an existing wire: value in, value out, and the Log signal taken from whatever outcome you want to record. The graph behaves identically with the node removed.
Log at `error` on a Failure branch, with the failing record's id in Data. That line carries the request id, so it lines up with the access log and the execution record.
antiPatterns: A Log node inside a Run Tasks loop over thousands of items. That is thousands of stdout lines and thousands of execution-record steps; the backend caps the copies it records per run, but the volume is still yours to think about.
Putting a credential in Message on purpose, on the assumption it will be scrubbed. The backend scrubs the values it issued; a token that arrived in a request body is not one of them.

inputs.name: read
inputs.description: Re-reads the clock. The outputs hold the instant of the last Read, not a live value

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation. This node has no other outcome — no Unchanged and no Failure — so it always fires together with Done, and wiring either one does the same thing. It is here on every action so that reaching for it is never a per-node decision

outputs.name: date
outputs.description: The instant of the last Read, for the other date nodes

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the outputs hold the freshly-read instant

outputs.name: iso
outputs.description: The same instant as an ISO-8601 string in UTC — the shape to put in a JSON body

outputs.name: timestamp
outputs.description: The same instant as milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC

enrichment.summary: The current date and time, as a Date, a millisecond timestamp and an ISO string. Re-read on demand.
enrichment.description: Now reads the wall clock when the node is created and again on every Read, and publishes the same instant in three shapes: a Date for the other date nodes, a millisecond timestamp for arithmetic and storage, and an ISO-8601 UTC string for a JSON body. The outputs hold the instant of the last Read — they are not a live clock, so a graph that wants a ticking value pairs this with a Timer. It reads Date.now(), which is the same clock in the browser, on the SSR server and in a cloud function.
enrichment.whenToUse: Stamping when something happened, comparing a stored date against the present, or computing a deadline together with Date Add. In a cloud function it is the server's clock, which is the one you want for anything a client should not be able to lie about.

ports.read: Signal; re-reads the clock and updates all three outputs.
ports.date: The instant of the last Read, for wiring into Date Add, Date Compare, Date Parts or Date To String.
ports.timestamp: The same instant as milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC.
ports.iso: The same instant as an ISO-8601 string in UTC — the shape to put in a JSON body or a record.
ports.done: Fires once the outputs hold the freshly-read instant.
ports.completed: Fires after every Read. This node has no other outcome.

patterns: Request receive → Now Read, then Date → Date Compare: 'is this due date in the past', answered on the server's clock.
Now Date → Date Add (+30 days) → Date To String: a deadline, rendered.
antiPatterns: Expecting the outputs to advance on their own. They hold the last Read; wire a Timer if you want them to tick.

inputs.name: object
inputs.description: The Object to watch. Changes to its keys are reported as they happen; sending a different Object reports Object Replaced. A plain JavaScript object that is not a Noodl Object cannot be watched key-by-key — only its replacement is reported

outputs.name: key
outputs.description: The key the last Key Added or Key Changed was about; empty after Object Replaced, which is about no single key

outputs.name: keyAdded
outputs.description: Fires when a key that did not exist on the watched Object now does

outputs.name: keyChanged
outputs.description: Fires when a key that already existed on the watched Object is given a different value

outputs.name: objectReplaced
outputs.description: Fires when a different Object arrives on the input, including the first one and including an explicit clear; Key is empty and Value / Previous Value carry the Objects themselves

outputs.name: previousValue
outputs.description: The value that key held before — empty when the key has just been added — or, after Object Replaced, the Object that was being watched before

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: The new value of that key — or, after Object Replaced, the Object that just arrived

enrichment.summary: Reports what changed inside an Object: which key was added or edited, its new value and its old one.
enrichment.description: Object Changed watches one Noodl Object and reports its changes as they happen, rather than only noticing that a different Object arrived. `keyAdded` (Key Added) fires when a key that did not exist now does; `keyChanged` (Key Changed) fires when an existing key is given a different value; `objectReplaced` (Object Replaced) fires when a different Object arrives on the input, including the very first one. Each signal is accompanied by `key` (Key), `value` (Value) and `previousValue` (Previous Value), written before the signal is sent so a downstream node reading them on the signal sees the change the signal is about. Writing a key the value it already holds reports nothing — the runtime itself suppresses it. Only Noodl Objects broadcast their edits; a plain JavaScript object is accepted but only its replacement can be reported, and an Array is declined outright because Array Changed is the node for it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it when a graph must react to *what* changed inside an Object rather than merely that it changed — logging an audit trail, saving only the field that was edited, or driving a different branch for a newly added key than for an edited one. Value Changed is the right node when only the fact of a change matters, or when the input is not an Object: it compares identity, so an Object edited in place is not a change there. Reach for Array Changed when the input is an Array.

ports.object: Accepts a Noodl Object. An empty (`undefined`) input abstains and leaves the current Object watched; `null` clears it, which reports Object Replaced and unsubscribes.
ports.key: Empty after Object Replaced, which is about no single key — deliberately cleared rather than left holding the previous key change.
ports.value: After Object Replaced this carries the Object that just arrived, not a key's value.
ports.previousValue: Empty when the key has just been added; after Object Replaced it carries the Object that was being watched before.

patterns: An Object's `keyChanged` → a Function's `do`, with `key` and `value` wired in: react to one edited field without re-reading the whole Object.
`keyAdded` and `keyChanged` into separate branches: treat a first-time value differently from a correction.
antiPatterns: Wiring an Array to Object. The node declines it, because an array's change event carries no key; use Array Changed.
Expecting it to report edits to a plain JavaScript object. Only Noodl Objects broadcast their writes — build the value as an Object node if you need per-key reporting.

inputs.name: apply
inputs.description: Writes Optimistic Value at Key now and opens a transaction the server response will resolve

inputs.name: commit
inputs.description: Confirms the update, so the optimistic value becomes the truth

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Reason reported on Error when this update is rolled back; wire the server error here

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: Key to write optimistically; an Apply with no key is refused rather than dropped

inputs.name: onDispose
inputs.description: What happens to updates still in flight when this node is removed: put the old value back, or keep the value that was shown

inputs.name: optimisticValue
inputs.description: Value to show immediately, before the server has confirmed anything

inputs.name: rollback
inputs.description: Puts the old value back, unless something else has written the key since

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store holding the key this update writes

inputs.name: timeout
inputs.description: Milliseconds to wait for an answer before rolling back on its own; 0 waits forever

inputs.name: transactionId
inputs.description: Names the update to commit or roll back when several are in flight; leave blank to generate one and resolve to the oldest

outputs.name: applied
outputs.description: Fires once the optimistic value is in the store and the transaction is open

outputs.name: committed
outputs.description: Fires once an update has been confirmed and its value is the truth

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the action did its work: an Apply that opened a transaction, a Commit that confirmed one, or a Rollback that put the old value back

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last update failed or was undone; blank once an Apply succeeds

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the node refused to act: no Key, a transaction id already open, or no such update to resolve

outputs.name: isCommitted
outputs.description: True when the last update to resolve was confirmed

outputs.name: isPending
outputs.description: True while at least one update is waiting for an answer

outputs.name: isRolledBack
outputs.description: True when the last update to resolve was undone, whether by Rollback, by the deadline, or by disposal

outputs.name: pendingCount
outputs.description: How many updates are open at once, which can be more than one when responses come back out of order

outputs.name: previousValue
outputs.description: What the key held immediately before the most recent Apply; blank when the key did not exist

outputs.name: rolledBack
outputs.description: Fires once an update has been undone, including when the value was left alone because something newer had written the key

outputs.name: timedOut
outputs.description: Fires alongside Rolled Back when it was the deadline rather than the graph that ended the update

outputs.name: transactionId
outputs.description: Id of the most recent Apply; carry it through the request and hand it back to resolve that update specifically

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when a Rollback resolved its transaction without restoring anything, because something else had already written the key — the value this update wrote was gone already, so there was nothing to undo. Rolled Back fires too, and Error says why

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: What the key holds right now, following writes made by anything, not only by this node

enrichment.summary: Writes a store key immediately, then commits or rolls it back when the server answers — so the UI responds now, not after the round trip.
enrichment.description: Applies `optimisticValue` to `key` the moment Apply fires, and holds the change open until Commit or Rollback resolves it. A rollback restores what was there before, and restores *absence as absence* — a key the update introduced is deleted rather than left holding `undefined`. Several updates can be open at once, each with its own transaction id and its own deadline. Two behaviours are worth knowing before relying on it. First, if a plain write changes the same key while an update is open, rollback **keeps the newer value**: `rolledBack` still fires so the failure branch runs, and `error` explains that the value was left alone, because silently reverting a write the user made after the fact is worse than a stale optimistic value. A newer *optimistic* update is not treated as supersession — the store's own newest-writer rule already resolves that correctly. Second, disposal resolves rather than leaks: a node deleted with updates still open rolls them back by default (or commits them, under On Dispose), clears its timers, and fires nothing into the dead node. All three actions also report an outcome: `done` for an Apply, Commit or Rollback that did its work, `unchanged` for the superseded rollback above — the value this update wrote was already gone, so there was nothing to undo — and `failure` when the node refused to act, with `completed` after any of them. The deadline is the one route that reports no outcome, because nobody invoked it: it announces itself on `rolledBack` and `timedOut` alone.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any action where waiting on the network makes the UI feel slow and the write is very likely to succeed: toggling a like, accepting an invite, checking off a task, reordering a list. Do not use it where a wrong-then-corrected value would mislead — a bank balance, a booking confirmation, a payment state. There, a pending indicator is the honest option.

ports.storeName: The store to write to. Defaults to `app`.
ports.key: The key held open by this update.
ports.optimisticValue: The value shown immediately, before the server has agreed to it.
ports.errorMessage: The message reported on Error if the update rolls back. Set it to the server's reason when you have one.
ports.transactionId: Identifies this update, so several in flight can be committed or rolled back individually. Left empty, one is generated and reported on the output of the same name.
ports.timeout: Milliseconds before the update rolls itself back. Default 30000; 0 disables it. A deadline matters here — without one, a request that never answers leaves the optimistic value on screen forever.
ports.onDispose: What an open update does when the node is deleted: roll back (the default, and the safe reading) or commit.
ports.apply: Applies the optimistic value and opens the update.
ports.commit: Confirms the update. The value stays and the update closes.
ports.rollback: Rejects the update, restoring the previous value unless a newer plain write superseded it.
ports.value: The current value of the key.
ports.previousValue: What the key held before this update, i.e. what a rollback would restore.
ports.isPending: True while at least one update from this node is open.
ports.pendingCount: How many updates from this node are open — the number to show as 'saving'.
ports.timedOut: Fires when an update rolled back because its deadline passed rather than because the server rejected it. Fires after `rolledBack`.
ports.error: Carries the rollback reason, including the explanation when a newer write was kept in preference to reverting it.

patterns: Apply on the click, Commit on the request's success, Rollback on its failure — with `errorMessage` wired from the server's reason so the message the user sees is the real one.
`pendingCount` → a subtle 'saving' indicator, rather than a blocking spinner: the point of the pattern is that the UI already moved.
Leave `transactionId` empty and read the output when several updates can be in flight, instead of inventing ids by hand.
antiPatterns: Using it for state where being briefly wrong misleads — money, confirmations, availability. Optimism is a UX choice about likely-successful writes, not a way to avoid showing pending state.
Setting `timeout` to 0 on a network call: a request that never answers then leaves the optimistic value on screen permanently.
Expecting Rollback to always restore the old value. If the user changed the key in the meantime, their write is kept and `error` says so.

inputs.name: fetch
inputs.description: Republishes every property from the parent now. This is additional to the outputs updating on their own; untick Parent object under Run On Value Change to stop that

inputs.name: properties
inputs.description: Names of the parent values to expose, each becoming a matching input and output

inputs.name: runOnChange-object
inputs.description: Whether a new value on Parent object re-runs this node. On by default; untick to make this input passive so only the control signal runs it

inputs.name: targetComponent
inputs.description: Which ancestor to read from; leave blank for the nearest one that has a Component Object

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires when a property on the resolved parent is written, unless Fetch is connected

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once a Fetch you triggered has republished every property, after Fetched

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Which ancestor was looked for and why it was not found

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when no parent Component Object could be found, so there is nothing to read

outputs.name: fetched
outputs.description: Fires whenever every property is republished, whether by Fetch or by the parent being re-resolved

dynamicPorts.description: Property ports mirror the parent component object's property schema.

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Parent Component Object: reads the enclosing parent component's instance-scoped object from inside a child component.
enrichment.description: Parent Component Object opens the same per-instance store as the parent's Component Object, from within a child. Properties declared on the node become value outputs that update reactively as anything writes the parent's object; `changed` fires per write. This is how reusable child components (controls, toolbars, wizard steps) participate in their host's state without dedicated ports for every value.
enrichment.whenToUse: Child components that are conceptually part of their parent and share its state — wizard controls, list toolbars. For unrelated components use Objects by id or events; for one-off values a Component Input is more explicit.

ports.properties: Declared property names; each becomes a reactive value output.
ports.changed: Signal; the parent's object was written by anyone.
ports.fetch: Signal input; republishes every property from the resolved parent now, firing `fetched` and then `done` — or `failure` when no parent Component Object is bound. Additive: untick Parent object under Run On Value Change to stop the node also republishing on change.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Property ports are generated from the per-instance `properties` list (runtime-discovered). Resolution walks up to the nearest ancestor component instance — the node is inert at the app root.

inputs.name: delimiter
inputs.description: The character between cells. Use ; for a European export, or a tab for TSV

inputs.name: hasHeader
inputs.description: When ticked the first row names the columns and Items is an array of records. Untick it and Items is an array of rows, each an array of cells

inputs.name: text
inputs.description: The CSV text to parse. A leading byte-order mark — which is what Excel writes when it saves UTF-8 — is stripped, so the first column keeps its name

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires once Items and Count hold the freshly parsed CSV

outputs.name: count
outputs.description: How many rows the last successful parse produced, not counting the header row

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the CSV could not be parsed, naming the line it gave up on; empty until a parse fails

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the CSV could not be parsed, leaving Items and Count as they were

outputs.name: items
outputs.description: The parsed rows — records when Has Header is ticked, arrays of cells when it is not. Every cell is a string, including columns that look numeric. Unchanged while the CSV cannot be parsed

enrichment.summary: Turns CSV text that arrived at runtime into an array — records when the first row is a header, rows of cells when it is not.
enrichment.description: Parse CSV reads CSV text into an array. With Has Header ticked (the default) the first row names the properties and Items is an array of records; untick it and Items is an array of rows, each an array of cells. It handles the awkward parts of the format properly: quoted cells, cells containing the delimiter, cells containing newlines, and doubled quotes. Every cell comes out a string — there is no type inference, so a column that looks numeric yields "42" and not 42; use an Expression or Array Map if you need numbers. A leading byte-order mark, which is what Excel writes when it saves UTF-8, is stripped so the first column keeps its name. A quote the parser cannot pair is a Failure with the line number, not a half-read file: without that check the text around the stray quote simply disappears and the array looks plausible. This is the same parser Static Array has always used, so an authored CSV and a received one cannot disagree. In a cloud function, remember the request body limit is 10 MB — a bigger file has to arrive through file storage instead.
enrichment.whenToUse: A CSV arriving from anywhere at runtime: a request body, an upload, an HTTP response, a file read from storage. For a CSV you type in yourself, Static Array is the node — it is this parser with an editor field in front of it.

ports.text: The CSV text to parse. A leading byte-order mark is stripped.
ports.hasHeader: When ticked the first row names the columns and Items is records; when unticked Items is rows of cells.
ports.delimiter: The character between cells. Default ','; use ';' for many European exports or a tab for TSV.
ports.items: The parsed rows. Records when Has Header is ticked, arrays of cells when it is not. Every cell is a string. Left unchanged when a parse fails.
ports.count: How many rows the last successful parse produced, not counting the header row.
ports.changed: Fires once Items and Count hold the freshly parsed CSV.
ports.failure: Fires when the CSV could not be parsed, leaving Items and Count as they were.
ports.error: Why the parse failed, naming the line it gave up on. Empty until a parse fails.

patterns: Request `pm-csv` → Parse CSV `text`; Parse CSV `items` → Array Filter → To CSV → Response: the whole 'someone sent us a spreadsheet' shape, with no Function node.
Wire `failure` somewhere that answers the caller. A function whose only wired path is the happy one hangs forever when the file is malformed (CWF-018).
antiPatterns: Expecting numeric columns to arrive as numbers. Every cell is a string; convert explicitly.
Splitting on commas with a String node instead. That breaks on the first quoted cell containing a comma, which is the first real file you will meet.
Posting a CSV larger than 10 MB to a cloud function. The body limit rejects it with a 413 before the graph runs.

inputs.name: extract
inputs.description: Runs Pattern over Text and reports what it found

inputs.name: extractAll
inputs.description: Collects every match into Matches instead of stopping at the first one

inputs.name: flags
inputs.description: Regex flags i, m, s, u and y; g is controlled by Extract All and a g written here is ignored

inputs.name: pattern
inputs.description: A JavaScript regular expression without the surrounding slashes; capture groups appear on Groups

inputs.name: text
inputs.description: The text to search

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the extract has run, whether it matched or not — Found and Not Found say which

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the pattern could not be used: it is blank, or it is not a valid regular expression

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the pattern itself is unusable, which is a bug to fix rather than a result

outputs.name: firstGroup
outputs.description: The first capture group of the first match, which is the whole answer for a pattern like (\d+)%

outputs.name: found
outputs.description: Fires when the pattern ran and matched at least once

outputs.name: groups
outputs.description: Capture groups of the first match; an optional group that did not participate is a blank string, not a hole

outputs.name: match
outputs.description: The first match, or blank when nothing matched

outputs.name: matchCount
outputs.description: How many matches were found, which is at most one unless Extract All is on

outputs.name: matches
outputs.description: Every match when Extract All is on, otherwise just the first

outputs.name: namedGroups
outputs.description: Named capture groups of the first match, keyed by name

outputs.name: notFound
outputs.description: Fires when the pattern ran and matched nothing, which is an ordinary outcome rather than a mistake

enrichment.summary: Pattern Extractor: pulls matches and capture groups out of text with a regular expression, without needing a Function node.
enrichment.description: Runs `pattern` over `text` on each `extract` and publishes the first match, its capture groups (numbered and named), and — with Extract All on — every match. An optional group that did not participate becomes an empty string rather than a hole in the array, so downstream indexes stay stable. `firstGroup` is a convenience for the overwhelmingly common single-group case. A pattern that will not compile is a result, not an exception: `ok` becomes false, `error` explains, and the `failure` signal fires — distinct from `notFound`, which is a normal outcome. Note that a catastrophically backtracking pattern is still the author's problem; this runs the platform regex engine and cannot bound it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Extracting a value from text that is not structured data: a percentage out of a progress line, a tool name out of an agent status message, a field out of a log record. Prefer JSON Stream Parser when the payload really is JSON, and String Format or Substring for fixed-position work that needs no pattern.

ports.text: The text to search. Non-strings are stringified, since stream payloads are typed `*`.
ports.pattern: A JavaScript regular expression without the surrounding slashes.
ports.flags: i, m, s, u. The global flag is controlled by Extract All and is stripped from here, so `match` cannot become stateful across calls.
ports.extractAll: Collect every match rather than only the first. Groups still describe the first match.
ports.match: The first match, or an empty string when nothing matched.
ports.groups: Numbered capture groups of the first match; unmatched optional groups are empty strings.
ports.firstGroup: Group 1 of the first match — the value you want in the common `(\d+)%` case.
ports.namedGroups: Named capture groups of the first match, as an object.
ports.error: Empty unless the pattern would not compile.
ports.found: Fires when there was a match.
ports.notFound: Fires when the pattern compiled but matched nothing — a normal outcome, not an error.
ports.failure: Fires only when the pattern itself is unusable, so a broken pattern cannot hide as 'no match'.
ports.done: Fires after both Found and Not Found — both mean the extract ran. There is deliberately no Unchanged: a miss is a result, not a post-condition that already held.

patterns: Stream text → `text`, pattern `(\d+)%`, `firstGroup` → Number → a progress bar.
Named groups turn one pattern into several outputs without chaining extractors: `(?<tool>\w+)\s+(?<state>\w+)`.
`failure` → a visible warning during authoring catches a mistyped pattern that would otherwise read as 'never matches'.
antiPatterns: Parsing JSON with a regex instead of using JSON Stream Parser.
Treating `notFound` as an error state — most streams contain lines the pattern is not meant to match.
Building a pattern from user input without bounding it; nested quantifiers can hang the frame.

inputs.name: encoding
inputs.description: How the bytes are rendered as text. Base64 URL is the safe one for a URL or a token

inputs.name: generate
inputs.description: Generates a fresh block of random bytes

inputs.name: length
inputs.description: How many random BYTES to generate (not characters — hex renders each byte as two). 1 to 4096

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once fresh random bytes are available on Value

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why no random bytes were produced

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when there is no cryptographic random source here, or Length is out of range. This node will not quietly substitute Math.random()

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: The random bytes rendered in Encoding, replaced on every New

enrichment.summary: A block of cryptographically random bytes as hex, base64 or base64url. Never falls back to Math.random().
enrichment.description: Random Bytes fills Length bytes from the platform's cryptographic random source (crypto.getRandomValues) and renders them in Encoding. If there is no such source it fails loudly rather than substituting Math.random() — a silent downgrade there produces output that looks identical and is worthless. Length counts BYTES, not characters: 32 bytes is 64 hex characters or 43 base64url characters. A length outside 1-4096 is refused rather than clamped.
enrichment.whenToUse: A nonce, a CSRF token, a PKCE verifier, an invite code, a one-time download key — anything that has to be unguessable. For an identifier that only has to be unique, the UUID node says so more clearly.

ports.length: How many random bytes to produce, 1-4096. Default 32.
ports.encoding: hex (default), base64 or base64url. Base64 URL is the one that is safe in a URL.
ports.value: The random bytes rendered in Encoding, replaced on every New.
ports.done: Fires once Value holds fresh bytes.
ports.failure: Fires when there is no cryptographic random source, or Length is out of range.
ports.error: Why no bytes were produced.

patterns: New → Done → store or send. The value is replaced on every New, so read it from the Done path rather than later.
antiPatterns: Treating Length as a character count. 16 bytes of hex is 32 characters.
Using this where a UUID is what the other system expects — the shapes are not interchangeable.

ssr.note: An event stream cannot be consumed during a server render; the node connects in the browser after hydration.

inputs.name: autoConnect
inputs.description: Opens the stream as soon as a URL is available, without waiting for a Connect signal

inputs.name: autoReconnect
inputs.description: Retries after a failure with a growing backoff; turning it off reports the failure and stops

inputs.name: body
inputs.description: Request body, sent as JSON unless it is already a string; ignored for GET and HEAD

inputs.name: connect
inputs.description: Opens the stream, replacing any connection already open and resetting the retry count

inputs.name: dedupeById
inputs.description: Drops events whose id has already been seen, so a reconnect that resumes cannot re-deliver messages

inputs.name: disconnect
inputs.description: Closes the stream and stops retrying

inputs.name: eventTypes
inputs.description: Comma-separated named event types to subscribe to; only needed for the EventSource transport, as Fetch delivers every type

inputs.name: headers
inputs.description: Request headers as an object, for bearer tokens and the like; ignored by the EventSource transport, which cannot set them

inputs.name: maxReconnectDelay
inputs.description: Ceiling on the backoff in milliseconds, however many failures there have been

inputs.name: maxRetries
inputs.description: Consecutive failures allowed before the connection gives up and reports an error; 0 keeps retrying

inputs.name: method
inputs.description: HTTP method for the request; anything other than GET needs the Fetch transport

inputs.name: reconnectDelay
inputs.description: First retry delay in milliseconds, doubling per consecutive failure up to Max Reconnect Delay

inputs.name: reconnectOnStreamEnd
inputs.description: Reconnects when the server closes the stream cleanly; off by default because reconnecting an agent stream re-issues the request

inputs.name: textPath
inputs.description: Where the text lives inside a JSON payload, as a dot path such as choices.0.delta.content; leave blank for a stream of bare text

inputs.name: transport
inputs.description: How the stream is fetched: Fetch carries headers and a body, EventSource lets the browser handle reconnection, Auto prefers Fetch

inputs.name: url
inputs.description: Endpoint to stream from; changing it while connected reconnects to the new one

inputs.name: withCredentials
inputs.description: Sends cookies and HTTP auth to a cross-origin endpoint, which the server must also allow

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: connected
outputs.description: True only while the stream is open and frames may arrive

outputs.name: connectionState
outputs.description: Where the connection is: idle, connecting, open, reconnecting, closed or error

outputs.name: data
outputs.description: The event payload, parsed as JSON when it is JSON and handed over as text when it is not

outputs.name: deliverySemantics
outputs.description: What this stream actually guarantees, derived from whether the server sends ids: at-most-once, at-least-once or at-least-once-deduped

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the action finished: a Connect whose stream opened, or a Disconnect that stopped one

outputs.name: duplicatesSuppressed
outputs.description: How many replayed events Dedupe By Id has dropped on this connection

outputs.name: eventType
outputs.description: The event name the server sent, or message when it sent none

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the stream could not be opened, or gave up retrying. Last Error carries the reason

outputs.name: lastError
outputs.description: What went wrong most recently, including the reason a retry was scheduled

outputs.name: lastEventId
outputs.description: The furthest id the server has reported, which is the point a reconnect resumes from

outputs.name: lastMessageTime
outputs.description: When the last event arrived, as milliseconds since the epoch; useful for spotting a stalled stream

outputs.name: messageCount
outputs.description: How many events have been delivered on this connection, not counting suppressed duplicates

outputs.name: onClose
outputs.description: Fires when the stream has stopped for good, whether it ended cleanly or gave up

outputs.name: onError
outputs.description: Fires when the stream failed or dropped, whether or not a retry is going to follow

outputs.name: onMessage
outputs.description: Fires once per event, after Data, Raw and Text already hold it

outputs.name: onOpen
outputs.description: Fires when the stream has been established

outputs.name: raw
outputs.description: The event payload exactly as it arrived, before any parsing

outputs.name: retryCount
outputs.description: Consecutive failed attempts in the current outage; back to zero once the stream opens

outputs.name: text
outputs.description: The one data output guaranteed to be a string: Raw when no Text Path is set, the field at that path when one is, blank when it does not resolve

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when there was nothing to do: a Disconnect with no stream running, or a Connect a later Connect or Disconnect superseded before it opened

enrichment.summary: Server-Sent Events: consumes a streaming HTTP endpoint, with connection state, retries and errors as graph outputs.
enrichment.description: Opens a `text/event-stream` connection and turns each event into outputs plus an `onMessage` signal. Two transports: Fetch (the default under 'Auto') can send headers, a method and a body, receives every event type, resumes with an explicit `Last-Event-ID`, and can tell a finished stream from a dropped one; EventSource is the browser's own client, which cannot set headers or POST, needs named event types declared up front on `eventTypes`, and reconnects on its own schedule. Failures never disappear: `connectionState` moves through idle/connecting/open/reconnecting/closed/error, `retryCount` counts consecutive failures, `lastError` carries the message and `onError` fires. Retries use exponential backoff from `reconnectDelay` up to `maxReconnectDelay`, honouring a server `retry:` field when one arrives. A 4xx is terminal (retrying cannot help); 5xx, 408 and 429 are retried. Deleting the node or navigating away aborts the request and clears every timer.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any server-push stream: AI/agent responses streamed token by token, progress on a long-running job, live notifications, dashboard metrics. Use the Fetch transport whenever the endpoint needs an Authorization header or a request body — the usual shape for an AI backend. Use REST2 or HTTP Request for ordinary request/response, and a WebSocket node when the client must also send on the same connection. Client-only: the node stays inert during server-side rendering and connects after hydration.

ports.url: Stream endpoint. Required before Connect does anything; an empty URL reports an error rather than failing silently.
ports.transport: 'Auto' picks Fetch wherever fetch exists. Choose 'EventSource' only to get the browser's own reconnection behaviour.
ports.method: Fetch transport only. POST is the common case for an AI endpoint that takes a prompt.
ports.headers: Fetch transport only — an object of header name to value. EventSource cannot send headers at all.
ports.body: Fetch transport only. An object is JSON-encoded and Content-Type is set unless Headers already sets it.
ports.eventTypes: Comma-separated named event types. Only needed for EventSource, which delivers a named event only to a listener registered in advance.
ports.textPath: Where the text lives inside a JSON payload, as a dot path — `choices.0.delta.content` for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Blank for a stream that sends bare text. Whatever it names appears on `text`.
ports.autoConnect: Connects once the URL and the rest of the inputs have landed, without needing a Connect signal.
ports.autoReconnect: Retry after a failure. Off means a single failure goes straight to the error state.
ports.reconnectOnStreamEnd: Off by default. An agent response stream is finite, and reconnecting would re-issue the request and start the response again.
ports.maxRetries: 0 keeps retrying. Otherwise the connection reports an error naming the budget it spent.
ports.dedupeById: Drops events whose id was already seen, so a resumed reconnect cannot re-deliver messages. Turn off only if the server reuses ids for distinct events.
ports.connectionState: idle, connecting, open, reconnecting, closed or error. 'error' is terminal; 'reconnecting' means another attempt is coming.
ports.connected: True only while the stream is open — false during connect, backoff and after a terminal failure.
ports.data: The event payload, parsed as JSON when it parses and left as the raw string when it does not (so a `[DONE]` sentinel arrives intact). An *object* for a JSON payload — feed a Text node or a Text Accumulator from `text`, not from here.
ports.raw: The payload exactly as sent, before any JSON parsing.
ports.text: The one data output that is always a string: the payload as sent when `textPath` is blank, or the field at that path when it is set. A missing field, a non-JSON sentinel or a path landing on an object all read as empty rather than as `[object Object]`.
ports.eventType: The `event:` field of the last event, or 'message' when the server sent none.
ports.lastEventId: The furthest `id:` the server has sent; this is what a reconnect resumes from.
ports.deliverySemantics: 'at-most-once' when the server sends no ids (gap events are lost), 'at-least-once' when it does, 'at-least-once-deduped' when ids are present and Dedupe By Id is on.
ports.duplicatesSuppressed: How many replayed events were dropped after a resume. Non-zero is normal after a reconnect.
ports.onMessage: Fires once per event, after the Data outputs have updated — so an accumulator wired `text` → `chunk` and `onMessage` → `add` sees the chunk first.
ports.onClose: Fires when the stream stops, whether cleanly or with a terminal error, so a Close handler always runs.
ports.onError: Fires on every failure, including ones the node is about to retry.
ports.done: Signal; this invocation finished — a Connect whose stream opened, or a Disconnect that stopped one that was running. ⚠️ A first attempt that fails and a retry that then opens is one Done, not a Failure and then a Done: the invocation is not over until the stream is up or the connection has given up.
ports.unchanged: Signal; there was nothing to do — a Disconnect with no stream running, or a Connect that a later Connect, a Disconnect or a URL change superseded before it opened.
ports.failure: Signal; the stream could not be opened, or gave up retrying. Last Error carries the reason.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every Connect and Disconnect the author triggered, whatever the outcome. ⚠️ Auto Connect and a URL change also open streams, and neither reports.

patterns: SSE `text` → Text Accumulator `chunk` and SSE `onMessage` → Text Accumulator `add`, with an empty delimiter, renders an AI response as it is written. Set `textPath` to `choices.0.delta.content` for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and leave it blank for a stream of bare tokens; either way `text` is a string.
`data` is for the payloads that are meant to be objects: a JSON Stream Parser, or an Action Dispatcher's `action` input.
SSE `connectionState` → String Mapper → a status label makes reconnection visible instead of leaving the UI apparently frozen.
POST the prompt in `body` with an Authorization header rather than putting a token in the query string, which the EventSource-only approach forces.
antiPatterns: Turning on Reconnect On Stream End for a finite agent response — the request is re-issued and the answer regenerates in a loop.
Ignoring `connectionState` and wiring only the data outputs: a silently failing reconnection then looks identical to a slow server.

Wiring `data` into anything that expects text. `data` is JSON-parsed, so for the commonest agent shape (`data: {"delta":"Hi"}`) it is an object; a Text Accumulator refuses it and reports the mis-wiring rather than appending `[object Object]`. Use `text`.
Leaving `textPath` blank on a JSON-envelope stream and wiring `raw` instead — the answer then reads as a run of JSON fragments.
Using the EventSource transport when the endpoint needs an Authorization header, then smuggling the token through the URL.

outputs.description: Fires after every invocation. This node has no other outcome — no Unchanged and no Failure — so it always fires together with Done, and wiring either one does the same thing. It is here on every action so that reaching for it is never a per-node decision

enrichment.description: The writing half of Component Object: property values set on this node's declared inputs are committed to the enclosing component instance's object when `store` fires, and every Component Object / Parent Component Object reader of that instance sees the change immediately. `done` confirms the write, and `completed` follows it on every invocation.
enrichment.whenToUse: Mutating instance-scoped state: resetting a wizard, recording a selection local to this instance. For state shared across instances or screens use Objects (Model2) or Variables instead.

ports.done: Signal; the write completed.
