inputs.name: clearHistory
inputs.description: Throws the history away and starts again from the live state

inputs.name: coalesceMs
inputs.description: Window in milliseconds within which successive changes to the same keys fold into one undo step; 0 records every change separately

inputs.name: enabled
inputs.description: Turning this off pauses recording and keeps the entries already collected

inputs.name: maxHistory
inputs.description: How many entries to keep before the oldest is dropped, never below two and never dropping the current one

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the global store to record; one tracker per store is enough, and two on the same store share one history

inputs.name: trackKeys
inputs.description: Comma-separated keys to record; leave blank to record the whole store, and note that changing this clears the history

outputs.name: byReferenceKeys
outputs.description: Comma-separated keys an undo cannot fully restore because they hold live objects rather than data

outputs.name: canRedo
outputs.description: True when an undo has been made and there is a later entry to step forward to

outputs.name: canUndo
outputs.description: True when there is an earlier entry to step back to

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: currentIndex
outputs.description: Where in the history the store is sitting; -1 when nothing is being tracked

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the history has been thrown away and re-baselined from the live state

outputs.name: fullyRestorable
outputs.description: False when some entry holds a Collection, a Model or a function, which a snapshot can only keep by reference

outputs.name: history
outputs.description: One entry per recorded change, each with its index, timestamp, description and changed keys, but not its state

outputs.name: historyChanged
outputs.description: Fires whenever an entry is added, the position moves, or the history is cleared

outputs.name: historySize
outputs.description: How many entries the history holds, including the baseline it started from

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when there was nothing to throw away, because the history was already just its baseline

enrichment.summary: Records a bounded history of a store's state so it can be undone, redone or stepped through, and reports what it cannot fully restore.
enrichment.description: Watches a store and records an entry per commit, keeping `entries[currentIndex]` always equal to live state. History is bounded by `maxHistory` (default 50): the oldest entry is dropped first, never the current one, and lowering the bound while you are mid-travel drops the redo tail instead. A new write truncates the redo stack, as undo/redo everywhere does. An undo is an ordinary store commit — every other subscriber sees it as a normal change, not a special replay — so nothing in the graph needs to know time travel exists. Where it is honest rather than magical: values that can only be captured by reference (Models, Collections, functions, cyclic objects) are *not* deep-copied, so undoing does not restore their internal state. `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` say exactly which keys those are, rather than letting the feature quietly under-deliver. Coalescing (`coalesceMs`, off by default) folds rapid same-key writes into one entry so undo steps match user intent instead of keystrokes — and never folds into the entry a navigation just landed on, which would destroy the state you had just undone to.
enrichment.whenToUse: Undo/redo over shared state — a form, an editor, a builder, a drawing surface — and stepping back through state while debugging. Place one per store you want tracked; wire the Undo / Redo node to the buttons. For a single named checkpoint rather than a moving history, use State Snapshot. Check `fullyRestorable` before advertising undo over state that holds Collections or Models.

ports.storeName: The store to track. Tracking is reference-counted, so a second State History node on the same store does not wipe the first one's history.
ports.trackKeys: Comma-separated keys to track; empty tracks the whole store. Only tracked keys are restored, so a filtered history leaves everything else alone.
ports.maxHistory: Entries kept, default 50, floor 2. This is a memory bound: an unbounded history in a long-running app grows without limit.
ports.coalesceMs: Window in which consecutive writes to the same keys fold into one entry. 0 (default) records every commit separately. Set it to roughly a typing pause when undo should step by word rather than by character.
ports.enabled: False pauses recording without discarding history. Resuming records an entry if state drifted while paused, so the history never claims a change did not happen.
ports.clearHistory: Discards every entry and starts again from live state.
ports.done: Signal; the history was thrown away and re-baselined.
ports.unchanged: Signal; there was nothing to throw away, because the history was already just its baseline.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after either outcome. There is no Failure port — this node is the tracker for its own store name, so there is no store it can be asked for and fail to find.
ports.currentIndex: Where in the history live state sits. Not at the end means you are mid-travel and a new write will truncate the redo tail.
ports.canUndo: Whether an earlier entry exists — wire it to the Undo button's enabled state rather than guessing.
ports.fullyRestorable: False when any tracked key in the history could only be captured by reference, so undo cannot fully restore it.
ports.byReferenceKeys: Which keys those are. Show this rather than letting an author believe undo is total.
ports.history: Entry descriptors (not the states themselves) for building a timeline UI, each flagged with whether it is partial.
ports.historyChanged: Fires when an entry is added, dropped, or the current position moves.

patterns: `canUndo`/`canRedo` → the buttons' enabled state, so the affordance matches reality.
`coalesceMs` around 300–500 for text input, so an undo removes a word rather than a letter.
`history` → a Repeater for a visible timeline, with `currentIndex` marking where you are.
Surface `byReferenceKeys` in a developer-facing view when the store holds Collections, instead of discovering the limit through a confusing undo.
antiPatterns: Leaving `maxHistory` unbounded-by-intent in a long-running app: every entry is retained state.
Assuming undo restores everything. A key listed in `byReferenceKeys` shares its object with the entry, so its internal state was never copied.
Tracking the whole store when only a form's keys need undoing — unrelated writes then become undo steps the user did not make.

inputs.name: jumpTo
inputs.description: Moves the store to the entry named by Target Index

inputs.name: redo
inputs.description: Steps the store forward one entry, or fires Unchanged when it is already at the end

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store to step through; a State History node must already be tracking it

inputs.name: targetIndex
inputs.description: Entry to move to when Jump To is signalled, counting from zero; ignored by Undo and Redo

inputs.name: undo
inputs.description: Steps the store back one entry, or fires Unchanged when it is already at the beginning

outputs.name: byReferenceKeys
outputs.description: Comma-separated keys the restored entry put back as the same live object rather than as a copy

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the step actually moved the store

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last step failed; blank once one succeeds

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the step could not be made, because nothing is tracking the store or Target Index is outside the history

outputs.name: fullyRestorable
outputs.description: False when the entry just restored held live objects a snapshot could only keep by reference

outputs.name: jumped
outputs.description: Fires once the store holds the entry Target Index named

outputs.name: redone
outputs.description: Fires when a step forward actually happened, and not when the history was already at its end

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when the history had nowhere to go — an Undo at the beginning or a Redo at the end. Not a failure: this is an ordinary end-stop, and it used to be silent

outputs.name: undone
outputs.description: Fires when a step back actually happened, and not when the history was already at its beginning

enrichment.summary: Moves a store backwards, forwards, or to a specific point in the history recorded by a State History node.
enrichment.description: Drives the history that a State History node on the same store is recording; it records nothing itself, so a store with no State History node has nothing to undo and says so on Error rather than failing quietly. Undo and Redo step one entry; Jump To moves straight to `targetIndex`, which is what a timeline UI needs. Each move is an ordinary store commit, so subscribers and bindings update exactly as they do for any other change. After every move, `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` describe *the restore that just happened* — not the whole history — so an author can tell the user when a particular step could not be fully reversed instead of leaving them to notice.
enrichment.whenToUse: Wire it to Undo and Redo buttons, a keyboard shortcut, or a timeline UI. One node can serve all three: Undo, Redo and Jump To are separate signals on the same node. Take the buttons' enabled state from the State History node's `canUndo`/`canRedo` rather than from here.

ports.storeName: The store to move. A State History node must already be tracking it.
ports.targetIndex: Where Jump To goes. Out-of-range values are reported on Error rather than clamped silently, so a broken timeline UI is visible.
ports.redo: Steps forward one entry. Nothing happens if a write has since truncated the redo tail.
ports.jumped: Fires after a successful Jump To.
ports.fullyRestorable: Whether the restore that just happened was complete. False means some key could only be restored by reference.
ports.byReferenceKeys: Which keys in the restore that just happened could not be deep-restored.
ports.error: Carries the reason a move did nothing: no history for that store, nothing to undo or redo, or an out-of-range target.

patterns: State History `canUndo` → the Undo button's enabled state, and this node's `undo` → its click. The recording node owns the availability; this one owns the action.
`jumpTo` with `targetIndex` from a Repeater index, for a clickable timeline.
Show `byReferenceKeys` after a move where `fullyRestorable` is false, rather than leaving the user to discover the gap.
antiPatterns: Expecting it to work without a State History node on the same store — it drives a history, it does not keep one.
Wiring Undo to a button whose enabled state ignores `canUndo`: the button then does nothing at the end of the history.
Treating a failed move as impossible. Read `error` — out-of-range jumps and truncated redo tails are both normal.

inputs.name: restore
inputs.description: Puts a checkpoint back as an ordinary write, so it appears in the history and can itself be undone

inputs.name: save
inputs.description: Copies the store as it is now and keeps it under Snapshot Name

inputs.name: snapshotData
inputs.description: A previously exported Snapshot to restore instead of the named one; leave blank to restore by name

inputs.name: snapshotName
inputs.description: Name to save this checkpoint under, and the name Restore looks up; required to save

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: Names the store to snapshot or restore into

outputs.name: byReferenceKeys
outputs.description: Comma-separated keys the checkpoint holds as live objects, so restoring will not undo changes made to them since

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once a Save or Restore you triggered has finished, whichever of the two it was

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last save or restore failed; blank once one succeeds

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the checkpoint could not be saved or put back, most often an unnamed or unknown checkpoint

outputs.name: fullyRestorable
outputs.description: False when the checkpoint holds a Collection, a Model or a function, which it can only keep by reference

outputs.name: restored
outputs.description: Fires once the store holds the checkpoint again

outputs.name: saved
outputs.description: Fires once the checkpoint has been taken and Snapshot holds it

outputs.name: snapshot
outputs.description: The checkpoint just saved or restored, as plain data that can be written to a file and fed back into Snapshot Data

enrichment.summary: Saves a named snapshot of a store and restores it later — a checkpoint, rather than the moving history State History keeps.
enrichment.description: Save captures the store as it is now; Restore writes it back as a single commit that subscribers see as an ordinary change. A snapshot is copied in on restore, so **the same snapshot can be restored any number of times** — which is what makes it usable as a reset point rather than a one-shot. `snapshot` outputs the captured value, and `snapshotData` accepts one back, so a snapshot can be round-tripped through JSON: persisted, sent to a server, or restored in another session. As with State History, values that could only be captured by reference are not deep-copied, and `fullyRestorable` / `byReferenceKeys` name them rather than letting the checkpoint quietly under-deliver. Errors are reported on the Error output instead of thrown out of a signal handler.
enrichment.whenToUse: A discrete checkpoint: 'reset this form', 'revert to the last saved version', 'restore the state I shipped this bug report with'. Use State History instead when you want undo/redo over every change; use this when you want one or two named points you return to deliberately. The `snapshot`/`snapshotData` pair is also the straightforward way to persist state across sessions or attach it to a bug report.

ports.storeName: The store to capture or restore.
ports.snapshotName: A label for the snapshot, so several checkpoints are distinguishable in a UI.
ports.snapshotData: A snapshot captured earlier, fed back in to be restored — the input side of the round trip through JSON.
ports.restore: Writes a snapshot back as one commit. Safe to fire repeatedly; the snapshot is copied in, not consumed.
ports.snapshot: The captured snapshot, for persisting, transmitting, or feeding into another Restore.
ports.fullyRestorable: Whether this snapshot can be fully restored, or holds values captured only by reference.
ports.done: Fires after a Save or a Restore you triggered succeeded, whichever it was — wire this when one chain follows both verbs.
ports.error: Carries a refused save or restore — an unknown store, or snapshot data that could not be read.

patterns: Save when a form opens, Restore on the Cancel button — a reset that needs no knowledge of the form's fields.
`snapshot` → JSON → persisted, then back through `snapshotData` on the next load, for state that survives a reload without a live store.
Attach a snapshot to a bug report so the state is reproducible rather than described.
antiPatterns: Using it for undo. It is a checkpoint, not a stack — State History keeps the ordered history.
Assuming a restore is total when `fullyRestorable` is false: keys in `byReferenceKeys` share their object with the snapshot.
Saving on every change. That is a history with extra steps, and unbounded — State History bounds itself.

ssr.note: Interval-based flushing needs a running timer, so it only happens in the browser. Add, Flush and size-based flushing behave normally.

inputs.name: add
inputs.description: Buffers the current Data, flushing straight away if that reaches Flush Size

inputs.name: clear
inputs.description: Discards the buffer and resets both counters without flushing

inputs.name: data
inputs.description: The next item to buffer, of any type; its value is retained between pulses of Add

inputs.name: flush
inputs.description: Hands the whole buffer to Flushed Data now; an empty buffer is a legitimate no-op

inputs.name: flushInterval
inputs.description: Flush automatically this often in milliseconds while items are buffered; 0 disables interval flushing

inputs.name: flushSize
inputs.description: Flush automatically once this many items are buffered; 0 disables size-based flushing

inputs.name: maxSize
inputs.description: Hard cap on buffered items; overflow drops the oldest and is counted on Dropped Items; 0 means no cap

outputs.name: buffer
outputs.description: Items waiting to be flushed, oldest first

outputs.name: bufferSize
outputs.description: How many items are waiting, which is what Flush Size is compared against

outputs.name: cleared
outputs.description: Fires once the buffer has been discarded

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once an Add, Flush or Clear you triggered has changed the buffer

outputs.name: droppedItems
outputs.description: How many items Max Size has discarded from the front since the last Clear

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last Add was refused; blank until one is

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when Add ran before any value had arrived on Data, so nothing was buffered

outputs.name: flushCount
outputs.description: How many flushes have happened since the last Clear

outputs.name: flushed
outputs.description: Fires once Flushed Data holds a new batch, and not for a flush that found nothing

outputs.name: flushedData
outputs.description: The batch handed over by the most recent flush; a stable array that later Adds do not mutate

outputs.name: overflowed
outputs.description: Fires when Max Size has just discarded something

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when a Flush found nothing to send, or a Clear found nothing to discard — an idle buffer doing exactly what it should

enrichment.summary: Stream Buffer: batches items arriving faster than the UI wants to react, flushing on a count, an interval, or on demand.
enrichment.description: Each `add` appends the current `data` to a buffer. The buffer empties when `flushSize` items have collected, when `flushInterval` milliseconds have passed since the first item after the last flush, or when `flush` fires — whichever comes first. `flushedData` is a detached array, so a later Add cannot mutate what a downstream node is already rendering. The interval timer is armed only while items are waiting, is re-armed rather than left stale when the interval changes, and is cleared on a manual flush and when the node is deleted. `maxSize` caps the buffer, dropping the oldest and reporting it on `droppedItems` with an `overflowed` signal. A `flush` that finds nothing, and a `clear` with nothing to discard, report `unchanged` — an idle buffer doing exactly what it should, not a failure.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any producer that outruns the UI: a token stream driving a Repeater, high-rate telemetry, a log feed. Batching turns hundreds of small graph updates a second into a few. Not needed when updates are already infrequent, and not a substitute for Text Accumulator when the thing being batched is text that should be concatenated rather than listed.

ports.data: The item to buffer on the next Add. Any type.
ports.add: Appends the current item. Wire the stream's message signal here.
ports.flushSize: Flush once this many items are buffered. 0 disables size-based flushing.
ports.flushInterval: Flush this many milliseconds after the buffer stops being empty. 0 disables interval flushing. Only fires in the browser, never during a server render.
ports.maxSize: Hard cap on buffered items. Overflow drops the oldest; 0 means no cap.
ports.flushedData: The batch released by the last flush — a fresh array each time.
ports.droppedItems: Running count of items lost to the cap. Non-zero means the consumer cannot keep up.
ports.flushed: Fires after each flush, once Flushed Data has updated.
ports.overflowed: Fires when the cap dropped items.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `onMessage` → `add` with `flushInterval` 250 and `flushedData` → For Each: a live list that repaints four times a second instead of hundreds.
`flushSize` and `flushInterval` together give 'whichever comes first', which keeps both a burst and a trickle responsive.
The stream's `onClose` → `flush` releases the tail of a batch that never reached the flush size.
antiPatterns: Relying on Flush Interval during server-side rendering — timers never advance there, so only Add, Flush and size-based flushing work.
Using this to concatenate streamed text; Text Accumulator is the node for that.
Setting Flush Size to 1, which is the same as no buffer at all plus an extra hop.

inputs.name: add
inputs.description: Appends the current Chunk, which is retained between pulses, so a second Add with no new chunk appends it again

inputs.name: chunk
inputs.description: The next fragment of text to append; wire a stream Text output, not its Data output, which is JSON-parsed and is usually an object

inputs.name: clear
inputs.description: Empties the buffer, the messages and both dropped counts

inputs.name: delimiter
inputs.description: Message boundary to split complete messages off; leave empty to accumulate everything, which is what a token stream wants

inputs.name: maxLength
inputs.description: Cap on the pending buffer in characters; overflow drops the oldest and is counted on Dropped Characters

inputs.name: maxMessages
inputs.description: Cap on retained complete messages, oldest dropped first; 0 keeps them all, which grows forever

outputs.name: accumulated
outputs.description: Everything appended since the last Clear that has not yet been split off as a complete message

outputs.name: byteCount
outputs.description: Length of Accumulated in UTF-8 bytes, which differs from Character Count for anything outside ASCII

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires whenever an Add appended something, which is the cue to redraw

outputs.name: characterCount
outputs.description: Length of Accumulated in characters

outputs.name: cleared
outputs.description: Fires once the buffer and the messages have been emptied

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once an Add or Clear you triggered has changed the buffer

outputs.name: droppedCharacters
outputs.description: How many characters Max Length has discarded from the front since the last Clear

outputs.name: droppedMessages
outputs.description: How many complete messages Max Messages has discarded since the last Clear

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last chunk was refused; blank once a chunk of text arrives

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when a chunk was not text and nothing was appended, which usually means the wrong stream output is wired

outputs.name: lastMessage
outputs.description: The most recent complete message, which is what a chat surface usually wants

outputs.name: messageCount
outputs.description: How many complete messages are being retained, which is not how many have arrived

outputs.name: messageReceived
outputs.description: Fires once per Add that completed at least one message, not once per message

outputs.name: messages
outputs.description: Complete messages split off the delimiter, oldest first, capped at Max Messages

outputs.name: overflowed
outputs.description: Fires when Max Length or Max Messages has just discarded something

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when an Add had no text to append — an empty chunk, or one already refused — or a Clear found nothing to discard

enrichment.summary: Text Accumulator: collects stream fragments into growing text, and splits complete messages off a delimiter.
enrichment.description: Each `add` appends the current `chunk` to a buffer. With an empty delimiter nothing is ever split and `accumulated` is simply the text so far — the mode a token stream wants. With a delimiter (newline by default) every complete piece moves to `messages` and only the unfinished tail stays in `accumulated`, so a message split across chunk boundaries reassembles correctly. Both stores are bounded: `maxLength` caps the pending buffer and `maxMessages` caps the retained list, dropping the oldest first and reporting the loss on `droppedCharacters` / `droppedMessages` plus an `overflowed` signal rather than growing without limit in a long-lived session. An empty chunk appends nothing, so a stream's keep-alive frames do not fire `changed` — the Add reports `unchanged` rather than nothing at all.
enrichment.whenToUse: Assembling anything that arrives in pieces: AI tokens into a displayable answer, log lines out of a chunked feed, NDJSON lines before parsing them. Pair it with Server-Sent Events or any node that emits fragments. Not needed when each event is already a whole value — wire that straight to its consumer.

ports.chunk: The fragment to append. Text, numbers and booleans are accepted; an object or an array is refused and named on `error`, because it means a JSON-parsed `data` output was wired here where the stream's `text` output was wanted.
ports.add: Appends the current chunk. Wire the stream's `onMessage` here; the chunk value arrives first.
ports.delimiter: Message boundary. Empty means no boundaries — accumulate everything, which is what a token stream needs.
ports.maxLength: Cap on the pending buffer in characters. Overflow drops the oldest and reports it; 0 disables the cap.
ports.maxMessages: Cap on retained complete messages. 0 keeps them all, which grows forever in a long session.
ports.accumulated: The text not yet terminated by a delimiter. With no delimiter this is the whole stream so far.
ports.lastMessage: The most recent complete message, for the common case of only wanting the newest.
ports.byteCount: UTF-8 size of the pending buffer, which differs from Character Count for anything non-ASCII.
ports.changed: Fires on every non-empty Add, so a Text node repaints as the stream arrives.
ports.messageReceived: Fires once per Add that completed at least one message — not once per message.
ports.overflowed: Fires when a cap dropped data. Wire it if losing the oldest content matters.
ports.error: Empty until something that is not text arrives on `chunk`, then a message naming what came and which output to wire instead. Clears on the next usable chunk and on Clear.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `text` → `chunk`, `onMessage` → `add`, delimiter empty, `accumulated` → Text `text`: an answer that types itself out.
Delimiter `\n` with `messages` → For Each renders a growing log without re-parsing the whole buffer each time.
The stream's `onOpen` → `clear` resets the accumulator when a new response starts.
antiPatterns: Wiring a stream's `data` output into `chunk`. `data` is JSON-parsed and is an object for an OpenAI-style payload; wire `text` (with the stream's `textPath` set) or a Function node that picks out the string field.
Leaving `maxMessages` at 0 in a session that runs for hours — the array grows until the tab does.
Wiring `add` from a signal that fires before `chunk` is set (a Function's own output, say) — the last chunk gets appended twice and the newest not at all.

inputs.name: columns
inputs.description: Which properties to write, in order, comma separated. Leave it empty and every property found on the records is written, in the order they were first seen

inputs.name: delimiter
inputs.description: The character between cells. Any cell containing it is quoted automatically

inputs.name: includeHeader
inputs.description: Write the column names as the first row

inputs.name: items
inputs.description: The array to write. Records become rows; an array of arrays is written cell for cell

outputs.name: changed
outputs.description: Fires once CSV holds the freshly written text

outputs.name: count
outputs.description: How many data rows were written, not counting the header row

outputs.name: text
outputs.description: The array as CSV text. Cells containing the delimiter, a quote or a newline are quoted and their quotes doubled, so this round-trips back through Parse CSV unchanged

enrichment.summary: Writes an array out as CSV text, quoting any cell that needs it.
enrichment.description: To CSV turns an array into CSV text. Records become rows: leave Columns empty and every property found on the records is written, in the order they were first seen, or name the columns yourself to fix the order and drop the rest. An array of arrays — what Parse CSV produces with Has Header unticked — is written cell for cell with no header invented. The correctness of a CSV writer is entirely about quoting, and this one gets it right: any cell containing the delimiter, a quote or a newline is wrapped in quotes with its own quotes doubled, so the output reads back through Parse CSV unchanged. The record `id` the runtime mints is not written unless you name it in Columns, because it is not a column you put there.
enrichment.whenToUse: Answering with a spreadsheet: a cloud function replying to an export request, a download button in a browser app, a file written to storage. Pair it with Parse CSV for 'read a supplier's file, filter it, send it back'.

ports.items: The array to write. Records become rows; an array of arrays is written cell for cell.
ports.columns: Which properties to write, in order, comma separated in one string. Empty means every property found, in first-seen order.
ports.delimiter: The character between cells. Any cell containing it is quoted automatically.
ports.includeHeader: Write the column names as the first row. Ignored for an array of arrays, which has no column names.
ports.count: How many data rows were written, not counting the header row.
ports.changed: Fires once CSV holds the freshly written text.

patterns: Query Records `items` → To CSV `items`; To CSV `text` → Response `pm-csv`: an export endpoint in three nodes.
Parse CSV → Array Filter → To CSV: read, narrow, write back. The round trip is exact, including cells containing commas, quotes and newlines.
antiPatterns: Building CSV by joining strings in an Expression or Function node. That is the quoting rule reimplemented, and it is wrong the first time a cell contains a comma.
Passing an array of arrays and expecting a header row. There are no column names to write; use records if you want one.

inputs.name: generate
inputs.description: Generates a fresh UUID, replacing the one on Id

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once a new UUID is available on Id

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why no UUID could be generated

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when there is no cryptographic random source here, leaving Id as it was

outputs.name: uuid
outputs.description: A random version-4 UUID, generated once when the node is created and again on every New. Use this rather than Unique Id wherever the id has to be globally unique or unguessable

enrichment.summary: A random version-4 UUID from the platform's cryptographic random source. Not the same thing as Unique Id.
enrichment.description: UUID emits a standard RFC 4122 version-4 identifier — 36 characters, 122 random bits — generated once when the node is created and again on every New. It uses crypto.randomUUID where that exists and builds the same layout from crypto.getRandomValues where it does not (a browser on a non-secure origin), so it is never weaker, only differently reached. It is deliberately a second node beside Unique Id rather than a replacement: Unique Id is 10 characters from Math.random(), which is right for keying a rendered list and wrong for a record id, an idempotency key or anything an attacker might try to guess.
enrichment.whenToUse: A record id, an idempotency key, a correlation id across services, a filename that must not collide. Anywhere the id leaves this page or has to be unguessable.

ports.generate: Signal (New); mints a fresh UUID, replacing the one on Id.
ports.uuid: The current UUID. Populated at creation, so it is never blank before the first New.
ports.done: Fires once Id holds a fresh UUID.
ports.failure: Fires when there is no cryptographic random source here, leaving Id as it was.
ports.error: Why no UUID could be generated.

patterns: Create Record with Id wired from this node: an id minted client-side lets the same request be retried safely.
antiPatterns: Using Unique Id where this node is meant. Ten characters of Math.random() is not an identifier to key a database on.

ssr.note: A WebSocket cannot be meaningfully opened during a server render and would leak a socket per request; the node connects in the browser after hydration.

inputs.name: autoConnect
inputs.description: Connect as soon as a URL is available, without waiting for a Connect signal

inputs.name: autoReconnect
inputs.description: Retries after an unsolicited close with a growing backoff; turning it off reports the close as an error

inputs.name: connect
inputs.description: Opens the socket, replacing one already open without reporting a close

inputs.name: disconnect
inputs.description: Closes the socket and cancels any pending reconnect

inputs.name: heartbeatInterval
inputs.description: Milliseconds between heartbeats while the socket is open; 0 disables it, and only enable it if your server expects the message

inputs.name: heartbeatMessage
inputs.description: Application text sent as the heartbeat; it is not a protocol ping frame

inputs.name: heartbeatReply
inputs.description: Exact text the server answers a heartbeat with; it is measured as Latency, hidden from On Message, and its absence is treated as a dead connection

inputs.name: jitter
inputs.description: Spreads reconnect attempts randomly across the second half of each backoff window, so a fleet does not return in lockstep

inputs.name: maxQueueSize
inputs.description: Messages the queue holds before further Sends are refused and counted as dropped; 0 or less is unlimited and can grow during a long outage

inputs.name: maxReconnectDelay
inputs.description: Ceiling on the backoff in milliseconds, however many attempts there have been

inputs.name: maxRetries
inputs.description: Reconnect attempts allowed per outage; 0 disables retrying and a negative value means unlimited

inputs.name: message
inputs.description: Value to send; objects are JSON-serialised, and ArrayBuffers and typed arrays go as binary frames

inputs.name: messageType
inputs.description: Auto sends binary values as binary and everything else as text; Binary encodes text and objects as UTF-8 first

inputs.name: protocols
inputs.description: Comma-separated WebSocket subprotocols to offer during the handshake

inputs.name: reconnectDelay
inputs.description: First backoff delay in milliseconds; each further attempt doubles it up to Max Reconnect Delay

inputs.name: send
inputs.description: Hands the current Message to the socket, or applies the When Disconnected policy

inputs.name: url
inputs.description: Endpoint to connect to, which must start with ws:// or wss://; changing it reconnects to the new one

inputs.name: whenDisconnected
inputs.description: What a Send does while the socket is not open: hold it in order, discard and count it, or also report an error

outputs.name: closeCode
outputs.description: WebSocket close code from the last close, or 1006 when the socket died without one

outputs.name: closeReason
outputs.description: Reason the server gave for closing, which is often blank

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: connected
outputs.description: True only while the socket is open and messages can be sent without queueing

outputs.name: connectionState
outputs.description: Where the connection is: idle, connecting, open, reconnecting, closed or error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the action finished: a Connect whose socket opened, a Send accepted for delivery (sent, or queued for the next open), or a Disconnect that closed something

outputs.name: droppedCount
outputs.description: Messages that will never be sent, whether discarded by policy, by a full queue, or by the node being removed

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the action could not be performed — no URL, a URL that is not ws:// or wss://, a connection that gave up, or a refused Send. Last Error carries the reason

outputs.name: lastError
outputs.description: What went wrong most recently, including why a reconnect was scheduled or abandoned

outputs.name: latency
outputs.description: Round trip of the last heartbeat in milliseconds; 0 until one has been measured

outputs.name: onClose
outputs.description: Fires whenever the socket goes down, whether or not a reconnect is going to follow

outputs.name: onError
outputs.description: Fires when something went wrong: a failed connect, a refused send, a dead heartbeat, or a give-up

outputs.name: onMessage
outputs.description: Fires once per message, after Received already holds it; heartbeat replies are not messages

outputs.name: onMessageSent
outputs.description: Fires when a message has been handed to the socket, including a queued one flushed on reopen; not for heartbeats

outputs.name: onOpen
outputs.description: Fires every time the socket opens, including after a reconnect

outputs.name: onReconnect
outputs.description: Fires on every open after the first; a WebSocket cannot resume, so this is the cue to re-fetch rather than assume continuity

outputs.name: queueSize
outputs.description: Messages held because the socket was not open when Send ran

outputs.name: received
outputs.description: The last message, parsed as JSON when it is JSON and handed over as text when it is not

outputs.name: receivedIsBinary
outputs.description: True when the last message was a binary frame, in which case Received holds the buffer

outputs.name: receivedRaw
outputs.description: The last text message exactly as it arrived; blank for a binary frame

outputs.name: retryCount
outputs.description: Attempts made during the current outage; back to zero once the socket opens

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when there was nothing to do: a Disconnect with nothing open, a Send discarded by the Drop policy, or a Connect a later Connect or Disconnect superseded before it opened

enrichment.summary: Two-way WebSocket connection: send and receive text, JSON or binary, with connection state as graph outputs.
enrichment.description: A bidirectional transport for agent chat, collaboration, telemetry and any other stream where the client also talks back. `url` plus `autoConnect` opens the socket; `Connect`/`Disconnect` do it by hand. `Send` transmits whatever is on `message` — a string goes as text, an object is JSON-serialized, an ArrayBuffer or typed array goes as a binary frame, and `messageType: binary` UTF-8 encodes text first. Received text is JSON-parsed onto `received` with the original on `receivedRaw`; binary arrives on `received` as an ArrayBuffer with `receivedIsBinary` true. Everything about the connection's health is an output rather than a console message: `connectionState` moves through idle → connecting → open → reconnecting → closed/error, `retryCount` counts attempts within the current outage, `lastError` says what went wrong, `closeCode`/`closeReason` carry the server's own explanation, and `queueSize`/`droppedCount` account for every message that has not reached the wire. Reconnection is exponential backoff from `reconnectDelay`, doubling to `maxReconnectDelay`, with jitter, stopping after `maxRetries` — or immediately for close codes where retrying is futile (1002, 1003, 1007–1010, 1015). Giving up sets `connectionState` to error and fires `onError`; it is never silent.
enrichment.whenToUse: When the client needs to send as well as receive — chat with an agent, collaborative editing, live cursors, device control, order placement. If the server only pushes and the client never sends, Server-Sent Events is simpler and more firewall-friendly. This node is transport only: point it at your own endpoint, and use ordinary Object/Array/Function nodes to shape what flows through it. It is client-only, so it stays inert during server-side rendering and connects in the browser after hydration. ⚠️ **It is not the node for your project's own backend data.** NodeGX's built-in backend has no WebSocket server at all — realtime there is Server-Sent Events — and PocketBase, Parse and Supabase each speak something different again, so there is no URL to point this node at. Use **Subscribe To Changes**, which picks the transport from the backend's type and hides it.

ports.url: Must start with ws:// or wss://. Anything else is rejected as an error rather than attempted. Use wss:// in production. Browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, so tokens go in the query string or in a first message sent from On Open.
ports.autoConnect: Connects as soon as a URL exists — no Connect signal needed. With no URL the node simply stays idle; an explicit Connect with no URL is reported as an error.
ports.protocols: Comma-separated subprotocols offered during the handshake. Changing this, like changing the URL, rebuilds the connection.
ports.autoReconnect: Reconnect after any close the app did not ask for, including a clean 1000 (a server closing an idle connection is the commonest reason to want reconnection). Turn it off and an abnormal close lands in the error state instead.
ports.maxRetries: Attempts allowed per outage. 0 never retries; a negative value retries forever. When the budget runs out, `connectionState` becomes error, `lastError` names the count, and `onError` fires.
ports.heartbeatInterval: Off by default. WebSocket protocol ping frames are unreachable from a browser, so this sends Heartbeat Message as ordinary application data — only enable it if your server expects that exact message.
ports.heartbeatReply: The exact text the server answers with. It is measured as `latency`, hidden from On Message, and — if a heartbeat goes a whole interval unanswered — treated as a dead connection, closing and reconnecting. TCP can hold a half-open socket for minutes, so this is the only way to notice one.
ports.whenDisconnected: Queue (default) holds sends in order until the socket reopens; Drop discards and counts them; Report Error also sets Last Error and fires On Error. Whichever you pick, nothing vanishes without appearing in `queueSize` or `droppedCount`.
ports.maxQueueSize: When the queue is full the newest send is refused, not the oldest evicted — the queue stays an ordered prefix of what the app tried to say. 0 or less means unlimited, which can grow without bound during a long outage.
ports.message: Value to send, read at the moment Send fires. Objects are JSON-serialized; ArrayBuffers, typed arrays and Blobs are sent as binary whatever Message Type says.
ports.connectionState: idle | connecting | open | reconnecting | closed | error. 'reconnecting' spans the whole outage — the wait and every attempt — so it is a single state to render, not a flicker.
ports.retryCount: Attempts made during the current outage; back to 0 on a successful open or a manual Connect.
ports.queueSize: Messages waiting for the socket to reopen.
ports.droppedCount: Messages that will never be sent: dropped by policy, refused by a full queue, failed to encode, or still queued when the node was deleted.
ports.latency: Round trip of the last answered heartbeat, in ms. Stays 0 unless both Heartbeat Interval and Heartbeat Reply are set.
ports.received: The parsed message. Valid JSON text becomes the value it describes; anything else stays a string; binary frames arrive as an ArrayBuffer.
ports.onMessage: Fires per received frame, after `received`/`receivedRaw` have updated. Heartbeat replies are transport bookkeeping and do not fire it.
ports.onMessageSent: Fires per message handed to the socket, including each one flushed from the queue. Heartbeats do not fire it.
ports.onReconnect: Fires on every open after the first. A WebSocket has no session resume, so a reconnect is a new session and the node cannot know what was missed — wire this to whatever re-fetches state, the way you would handle a resync.
ports.onClose: Fires whenever the socket goes down, including when a reconnect is about to be attempted; read `connectionState` to tell the two apart. A Connect that replaces a live socket does not fire it, because the app asked for that.
ports.onError: Fires for a rejected URL, a failed connect, a refused or failed send, a dead heartbeat, and the moment reconnection is abandoned.
ports.done: Signal; this invocation finished and changed something — a Connect whose socket opened, a Send accepted for delivery, or a Disconnect that closed a live socket. ⚠️ A Send that was queued rather than written reports Done too, because the value is still owed to the wire; On Message Sent is what says it actually went.
ports.unchanged: Signal; there was nothing to do — a Disconnect with nothing open, a Send the Drop policy discarded, or a Connect that a later Connect or a Disconnect superseded before it opened. None of these is an error and none of them raises.
ports.failure: Signal; the action could not be performed — no URL, a URL that is not ws:// or wss://, a connection that gave up retrying, or a Send refused by the Report Error policy, an empty Message, a full queue or an encoding error. Last Error carries the reason.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every Connect, Send and Disconnect the author triggered, whatever the outcome. ⚠️ Auto Connect and a URL change also open sockets, and neither reports — they are not invocations of a port, so a boot that fired Done would pulse every chain in the app.

patterns: `connectionState` → a status Text, and `lastError` → an error Text: an outage becomes something the user can see rather than a UI that has quietly stopped answering.
Leave `whenDisconnected` on Queue so a message typed during a reconnect is held in order and sent on reopen instead of lost.
`onOpen` → send an auth or subscribe frame: the queue is flushed after On Open, so the handshake always precedes the backlog.
`onReconnect` → re-fetch history or re-subscribe, since the new session replays nothing.
`droppedCount` → a Condition → a 'messages were lost' notice, for apps where silent loss is not acceptable.
antiPatterns: Assuming a message handed to Send arrived. `socket.send` only buffers, and a connection that dies before the frame leaves loses it with no way to say which — add application-level acknowledgements if that matters.
Turning on the heartbeat against a server that does not expect it: the message is ordinary application data and most servers will either ignore it or close the connection.
Using this where the client only listens — Server-Sent Events reconnects natively and passes through more firewalls.
Setting Max Queue Size to 0 on a long-lived page: an outage then grows the queue without bound.

Putting a long-lived secret in the URL. Browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, but a query-string token ends up in server logs; prefer a short-lived ticket, or authenticate with a first message from On Open.

ssr.note: The scheduler clock is frozen during server render; the value stays at its start and Finished never fires there.

enrichment.summary: The standard clickable button control, with label, optional icon, and hover/pressed/focus states.
enrichment.description: The Button control renders a styled, accessible button with a text `label` and optional icon. Its main product is the `onClick` signal; it also exposes its interaction state as boolean levels (`hoverState`, `pressedState`, `focusState`) for styling reactions, and an `enabled` input to disable it. Visual-state variants let hover/pressed/disabled styling be defined per state.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any tap/click affordance with a caption. For a custom-drawn clickable area, a Group's `onClick` works; prefer the Button control when you want built-in states, label/icon layout and accessibility. The legacy `Button` type is superseded by this control.

ports.label: The button caption string.
ports.onClick: Signal; the click event — wire this to the action (Condition `eval`, Navigate `navigate`, Send Event `sendEvent`, …).
ports.enabled: Boolean level input; false renders the disabled state and suppresses `onClick`. The current value is also mirrored as an output of the same name.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: icon ports appear when an icon source is chosen, and each visual state (hover, pressed, disabled, focused) contributes state-scoped styling ports. The catalog list is the superset; the editor shows the subset matching current parameters.
patterns: onClick → Condition `eval`: validate before acting.
onClick → RouterNavigate `navigate`: page navigation.
A boolean derived from form state → `enabled`: prevent invalid submits at the source.
antiPatterns: Simulating disabled state by hiding the button; drive `enabled` instead so layout and accessibility stay intact.

enrichment.summary: Checkbox control: a styled boolean toggle exposing checked as a level and onChange as an edge.
enrichment.description: The Checkbox control renders a toggle with full style/state theming. `checked` is both an input (set programmatically) and an output level holding the current value; `onChange` fires on each user toggle. Interaction state (`hoverState`, `pressedState`, `focusState`) and `enabled` behave as on the other controls, with per-visual-state styling ports.
enrichment.whenToUse: Boolean choices the user flips directly: settings, consent, done flags. For one-of-many choices use Radio Buttons in a Radio Button Group; for an on/off in logic without UI, use a Switch node.

ports.checked: Boolean level, input and output — bind data in, read the current value out.
ports.onChange: Signal; a user toggle happened (fires after `checked` updated). Trigger persistence here.
ports.enabled: Boolean level; false shows the disabled state and blocks interaction.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: label ports appear when the label is enabled, and each visual state (hover, pressed, disabled, focused) adds state-scoped styling ports. The catalog list is the superset the editor filters by current parameters.
patterns: `checked` → Set Object Properties value + `onChange` → its `store`: level carries the data, edge commits it.

enrichment.summary: Radio Button control: one selectable option; place several inside a Radio Button Group, which reports the chosen value.
enrichment.description: A Radio Button is one option in a mutually-exclusive set. Each carries a `value` parameter; the enclosing Radio Button Group enforces single selection among its child radio buttons and outputs the selected `value`. The button itself exposes `checked` (is this one selected) and the usual interaction/styling surface.
enrichment.whenToUse: Small option sets where all choices should be visible at once. The group, not the individual buttons, is what logic listens to; without a Radio Button Group ancestor the buttons cannot coordinate exclusivity.

ports.checked: Boolean level; whether this particular option is the selected one.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: label and per-visual-state styling ports appear per configuration, matching the other controls.
antiPatterns: Wiring logic to each radio button's `checked` — listen to the group's `value` instead.

enrichment.summary: Slider control: picks a number between min and max by dragging a thumb; value and valuePercent stream out live.
enrichment.description: The Slider renders a draggable range input bounded by `min`/`max` with `step` granularity. `value` (the number) and `valuePercent` (0–100 regardless of bounds) update continuously while dragging; `onChange` fires per change. Thumb and track are styleable separately, and the standard control surface (enabled, focus/hover/pressed states) applies.
enrichment.whenToUse: Continuous or stepped numeric input where feel matters more than precision: volume, brightness, price ranges. For exact numeric entry pair it with (or replace it by) a Text Input.

ports.value: Number level: the current position in min–max units (input to set, output to read).
ports.valuePercent: Number level 0–100; convenient for driving other visuals without knowing the bounds.
ports.onChange: Signal; fires as the user drags — expect high frequency; debounce before persistence.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: label and per-visual-state styling ports appear per configuration.
antiPatterns: Writing to a backend on every `onChange` while dragging — debounce with a Timer first.

enrichment.summary: Single-line or multi-line text entry control with label, icon, placeholder and focus handling; outputs the text as the user types.
enrichment.description: The Text Input control renders an editable text field (or text area, or email/number/password/URL input, chosen by the `type` enum). Its main product is `onTextChanged` (display name 'Text'), a string output that updates continuously as the user types; the `textChanged` signal fires on every such change and `onEnter` fires when the user presses Enter. Text can also be written programmatically: the `startValue` (Text) input holds the field text, and the `set` signal applies it on demand. Optional label and icon sections, per-state styling and focus control (`focus`/`blur` signals, `focusState` output) are built in.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any free-text entry. Use `type` instead of separate nodes for email/number/password fields. For multi-line text set `type` to textArea. For choosing among fixed options use a Dropdown (net.noodl.controls.options) or Radio Button Group instead. The legacy `Text Input` type is superseded by this control.

ports.onTextChanged: String output ('Text') with the field's current text; updates on every keystroke.
ports.onEnter: Signal; fires when the user presses Enter while the field is focused.
ports.startValue: String input ('Text'). When `set` is unconnected a new value applies immediately; when `set` is connected the value is held until `set` fires. While the field has focus, programmatic writes are ignored so they cannot fight the user's typing.
ports.set: Signal; applies the pending `startValue` to the field.
ports.focus: Signal; gives the field keyboard focus (`blur` removes it).
ports.type: Enum: text, textArea, email, number, password or url. textArea renders a multi-line editor.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: `width`/`height` appear per `sizeMode`, icon ports per `useIcon`/`iconSourceType`, label styling ports when `useLabel` is true, and border/shadow ports per border-style and `boxShadowEnabled` settings. The catalog list is the superset; the editor shows the subset matching current parameters.
patterns: `onTextChanged` → an Expression or Condition: validate as the user types.
`onEnter` → the same action as the submit button's `onClick`: keyboard-friendly forms.
A stored value → `startValue` with a load signal → `set`: prefill a form when data arrives.
antiPatterns: Polling the text with a timer — `onTextChanged` is already live; wire it directly.
Wiring `textChanged` (signal) where the text string is wanted; use `onTextChanged`.

enrichment.summary: External Link: opens a URL outside the app — same tab or new tab — when its signal fires.
enrichment.description: External Link leaves the app: when `do` fires, the browser navigates to `link`, in a new tab when `openInNewTab` is true. It performs no in-app routing. It reports `done` once the link has been handed to the browser, `failure` when there is no Link or a popup blocker refused the new tab, and `unchanged` during a server-side render where there is no browser to open anything in — with Open In New Tab off the page is replaced, so nothing downstream of `done` may still exist.
enrichment.whenToUse: Documentation links, third-party checkout, mailto/tel URLs. For anything inside the app use Navigate or Navigate To Path, which keep SPA state alive.

ports.link: The absolute URL (or mailto:/tel: scheme) to open.

antiPatterns: Pointing External Link at the app's own routes — the full page reload throws away application state that Navigate would keep.

enrichment.summary: Logs a user into the cloud backend with username and password, establishing the session the User node reflects.
enrichment.description: Log In sends the current `username` and `password` (string values) to the cloud backend when `login` (Do, signal) is triggered. On success the returned session is stored in the browser (it persists across reloads), the app-wide user service switches to the logged-in user — which updates every User node and fires their Logged In signal — and `done` (signal) fires. On a bad login or network problem `error` (string value) is set with the message and `failure` (signal) fires; nothing about the current session changes.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action node behind a login form. To read who is logged in, or to react to session changes, use the User node; to create an account use Sign Up (which also logs the new user in); to end the session use Log Out.

ports.login: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); performs the login after pending input updates, so username/password wired from inputs are current.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the session is established. Typical next step: navigate to the logged-in page.
ports.failure: Signal; fires on rejected credentials or request failure. Show `error` to the user.
ports.error: String value holding the backend's error message from the last failed attempt.

patterns: Text Input `text` → `username`/`password`, Button `onClick` → `login`, `done` → navigation: the standard login form.
`error` → a Text node's `text`: surface backend messages like 'Invalid username/password' directly.
antiPatterns: Driving logged-in UI from this node's `done` signal alone — state belongs to the User node's `authenticated` boolean, which also covers sessions restored on reload.

enrichment.summary: Ends the current user session on the cloud backend and clears it from the browser.
enrichment.description: Log Out ends the current session when its `login` input (displayed 'Do', signal) is triggered: the backend session is revoked, the stored session is removed from the browser, and the app-wide user service switches to logged-out — updating every User node (`authenticated` becomes false) and firing their Logged Out signal. `done` (signal) fires when this completes; `failure` (signal) fires with `error` (string value) set if the request fails.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action behind a log-out button or menu item. To react to the session ending (e.g. navigate to the login page), listen on this node's `done` or the User node's Logged Out signal.

ports.failure: Signal; fires if the logout request fails. Read `error` for the message.

patterns: Button `onClick` → `login` (Do), `done` → navigate to the public/login page.

enrichment.summary: Asks the backend to email a one-click sign-in link. Succeeds identically whether or not the address has an account.
enrichment.description: Request Magic Link posts `email` (string value) to the backend's `/auth/magic-link` when `send` (Do, signal) is triggered. The backend mails a single-use, short-lived link; clicking it signs the user in on the page named by `redirect` (defaulting to the page the request was made from), where the runtime picks up the one-time code and establishes an ordinary session. `done` (signal) means THE REQUEST WAS ACCEPTED — never that an account exists. The endpoint answers identically for known and unknown addresses on purpose, because a public endpoint that answers differently is an account-existence oracle. `failure` (signal) with `error` (string value) means the request itself failed: no backend configured, a network error, or the rate limit.
enrichment.whenToUse: For passwordless sign-in, and as a password-free recovery path on backends that use provider sign-in. Requires the backend to have SMTP configured (BAK-002) and magic links enabled in the Auth section — with either missing, the request is still accepted and no mail is sent, which is deliberate anti-enumeration and shows up in the backend's log rather than in the app.

ports.send: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); posts the request after pending input updates.
ports.email: String value; the address to mail.
ports.redirect: String value; where the link should land the user. Defaults to the current page. Must be same-origin with the backend or on its redirectAllowList — an off-list target means no mail is sent.
ports.done: Signal; the request was accepted. Show 'if that address has an account, a link is on its way'.
ports.failure: Signal; the request could not be made. Show `error`.
ports.error: String value with the reason the request failed.

patterns: Text Input `text` → `email`, Button `onClick` → `send`, `done` → a neutral confirmation message.
Put a Sign In With node on the landing page named by `redirect` so the app can react to the click's outcome.
antiPatterns: Showing 'check your inbox' only when the account exists — this node cannot tell you that, and a UI that appears to know re-creates the oracle the backend removed.
Treating `done` as 'signed in'. The sign-in happens when the user clicks the link, on a later page load.

enrichment.summary: Saves changes to the signed-in user's email, username and custom properties on the cloud backend.
enrichment.description: Set User Properties writes the current values of its `email` and `username` (string values) and its per-property inputs to the signed-in user when `store` (Do, signal) is triggered. On success the server confirms the update, the local user model changes — User nodes see the new values and fire their per-property Changed signals — and `done` (signal) fires. On failure `error` (string value) is set and `failure` (signal) fires. It requires a signed-in session; it is also available inside cloud functions, where it acts on the calling user.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action behind a profile/settings form for the logged-in user. To set properties at account creation use Sign Up's property inputs; to read properties use the User node. It cannot edit other users — do that server-side in a cloud function with appropriate trust.

enrichment.summary: Signs a user in via an identity provider (Google, GitHub, any OpenID Connect issuer) configured on the backend. Redirects away.
enrichment.description: Sign In With drives BAK-004's redirect flow. Triggering `signIn` (Do, signal) sends the whole browser to the backend's `/oauth/<provider>/start`, which redirects on to the identity provider — so nothing downstream of `Do` runs, and the graph on that page is torn down. The provider sends the user back to the URL given in `redirect` (defaulting to the page they left) carrying a one-time code, which the runtime's user service exchanges for an ordinary session before any node sees it. On that LATER page load this node fires `done` (signal) or `failure` (signal) with `error` (string value); `signingIn` (boolean value) is true while the exchange is in flight. `notice` (string value) is set in the one case where a sign-in succeeds but the user should be told something: the backend linked this identity to an existing account whose email address had never been verified, and removed that account's old password.
enrichment.whenToUse: For 'Sign in with Google/GitHub/SSO' buttons on an app served by a NodeGX backend. Configure the provider first in the Backend Services panel's Auth section (or via MCP) — a provider that is not configured refuses the redirect with an explanation rather than sending the user to a broken provider page. Use Log In for username/password, Request Magic Link for passwordless email, and the User node to read who is signed in.

ports.signIn: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); NAVIGATES THE BROWSER AWAY after pending input updates. Treat it as the end of the flow, not a step in it.
ports.provider: String value; the provider id configured on the backend ('google', 'github', or whatever the operator named their OIDC provider). Read the list from GET /auth/providers.
ports.redirect: String value; where the provider should send the browser back to. Defaults to the current page. Must be same-origin with the backend or listed in the backend's redirectAllowList, otherwise the sign-in is refused before it starts.
ports.done: Signal; fires on the RETURNING page load once the session exists.
ports.failure: Signal; fires on the returning page load when the sign-in was refused, cancelled, or could not be completed.
ports.signingIn: Boolean value; true between the return landing and the session being established. Drive a spinner from this.
ports.error: String value holding the reason the last sign-in failed.
ports.notice: String value; non-empty only when the backend linked to an existing unverified account and revoked its password. Show it.

patterns: Put the node on both the page the user leaves from and the page they come back to — `Do` on the first, `done`/`failure` on the second. Pointing `redirect` at the same page makes one node do both.
`done` → navigation, `error` → a Text node's `text`: the whole flow in three connections.
`signingIn` → a Group's `visible`: the return leg is a network round trip, so there is a real moment to cover.
antiPatterns: Wiring anything downstream of `Do` and expecting it to run — the page is gone.
Reading logged-in state from `done` alone; the User node's `authenticated` boolean is the state, and it also covers sessions restored on reload.
Hard-coding an app URL in `redirect` that is not on the backend's redirectAllowList — the refusal happens at the start of the flow, not the end.

enrichment.summary: Creates a new user account on the cloud backend and logs it in, with inputs for custom user properties.
enrichment.description: Sign Up creates a user from the current `username`, `password` and optional `email` (string values), plus one input per custom property on the User class, when `signup` (Do, signal) is triggered. On success the new account is immediately logged in — the session is stored in the browser, every User node updates, their Logged In signal fires — and `done` (signal) fires. On failure (e.g. username taken) `error` (string value) is set and `failure` (signal) fires, and no account is created.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action node behind a registration form. For signing in an existing user use Log In; for editing the signed-in user's properties later use Set User Properties.

ports.signup: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); performs the sign-up after pending input updates so all field values are current.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the account exists and the user is logged in — no separate Log In step is needed.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the backend rejects the sign-up. Show `error` to the user.
ports.error: String value holding the backend's error message, e.g. an already-taken username.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: The editor generates one value input per custom property in the User class schema (stored as `prop-<name>`, typed from the schema; built-ins like username, password, email and system fields are excluded). These set the new user's properties at creation time.
patterns: Text Inputs → `username`/`password`/`email`, Button `onClick` → `signup`, `done` → navigate into the app: the standard registration form.
Fill `prop-<name>` inputs at sign-up for properties every account must have, instead of a follow-up Set User Properties call.
antiPatterns: Triggering Log In from `done` — sign-up already establishes the session.

ssr.note: Sessions live in browser storage; a server render always sees a logged-out user.

enrichment.summary: Reads the currently signed-in user: id, username, email, custom properties, and an authenticated boolean, kept live across session changes.
enrichment.description: User mirrors the current session's user. Its value outputs — `id`, `username`, `email` (strings) and one output per custom property on the User class — always reflect the signed-in user, and `authenticated` (boolean) is true exactly while a user is signed in. The node tracks the app-wide user service: it updates when Log In or Sign Up succeeds, when a stored session is restored, and when Log Out runs or the session is lost, so a single connection from `authenticated` can gate an entire logged-in UI. `changed` (signal) fires when the user's data changes. Triggering `fetch` (signal) re-reads the user from the server, firing `fetched` and then `done` on completion, or `failure` with `error` (string value) set; `completed` follows either way. `fetched` is the value-level announcement — the twin Record node fires it on binding too — and `done` is this invocation's outcome. It also works inside cloud functions, where it reflects the calling user's session.
enrichment.whenToUse: The one node to read who is logged in and their properties, anywhere in the app. It performs no actions — pair it with Log In, Sign Up, Log Out and Set User Properties for those.

ports.authenticated: Boolean value; true while a user is signed in. The canonical driver for logged-in/logged-out UI, including sessions restored on page load.
ports.fetch: Signal input; re-fetches the current user from the server (e.g. after another device may have changed it). While connected, the node suppresses its automatic per-change outputs and updates on fetch instead.
ports.fetched: Signal; fires when a `fetch` round-trip completes successfully.
ports.changed: Signal; fires when any property of the current user's data changes locally.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Beyond the static ports, the editor generates one value output per custom property in the User class schema (stored as `prop-<name>`, typed from the schema) plus a `changed-<name>` signal per property (built-ins authData/password/username/email are excluded — username and email have static outputs). In the browser it additionally registers the signal outputs `loggedIn` (Logged In), `loggedOut` (Logged Out) and `sessionLost` (Session Lost), which fire on the corresponding session transitions; these do not exist in the cloud runtime.
patterns: `authenticated` → a Group's `visible` (and through an inverter to the login form): one boolean drives both faces of the UI.
`loggedOut`/`sessionLost` signal outputs → navigation to the login page: handle forced sign-outs globally.
antiPatterns: Storing the user id in your own variable at login time — read `id` from this node instead so restored and switched sessions stay correct.

enrichment.summary: Responsive multi-column layout: distributes its children into columns whose relative widths come from a layout string.
enrichment.description: Columns lays out its visual children in a grid of columns described by `layoutString`: a space-separated list of relative widths, so '1 2 1' means three columns where the middle one is twice as wide as the outer ones (default '1 2 1'). Children fill the columns in order and wrap into further rows when there are more children than columns. `marginX` (Horizontal Gap) and `marginY` (Vertical Gap) set the spacing in pixels (default 16), and `minWidth` (Min Column Width) makes the layout responsive: when the container gets too narrow to honour the minimum, columns fold away and content reflows into fewer, wider columns. `direction` flips the fill order between row and column, and `justifyContent` aligns partial rows. The node warns in the editor if `layoutString` is bound to a non-string.
enrichment.whenToUse: Card grids, dashboards, magazine-style layouts — anywhere content should reflow across a variable number of columns. For a fixed row or column of items a plain Group with `flexDirection` is simpler; for one instance per data record put a For Each inside the Columns.

ports.layoutString: String value of space-separated relative widths, e.g. '1 2 1'. The number of entries is the column count; each entry is that column's share of the width.
ports.minWidth: Number value in px (Min Column Width, default 0): below this per-column width the layout folds columns away and reflows — this is what makes the grid responsive.
ports.marginX: Number value in px (Horizontal Gap) between columns.
ports.marginY: Number value in px (Vertical Gap) between wrapped rows.

patterns: Responsive card grid: layoutString '1 1 1' + `minWidth` ~200 so three columns collapse to two, then one, as the viewport narrows.
For Each inside Columns: repeated component instances distribute across the columns automatically.

enrichment.summary: Adds a user to a named permission role from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only — the only way an account gains privilege.
enrichment.description: Add User To Role writes a membership row linking `userId` to `role`. `Roles` (every role the user is now in) and `roleCreated` are read back through the same resolver a permission rule's `role:` check uses, so this cannot answer a role the access check would disagree with. A `role` that does not exist is a `failure` unless `createRole` is on — off by default on purpose, because a mistyped role name that silently gets created is a grant that names nobody: the rule that was meant to reference it still says the old, correct name. `userId` is required and there is deliberately no fallback to whoever called the function; wiring a request parameter straight into it turns this into 'grant any role to any account' with an HTTP endpoint in front, so gate the function with a `call` rule (CWF-017) and check the caller's own id before wiring it in.
enrichment.whenToUse: In a cloud function that provisions or escalates privilege: making a newly signed-up user a `member`, promoting someone to `staff`, adding a subscriber to a `pro` role after a payment webhook confirms it. Never reachable from a browser graph — that would be one wire from a button to self-granted admin.

ports.role: Value; required. Name of the role to add the user to, matching what a permission rule writes after `role:` — letters, digits, underscore and hyphen only.
ports.userId: Value; required. Which account to grant the role to. A blank id is a `failure`, never a fallback to the function's own caller.
ports.createRole: Edit-only boolean, default off. Creates the role if it does not exist yet instead of failing. Leave off so a typo is a loud Failure naming the bad role, rather than a role no permission rule will ever reference.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum, default Unchanged. Set it to Failure if a signup function re-running and finding the user already a member should stop the chain instead of carrying on.
ports.add: Signal (Do); writes the membership. Nothing happens until this fires.
ports.roles: Value; every role the user is in once this call settles, read from the same resolver a permission rule's access check uses — this cannot disagree with what a rule sees.
ports.roleCreated: Value; true when this call also created the role, worth branching on since a brand-new role is named by no permission rule yet.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the user is in the role and Roles lists it.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when the user was already in this role, with Roles still listing it — so a signup function re-run does not go red. Set Treat Unchanged As to Failure if a repeat should be treated as a bug.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the membership could not be written — a blank Role or User Id, a user id nothing resolves, or a role that does not exist with Create Role If Missing left off.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt, whatever the outcome.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed.

patterns: Wire straight after Create User in a signup function to put every new account into a default role like `member` — `unchanged` and `done` both mean the account is now in that role, so wiring both to the same next step covers a re-run cleanly.
antiPatterns: Wiring a request parameter straight into `userId` (or `role`) on a function anyone may call. That is 'grant any role to any account' with an HTTP endpoint in front of it — give the function a `call` rule (CWF-017) and check inside the graph that the caller is entitled to make this particular grant.

Leaving Create Role If Missing on as a default habit. It turns a mistyped role name into a role that exists, has one member, and is named by no permission rule — a grant that silently never takes effect.
