enrichment.summary: Aggregate Records: computes min/max/sum/avg/distinct over a database class server-side, inside a cloud function.
enrichment.description: Aggregate Records runs an aggregation query against a cloud database class without transferring the records. It only exists in the cloud runtime, so it is used inside cloud function components. Pick the class in `collectionName` (Class), optionally narrow the records with a visual or JavaScript filter, then declare named aggregates in the `aggregates` list: for each name you choose a property and an operation — Min/Max/Sum/Avg for number properties, Distinct for string properties — and get an output carrying the computed value. `fetched` (Success, signal) fires when results arrive; `failure` (signal) fires and `error` (string value) is set on failure. The node also fetches automatically when its configuration inputs change, unless an explicit fetch signal is connected.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for counts, sums, averages and distinct-value lists over many records — computing these server-side is the point. To read the records themselves use DbCollection2 (Query Records); browser logic must reach this node through a cloud function called via CloudFunction2.

ports.fetched: Signal (displayed 'Success'); fires after the aggregate outputs have been updated with fresh results.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the aggregation fails. Read `error` for the message.
ports.aggregates: Edit-only name list; each name creates a Property/Operation input pair and a result output. Names must not contain spaces or special characters.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Ports are generated from the node's parameters and the database schema: `collectionName` (edit-only class enum), a filter port set that mirrors Query Records (visual `visualFilter` with `qp-<name>` query-parameter inputs, or a JavaScript filter with `storageFilterValue-<name>` inputs), a `storageFetch` ('Do', signal) action input, and per aggregate name `aggprop-<name>`/`aggop-<name>` edit-only inputs plus an `agg-<name>` output typed number (Min/Max/Sum/Avg) or string (Distinct). When `storageFetch` is not connected, any change to class, filter or query parameters schedules a fetch automatically.
patterns: Request `receive` → `storageFetch`, `agg-<name>` → Response result inputs, `fetched` → Response `send`: a stats endpoint the browser calls with CloudFunction2.
antiPatterns: Querying all records with DbCollection2 and summing them in graph logic — aggregate server-side instead and return only the numbers.

enrichment.summary: Creates a user account from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only — it does not exist in the browser.
enrichment.description: Create User writes a new `_User` row on this backend's own database, with the authority of the server rather than of whoever called the function. Set `username` (the identity Log In looks accounts up by), optionally wire `password` and `email`, list any extra columns in `properties` to get one input per name, then pulse `create` (Do). On success `done` fires and `userId` holds the new account's id. It mints no session and returns no session token, so it is not Sign Up and cannot hand a caller a logged-in session for an account it just made. A password that is never wired means no password hash is stored at all — the invite/passwordless account BAK-004 describes — and no password can match until one is set.
enrichment.whenToUse: In a cloud function that provisions accounts: an invite flow, a bulk import, a signup that has to validate something server-side first, or a partner integration that creates users on your behalf. Do NOT use it for a person signing themselves up in your app — that is the browser's Sign Up node, which sets the session as it goes. ⚠️ A function containing this node must carry a `call` rule in the backend's Permissions panel (CWF-017). With no rule the function's Request node decides: `Allow Unauthenticated` ticked means the open internet may create accounts, and unticked means any signed-in user may.

ports.username: Value; required. The account's identity. A blank one is a `failure`, never a silently-skipped write.
ports.email: Value; optional, and NOT checked for uniqueness — this backend's signup route does not check it either.
ports.password: Value, connection-only; optional. Hashed by the backend with the same function Log In verifies against. It cannot be set as a parameter, because a typed password would live in the project file a deploy ships.
ports.emailVerified: Value; whether the account counts as verified. This node never sends a verification email. Leave it false for an account that should go through the normal verification flow; tick it for one that must be able to log in immediately on a backend with `requireForLogin` on.
ports.properties: Edit-only string list. Each name becomes a `prop-<name>` input for one `_User` column. A protected name is a `failure` naming the key, not a silent drop.
ports.create: Signal (Do); creates the account. Nothing is written until this fires.
ports.userId: Value; the new account's id after `done`, or the EXISTING account's id after `unchanged`. Blank after `failure`.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the account exists.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when a user with this username already exists. This is the specific 'already exists' branch — `userId` carries the existing account, so a provisioning function is idempotent in one wire.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the account could not be created. `error` says why.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt, whatever the outcome.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed. It never contains a password or a hash.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum; set it to Failure in a project whose idiom is that a duplicate signup is a bug.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Every name listed in the `properties` parameter mints one input port called `prop-<name>`, in the Properties group, typed `*`. The set is derived from that parameter alone — nothing is discovered from the backend's `_User` schema, and no editor connection or running backend is involved — so an authoring tool can compute the port list from the project file exactly as the editor does. Names are de-duplicated and blanks dropped. A `prop-` name the backend refuses (objectId, createdAt, updatedAt, ACL, password, sessionToken, or anything starting with `_`) still mints a port; the refusal happens at run time, on the `failure` branch, with the key named.
patterns: Request `receive` → Create User `create`, with the Request node's parameter outputs wired into `username` and `password`: the ordinary shape of a server-side provisioning function.
Wire `unchanged` to the same Response as `done` when the function's job is 'make sure this account exists'. `userId` is correct on both branches.
Wire `failure` somewhere that answers the caller. A function whose only wired path is the happy one hangs until its timeout (CWF-018) the first time a username is taken.
antiPatterns: Leaving the function without a `call` rule. A cloud function holding this node and answering `public` is account creation for the open internet.
Returning `userId` from a `public` function on the `unchanged` branch. That turns the function into a username-enumeration oracle: it answers 'this one exists' for any name a caller tries.

Reaching for this instead of the browser's Sign Up node. Sign Up signs the person in; this deliberately does not, and bolting a Log In onto the response is how a signup flow ends up with two sources of truth for the session.

inputs.name: remove
inputs.description: Deletes the account named by User Id, and every session it holds

inputs.name: treatUnchangedAs
inputs.description: What this node reports when the action was valid and there was nothing to do. Unchanged (the default) keeps it a third outcome of its own. Done suits a project whose chains should carry on either way; Failure suits one whose idiom is that a no-op is a bug. Completed fires whatever this is set to.

inputs.name: userId
inputs.description: Which account to delete. Required — this node never falls back to the caller, and a blank id is a Failure rather than the deletion of whoever is signed in

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the account and its sessions are gone

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed. It never contains a password, a hash or a token

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the account could not be deleted, including when User Id is blank

outputs.name: sessionsRevoked
outputs.description: How many sessions the deleted account held. Zero after Unchanged

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when there is no user with this id — the account is already absent, which is the goal met

enrichment.summary: Deletes a named user account and every session it holds, from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only.
enrichment.description: Delete User removes the `_User` row whose id you give it, and every `_Session` row belonging to it, with the authority of the server. Sessions go first and that ordering is deliberate: a deleted user whose sessions survived would leave tokens that resolve to a row the backend can no longer fetch. `sessionsRevoked` reports how many went, which is also the honest answer to 'was anybody actually signed in as them?'. `userId` is required — a blank one is a `failure`, never the deletion of whoever called.
enrichment.whenToUse: In a cloud function that closes accounts: a moderation action, an account-deletion request the user made in your app, or the cleanup half of a provisioning job. There is no browser equivalent and there deliberately is not one.

ports.userId: Value; required. Which account to delete. A blank one is a `failure`; this node never falls back to the caller.
ports.remove: Signal (Do); deletes the account and its sessions. Nothing is deleted until this fires.
ports.sessionsRevoked: Value; how many sessions the deleted account held. Zero after `unchanged`.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the account and its sessions are gone.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when there is no user with this id. Not a failure — the post-condition already holds, so a moderation job re-run after a partial failure does not go red on its second pass.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the account could not be deleted, including when `userId` is blank.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum; set it to Failure if 'that account was already gone' should stop the chain.

patterns: Wire `done` and `unchanged` to the same Response when the function's job is 'make sure this account is gone'. Both mean it is.
antiPatterns: Wiring a request parameter straight into `userId` on a function anyone may call. That is 'delete any account by id' with an HTTP endpoint in front of it — give the function a `call` rule (CWF-017) and check inside the graph that the caller is entitled to delete that particular account.
Expecting a blank `userId` to delete the caller's own account. It is a failure; read the caller's id from the Request node's `userId` output and wire it in explicitly, so the graph says what it does.

inputs.name: read
inputs.description: Reads the roles this user is in

inputs.name: treatUnchangedAs
inputs.description: What this node reports when the action was valid and there was nothing to do. Unchanged (the default) keeps it a third outcome of its own. Done suits a project whose chains should carry on either way; Failure suits one whose idiom is that a no-op is a bug. Completed fires whatever this is set to.

inputs.name: userId
inputs.description: Object id of the account to act on, usually wired from Create User or a Request parameter; blank is a Failure rather than a fallback to whoever called the function

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once Roles holds every role this user is in

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the roles could not be read — a blank User Id, or a user id nothing resolves

outputs.name: roles
outputs.description: Every role this user is in once the operation has finished, read back through the same resolver the access check itself uses

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when the user is in no roles at all, which is the branch a membership check wants

enrichment.summary: Reads every permission role a user is currently in, from inside a cloud function. Cloud-only and read-only — nothing is written.
enrichment.description: Get User Roles answers 'what is this account allowed to do' without making a change to find out. `Roles` comes from the same resolver a permission rule's `role:` check evaluates, so this cannot answer `member` while a rule disagrees — it is the actual check, not a second opinion on it. `unchanged` fires (rather than `done` with an empty array) when the user is in no roles at all, because that is the branch a membership check actually wants to take, and an empty array arriving on a `done` wire is easy to mistake for a port nobody connected.
enrichment.whenToUse: Whenever a cloud function needs to decide something based on what a user is allowed to do — gating a branch on `role:staff`, showing a different response to a `pro` subscriber, or verifying a role grant actually took before reporting success to the caller. Also the honest way to check 'did Add User To Role actually work' without trusting its own report.

ports.userId: Value; required. Which account's roles to read. A blank id is a `failure`, never a fallback to the function's own caller.
ports.read: Signal (Do); performs the read. Nothing happens until this fires.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum, default Unchanged. Set it to Failure if a user with no roles at all should be treated as a check failing rather than a distinct outcome.
ports.roles: Value; every role this user is in, read through the same resolver the access check itself uses.
ports.done: Signal; fires once Roles holds every role this user is in — including when that's more than zero.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when the user is in no roles at all — the branch a membership check wants, rather than an empty array silently arriving on Done.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the roles could not be read — a blank User Id, or a user id nothing resolves.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt, whatever the outcome.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed.

patterns: Read this after Add User To Role or Remove User From Role to confirm the membership actually changed, rather than trusting the mutation's own Done — useful when a function's response needs to report the account's current role set, not just that one operation succeeded.
antiPatterns: Re-deriving 'is this user staff' from a cached copy of Roles taken earlier in a long-running function instead of reading it fresh — roles can change between the start of a function and a later branch inside it.

inputs.name: algorithm
inputs.description: Which SHA-2 digest the HMAC is built on. HMAC-SHA256 is what almost every webhook uses

inputs.name: encoding
inputs.description: How the signature bytes are rendered as text. Match whatever the other side sends

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: The shared secret. Wire this from a Secret node — never type a credential into the graph

inputs.name: sign
inputs.description: Computes the signature of Value under Key

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: The message to sign, as UTF-8 bytes. For a webhook signature this is the raw request body

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the signature has been computed and is available on Signature

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why no signature was produced. It names the problem, never the key

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the signature could not be computed — most often no Key

outputs.name: signature
outputs.description: The HMAC of Value, rendered in Encoding. Available once Done has fired

enrichment.summary: Keyed SHA-2 signature of a string. Cloud-only, because it takes a shared secret.
enrichment.description: HMAC signs the text on Value with the secret on Key and puts the result on Signature, rendered in the chosen encoding. It is the primitive behind webhook signature verification (compute the HMAC of the raw request body and compare it to the header the sender supplied) and behind signing an outbound API request. It is registered only in the cloud runtime, and that is the point: every real use holds a shared secret, and a browser node whose Key input can only be filled from a literal or a fetch is a secret in the page. It shares one implementation with JWT Sign and JWT Verify, so a token this backend mints and a signature this node checks cannot drift apart.
enrichment.whenToUse: Verifying a Stripe, GitHub or supplier webhook; signing a request some API requires signed; minting a tamper-evident download token. Wire Key from a Secret node.

ports.value: The message to sign. For a webhook signature this must be the RAW body, byte for byte, not a re-serialised object.
ports.key: The shared secret. Wire this from a Secret node.
ports.algorithm: SHA-256 (default), SHA-384 or SHA-512. Almost every webhook uses SHA-256.
ports.encoding: hex (default), base64 or base64url. Match whatever the other side sends.
ports.signature: The HMAC, valid once Done has fired.
ports.done: Fires once Signature holds the result.
ports.failure: Fires when the signature could not be computed — most often no Key.
ports.error: Why no signature was produced. It names the problem, never the key.

patterns: Secret Done → HMAC Do, with Value wired from the Request node's raw body: the standard webhook-verification shape.
antiPatterns: Re-serialising the request body before signing it. Any difference in key order or whitespace changes the signature.
Typing the key into the graph. It ends up in the exported project; use a Secret node.

inputs.name: algorithm
inputs.description: Which HMAC signs the token. RS256 is not offered yet — it needs a key-import pass of its own

inputs.name: claims
inputs.description: The payload object. `iat` is always added; `exp` is added when Expires In is set. Anything you put here is readable by whoever holds the token — a JWT is signed, not encrypted

inputs.name: expiresIn
inputs.description: Seconds until the token expires, stamped as `exp`. Leave empty for a token with no expiry — which is a decision, not a default

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: The signing secret. Wire this from a Secret node — never type a credential into the graph

inputs.name: sign
inputs.description: Signs the claims and puts the token on Token

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the token has been signed and is available on Token

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why no token was produced. It names the problem, never the key

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the token could not be signed — no Key, or claims that will not serialise

outputs.name: token
outputs.description: The signed JWT, available once Done has fired

enrichment.summary: Mint a signed JSON Web Token (HS256/384/512). Cloud-only — signing in a browser means the key is in the browser.
enrichment.description: JWT Sign serialises the Claims object into a JWT signed with the secret on Key. It always stamps `iat`; it stamps `exp` only when Expires In is set, so a token with no expiry is something you chose rather than something that happened. A JWT is signed, not encrypted: everything in Claims is readable by whoever holds the token. RS256 is not offered in this pass — it needs a PEM key import, still with no dependency, and is a slice of its own.
enrichment.whenToUse: Issuing a short-lived token your own system will check later — a download link, a callback nonce, a hand-off to a partner who has your shared secret. To authenticate your own users, do not mint tokens here: the Request node already resolves the caller from their session.

ports.claims: The payload object. Readable by anyone holding the token — put identifiers in it, never secrets.
ports.key: The signing secret. Wire this from a Secret node.
ports.expiresIn: Seconds until the token expires, stamped as exp. Leave empty for a token that never expires.
ports.token: The signed JWT, valid once Done has fired.
ports.done: Fires once Token holds the signed token.
ports.failure: Fires when the token could not be signed — no Key, or claims that will not serialise.
ports.error: Why no token was produced.

patterns: Secret Done → JWT Sign Do, then Token into a URL or a response: the whole shape of a signed link.
antiPatterns: Putting a secret in Claims. The payload is base64, not encryption — anyone with the token can read it.
Leaving Expires In empty for a token that reaches a user's browser. A token with no expiry is valid until the key changes.

inputs.name: algorithm
inputs.description: The algorithm the token MUST have been signed with. A token whose header says anything else is refused unread — that is what stops alg:none and algorithm confusion

inputs.name: clockTolerance
inputs.description: Seconds of leeway on exp and nbf, for issuers whose clock is not quite yours

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: The shared secret the issuer signed with. Wire this from a Secret node

inputs.name: token
inputs.description: The JWT to check, without any "Bearer " prefix

inputs.name: verify
inputs.description: Checks the token

outputs.name: claims
outputs.description: The token payload — set ONLY after the signature verified. Nothing in a token can be believed before that, so this is left alone on a failure rather than handed over unchecked

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the token verified and Claims holds its payload

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the token did not verify

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the token did not verify, for any reason — expired, not yet valid, wrong key, wrong algorithm, tampered with, or malformed. Error says which

outputs.name: valid
outputs.description: Whether the token verified. False whenever Failure fired, so either can be wired

enrichment.summary: Check a JWT somebody else issued: signature, algorithm, exp and nbf. Not how you authenticate your own users.
enrichment.description: JWT Verify checks a token against the secret on Key and, only if it verifies, puts the payload on Claims. It refuses a token whose header names any algorithm other than the one you selected — which is what stops both `alg: none` and algorithm confusion — and it checks nbf and exp with an optional clock tolerance. Nothing in a token can be believed before the signature check, so Claims is left alone on any failure rather than handed over unchecked. IMPORTANT: this is for OTHER people's tokens — a partner's signed webhook, an OIDC id_token, a link your own backend minted with JWT Sign. Your own callers are already resolved: the Request node outputs Authenticated and User Id from the session token before the graph runs.
enrichment.whenToUse: A partner hands you a signed token; an identity provider returns an id_token; you are checking back a link you minted with JWT Sign. Never for your own session tokens.

ports.key: The secret the issuer signed with. Wire this from a Secret node.
ports.algorithm: The algorithm the token MUST carry. A token claiming anything else is refused unread.
ports.clockTolerance: Seconds of leeway on exp and nbf, for issuers whose clock is not quite yours. Default 0.
ports.valid: True when the token verified; false whenever Failure fired.
ports.claims: The payload — set only after the signature verified.
ports.done: Fires when the token verified.
ports.failure: Fires when it did not, for any reason. Error says which.
ports.error: Why the token did not verify.

patterns: Request receive → Secret Do → JWT Verify Do, with Failure wired to a Response that answers 401.
Wire both Done and Failure. A function that only wires the happy path hangs when the token is bad.
antiPatterns: Using this to authenticate your own app's users. The Request node's Authenticated and User Id already did that.
Reading Claims off the Failure path. It is deliberately not set there.

inputs.description: How many members to return in one call; Total still reports the whole membership, so a clipped page is always visible as one

inputs.name: read
inputs.description: Reads the members of the role

inputs.name: role
inputs.description: Name of the role to list the members of, matching the name a permission rule uses after "role:" — letters, digits, underscore and hyphen only

inputs.name: skip
inputs.description: How many members to step over before this page — Skip 100 with Limit 100 is the second page

inputs.name: treatUnchangedAs
inputs.description: What this node reports when the action was valid and there was nothing to do. Unchanged (the default) keeps it a third outcome of its own. Done suits a project whose chains should carry on either way; Failure suits one whose idiom is that a no-op is a bug. Completed fires whatever this is set to.

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once Users and User Ids hold this page of the role membership

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the members could not be read — a blank Role, an unusable name, or a role that does not exist

outputs.name: total
outputs.description: How many members the role has in total, before Limit — compare it with the length of Users to know whether there is another page

outputs.name: users
outputs.description: The member records for this page, shaped exactly like the account record /users/me answers with, so a For Each over them reads the same property names the User node does

enrichment.summary: Lists the accounts in a permission role, from inside a cloud function. Cloud-only and read-only — the inverse of Get User Roles.
enrichment.description: Get User Roles answers 'which roles is this user in'. List Users In Role answers the other direction: 'who is in this role'. Both walk the same membership junction, and until this node existed only one direction was reachable — so 'show me the member list', the most ordinary screen in a membership app, could not be built at all except by maintaining a separate collection that duplicates the role table and goes stale the first time somebody changes a membership by hand. `Users` holds the member records in the same shape the User node reads, so a For Each over them uses the same property names. `Total` is the whole membership before `Limit`, so a clipped page is always visible as one rather than silently looking like the complete roster. `unchanged` fires when the role exists and nobody has joined it; a role that does not exist is a `failure` naming it, because answering an empty list for a misspelled role draws the empty-community screen for a typo.
enrichment.whenToUse: Whenever a cloud function needs the membership of a role rather than the roles of a member — rendering a members directory or a staff list, counting how many people hold a subscription tier, or fanning a notification out to everyone in a role. Compare `Total` with the length of `Users` to decide whether to ask for another page.

ports.limit: Value, default 100. How many members to return in one call. Turning ids into records is one fetch each, so this is bounded rather than unlimited; `Total` still reports the whole membership.
ports.skip: Value, default 0. How many members to step over before this page — Skip 100 with Limit 100 is the second page.
ports.read: Signal (Do); performs the read. Nothing happens until this fires.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum, default Unchanged. Set it to Failure if an empty role should be treated as a check failing rather than a distinct outcome.
ports.users: Value; the member records for this page, shaped like the account record /users/me answers with.
ports.userIds: Value; object ids of the members in this page, in the same order as Users.
ports.total: Value; how many members the role has in total, before Limit.
ports.done: Signal; fires once Users and User Ids hold this page of the membership.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when the role exists and has no members at all — the 'nobody has joined yet' branch.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the members could not be read — a blank Role, an unusable name, or a role that does not exist.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt, whatever the outcome.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed.

patterns: Put this behind a cloud function whose call rule names the role that may see the roster — a member list is other people's account records, and a cloud function runs as system, so the function's own permission rule is the only thing deciding who may read it.
Page a large role by wiring Skip from a page counter and comparing Total against the running count of rows already shown, rather than assuming one call returned everybody.
antiPatterns: Rendering Users straight onto a public page without a call rule on the function — the graph's Allow Unauthenticated port is what applies when no rule is written, and ticked means the whole membership roster is readable by anyone on the internet.
Treating the length of Users as the membership count; it is the size of one page, and Total is the number that answers 'how many members are there'.

inputs.name: treatUnchangedAs
inputs.description: What this node reports when the action was valid and there was nothing to do. Unchanged (the default) keeps it a third outcome of its own. inputs.name: userId
inputs.description: Object id of the account to act on, usually wired from Create User or a Request parameter; blank is a Failure rather than a fallback to whoever called the function

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the user is out of the role and Roles no longer lists it

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the membership could not be removed — a blank Role or User Id, or a store that would not write

outputs.name: roles

outputs.name: unchanged

enrichment.summary: Takes a user out of a named permission role from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only — the other half of Add User To Role.
enrichment.description: Remove User From Role deletes the membership row linking `userId` to `role`, so the app can revoke a privilege it once granted — a subscription lapsing, a moderator being stood down. `unchanged` covers two different post-conditions that both mean 'they are not in it': the user was never a member, or the role does not exist at all; `Error` says which, for a function that wants to tell them apart, while `Roles` and every wired-through branch treat them the same. Removing a role membership does **not** end that user's existing sessions — a session token is not a copy of the roles it had at sign-in, so the very next request that token makes already resolves the shorter list. There is no cache to invalidate and nothing to revoke separately.
enrichment.whenToUse: In a cloud function that de-provisions or downgrades access: ending a lapsed subscription's `pro` role, removing a stood-down moderator from `staff`. A de-provisioning job can safely re-run — both `unchanged` branches mean the desired end state already holds, the same reading Delete User gives an account id that is already gone.

ports.role: Value; required. Name of the role to take the user out of, matching what a permission rule writes after `role:`.
ports.userId: Value; required. Which account to remove the role from. A blank id is a `failure`, never a fallback to the function's own caller.
ports.remove: Signal (Do); writes the removal. Nothing happens until this fires.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum, default Unchanged. Set it to Failure if a de-provisioning job finding the user already out of the role should stop the chain instead of carrying on.
ports.roles: Value; every role the user is in once this call settles, read from the same resolver a permission rule's access check uses.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the user is out of the role and Roles no longer lists it.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when the user was not in this role, or the role does not exist at all — so a de-provisioning job re-run does not go red. Error says which of the two it was.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the membership could not be removed — a blank Role or User Id, or a store that would not write.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt, whatever the outcome.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed, or (on Unchanged) which of the two non-membership cases it was.

patterns: Wire a lapsed-subscription webhook straight to this node's `remove`, with `done` and `unchanged` both leading to the same next step — the account ends up without the role either way, which is the only thing that response needs to be true.
antiPatterns: Assuming removing a role also signs the user out of an active session. It does not — the next request that session's token makes already sees the shorter role list, but the session itself stays valid until it expires or is separately revoked.

inputs.name: params

enrichment.summary: Entry point of a cloud function component: receives the call's parameters and fires Received to start the server-side flow.
enrichment.description: Request is the entry node of a cloud function — it only exists in the cloud runtime, and a component containing one becomes callable from the browser through a Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) node. Declare the function's parameters as a name list in `params`; each name becomes an output carrying the value the caller sent, and a matching `in-<name>` input appears on the browser-side caller. When a call arrives the node checks authentication (rejecting unauthenticated calls unless `allowNoAuth` is true), publishes each parameter, then fires `receive` (Received, signal) — wire that signal into your logic and end the flow at a Response node. The caller's identity, parameters and headers are also placed on a 'Request' model readable elsewhere in the function.
enrichment.whenToUse: Place exactly one at the start of every cloud function component. It is meaningless in browser components — there, use Component Inputs for inputs and CloudFunction2 to call the function.

ports.receive: Signal; fires once per incoming call, after authentication has been checked and all parameter outputs hold the call's values. Start the function's logic from here.
ports.allowNoAuth: Boolean value (default false). When false, calls without a valid user session are rejected before the graph runs.
ports.auth: Boolean value; true when the call carried a valid user session.
ports.userId: Value holding the authenticated caller's user id (undefined for unauthenticated calls); use it to scope queries to the calling user.
ports.params: Edit-only name list declaring the function's parameters; drives both this node's outputs and the caller's inputs. Each name also gets three declaration rows in the Parameter Types group — Type, Required and Default — which together are the function's request contract (CWF-014). Leaving them alone is the behaviour every function had before that task: every parameter is Any, and optional.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Each name in the `params` stringlist becomes a runtime-registered output (stored as `pm-<name>`) holding that parameter's value from the current call. The same list is what CloudFunctionAdapter mirrors onto browser-side CloudFunction2 callers as `in-<name>` inputs, so editing `params` changes both sides. CWF-014: a name may also carry `ptype-<name>` (one of *, string, number, boolean, object, array, date), `preq-<name>` and `pdef-<name>`. When any of those is set the node checks the request body BEFORE the graph runs — a missing required field, or a value the declared type cannot take, is answered as HTTP 400 naming the field, and the graph does not run at all. A value the declared type can take losslessly is coerced first, so "42" reaches a number-typed output as the number 42, and an omitted parameter with a Default arrives holding it. A declared type also becomes the `pm-<name>` output's port type, so the wire out of it is checked like any other.
patterns: `receive` → your logic → Response `send`: every cloud function is this shape; the reply is not sent until a Response node sends it.
`userId` → a query filter parameter: trust the session-derived id, never an id passed in `params`, for per-user data.
antiPatterns: Leaving `allowNoAuth` false and then calling the function from a logged-out browser session — the call is rejected before `receive` ever fires.
Ticking Required on a parameter and giving it a Default too: the default wins and the request is never refused, which is almost certainly not what the tick meant.

Checking the request body inside the graph with Condition nodes and answering through a Response node with Status = Failure: that is a graph that ran. Declare the type on the parameter instead, and the request never starts.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Message returned to the caller; used only when Status is Failure

inputs.name: params
inputs.description: Names to return in the response body, each becoming an input to supply it

inputs.name: send
inputs.description: Sends the response and ends the request, which can only happen once

inputs.name: status
inputs.description: Whether the caller gets a 200 carrying Parameters or a 400 carrying Error Message

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires as the response goes out, and before the request scope is torn down

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the response could not be sent

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the response could not be sent, because there is no request in scope or one was already answered

dynamicPorts.description: Input ports mirror the result values declared for the cloud function (one input per response value).

declaredPortGroups.condition: status = success OR status NOT SET
declaredPortGroups.name: conditionalports/extended
