variables.param: one of the comma-separated entries in the `params` parameter

enrichment.summary: Exit point of a cloud function component: collects result values and sends the reply back to the caller.
enrichment.description: Response ends a cloud function — it only exists in the cloud runtime. Declare the function's result values as a name list in `params`; each name becomes an input to feed, and a matching `out-<name>` output appears on the browser-side Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) caller. Triggering `send` (Send, signal) replies to the pending call: with `status` 'success' (the default) it returns HTTP 200 with the collected result values, with `status` 'failure' it returns HTTP 400 carrying `errorMessage`, which the caller surfaces on its `error` output before firing `failure`. A function can contain several Response nodes — for example one success and one failure path — but exactly one should send per call.
enrichment.whenToUse: End every path through a cloud function with one. Without a `send`, the caller's request never completes. In browser components use Component Outputs instead.

ports.send: Signal input; sends the reply for the current call using the current status, result values and error message. Trigger it exactly once per call.
ports.status: Enum value 'success' or 'failure' (default 'success'); selects between a 200 reply with results and a 400 reply with `errorMessage`, and switches which inputs the editor shows.
ports.errorMessage: String value returned to the caller when `status` is 'failure'; it appears on the caller's `error` output.
ports.params: Edit-only name list declaring the result values; drives both this node's inputs and the caller's outputs.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Each name in the `params` stringlist becomes a runtime-registered input (stored as `pm-<name>`, type '*') collected into the success reply. Declared port groups make the ports conditional on `status`: `params` (and its `pm-` inputs) exist while status is 'success' or unset, `errorMessage` exists while status is 'failure'. CloudFunctionAdapter mirrors the union of all Response nodes' `params` onto the browser-side caller as `out-<name>` outputs.
patterns: Two Response nodes — one with status 'success', one with status 'failure' and an `errorMessage` — triggered from the two branches of a Condition: explicit success/failure replies.
Feed `pm-` inputs as values as your logic computes them; only `send` decides when the reply goes out.
antiPatterns: Finishing a function path without triggering any Response `send` — the browser-side caller hangs until the request times out.

inputs.name: fetch
inputs.description: Reads the secret and puts it on Value

inputs.name: name
inputs.description: Which stored secret to read. A cloud function can only ever read the project's own secrets — the backend's webhook, email, auth and admin credentials are not addressable from here

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the secret has been read and is available on Value

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the secret could not be read — names the secret and where to put it, never a value

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the secret is not provisioned on this machine, or the Name is unusable. A missing credential is loud here rather than an empty string that becomes a 401 from somebody else an hour later

outputs.name: value
outputs.description: The secret, available once Done has fired. Blank until then, and blank after a Failure

enrichment.summary: Reads one of the project's stored credentials by name, inside a cloud function. Cloud-only — it does not exist in the browser.
enrichment.description: Secret is the door to a stored credential from inside a cloud function. Set Name to the secret you want, pulse Do, and the value appears on Value with Done. The backend resolves the name against the `functions` section of its machine-local `secrets.json`, then falls back to a `NODEGX_SECRET_<NAME>` environment variable — the project author's own credentials, and nothing else: the backend's webhook, email, auth and admin credentials are not addressable from a graph at all. A name that resolves to nothing is a Failure with a message naming the secret and the two places to put it, never an empty string — a silently missing credential turns into somebody else's 401 an hour later. This node is registered only in the cloud runtime: a Secret node in a browser bundle would be a secret in a browser bundle.
enrichment.whenToUse: Whenever a cloud function calls a third-party API, signs something, or otherwise needs a credential. Wire Value straight into the HTTP Request node's header or the HMAC / JWT Sign node's Key — do not copy the credential into a parameter, a Function node script or a Response.

ports.name: The secret's name: 1-128 characters from letters, digits, '_', '.' and '-'. Only the name lives in the graph, so nothing here reaches the exported project.
ports.fetch: Signal (Do); reads the secret. Nothing is read until this fires.
ports.value: The secret, valid once Done has fired. Blank before that and blank after a Failure.
ports.error: Why the read failed — names the secret and where to provision it. It never contains a value.
ports.done: Fires once Value holds the secret.
ports.failure: Fires when the secret is not provisioned on this machine or Name is unusable.
ports.completed: Fires after every read, whatever the outcome.

patterns: Request `receive` → Secret `fetch`; Secret `done` → HTTP Request `fetch`, with Value wired into the Authorization header: the ordinary shape of calling a paid API from the server.
Wire `failure` somewhere that answers the caller. A function whose only wired path is the happy one hangs forever when the credential is missing (CWF-018).
antiPatterns: Wiring Value into a Response node's parameter. That writes the credential into your own API's reply — the one leak this node cannot prevent for you.
Reading a secret with a Function node and `process.env` instead. It works, but the name is then invisible to every tool that reads the graph.

inputs.name: html
inputs.description: HTML body sent alongside Text Body; optional, and ignored when Template is set

inputs.name: send
inputs.description: Sends the message

inputs.name: subject
inputs.description: Subject line of the message, and ignored when Template is set

inputs.name: template
inputs.description: Which stored template to render, or None to use Subject, Text Body and HTML Body instead

inputs.name: text
inputs.description: Plain-text body of the message, and ignored when Template is set

inputs.name: to
inputs.description: Address the message goes to; the send fails outright when this is blank

inputs.name: variables
inputs.description: Values substituted into the template placeholders, and ignored when Template is None

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the mail server has accepted the message for delivery

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the message could not be sent

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the message could not be sent, including when no mail service is configured

enrichment.summary: Sends an email through the backend's configured SMTP server from inside a cloud function or workflow.
enrichment.description: Send Email is a server-side-only action node (it only runs inside a cloud function, never in a browser component). Wire `send` to fire it: it either renders one of the backend's built-in templates (Password Reset, Verify Email) against the `variables` object, or sends the raw `subject`/`text`/`html` inputs directly. The send is synchronous from the graph's point of view — `done` or `failure` fires once the attempt (plus one automatic retry on transient failure) has finished. If the backend has no SMTP configured, or this component is somehow evaluated outside a nodegx-backend process, it fails loudly on `failure`/`error` — it never drops a send silently or queues it for later.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it wherever a workflow needs to notify someone by email — a signup confirmation, an order receipt, an internal alert. Do not use it for the account password-reset/verify-email flows the backend already runs (BAK-002) — those are automatic; wire this node only for YOUR OWN application notifications.

ports.template: 'none' sends the Subject/Text/HTML inputs as-is; 'passwordReset'/'verifyEmail' render the backend's built-in templates instead and ignore Subject/Text/HTML.
ports.variables: An object of `{{name}}` values for template interpolation; only read when Template is not 'none'.
ports.send: Signal; fires the send attempt (with its one documented retry on failure).
ports.error: The failure message, e.g. "Email is not configured for this backend..." — always a specific, actionable string, never a generic failure.

patterns: Request `receive` → Send Email `send` → Response `send`: a fire-and-notify cloud function, the same shape as the Request/Response round trip but with a side effect instead of (or in addition to) a computed value.
antiPatterns: Wiring this into a browser component — it has no effect there (no `_noodl_send_email` exists outside nodegx-backend) and the failure is confusing without knowing this node is cloud-only.
Assuming a fired `sent` means the recipient's inbox will show it soon — deliverability (SPF/DKIM/provider reputation) is the operator's SMTP provider's job, not this node's.

inputs.name: password
inputs.description: A new password for this account, hashed by the backend. Setting one revokes EVERY session this user has, including one that may be calling this function. Leave it unwired to change properties only. Connection-only — a password must not live in a project file

inputs.name: properties
inputs.description: Names of the user columns this node writes, each becoming an input to supply the value. A name the backend refuses — objectId, ACL, password, sessionToken, or anything starting with "_" — is a Failure naming the key, never a silent drop

inputs.name: store
inputs.description: Writes the values below to the account named by User Id

inputs.name: userId
inputs.description: Which account to change. Required — this node never falls back to the caller, and a blank id is a Failure rather than a write to whoever is signed in

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires once the account has been written

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed. It never contains a password, a hash or a token

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the account could not be written — a blank or unknown User Id, a property the backend refuses, or a username already taken by somebody else

outputs.name: sessionsRevoked
outputs.description: How many of this user's sessions the last write ended. Non-zero only when a Password was supplied

dynamicPorts.description: Declares conditional/expandable port groups whose visibility depends on parameter values (see declaredPortGroups). Some ports are discovered at runtime from user code, parameters or connected components, and are pushed to the editor per instance; the static port list below is incomplete for such instances.

parameterEncoding.reason: The port helper needs project context this generator cannot supply headlessly — a live component, a connected node, or a backend schema.

enrichment.summary: Writes properties (and optionally a new password) to a NAMED user from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only.
enrichment.description: Update User is Set User Properties' server-side sibling, and the difference is the whole point: Set User Properties writes to whoever is signed in and fails when nobody is, while this one writes to the account whose id you give it, with the authority of the server. `userId` is required — a blank one is a `failure` with a sentence saying so, and never a fallback to the caller, because the failure mode this split exists to prevent is 'accidentally edited the caller instead of the target'. List the columns to write in `properties` to get one input per name, pulse `store` (Do), and `done` fires once the row is written.
enrichment.whenToUse: In a cloud function that moderates or administers accounts: suspending a user, changing a plan after a webhook from a payment provider, resetting a password on request, correcting an imported record. Use the browser's Set User Properties node when a signed-in person is editing their own profile — that is the caller's own authority and does not belong on the server.

ports.userId: Value; required. Which account to write to. A blank one is a `failure`; this node never falls back to the caller.
ports.password: Value, connection-only; optional. A new password for the account, hashed by the backend. ⚠️ Setting one revokes EVERY session this user holds, including one that may be calling this function — there is no session that authorized the change, so there is no survivor to spare.
ports.properties: Edit-only string list. Each name becomes a `prop-<name>` input for one `_User` column. A protected name is a `failure` naming the key. Changing `username` to one another account already holds is a `failure` too, because Log In resolves accounts by username.
ports.store: Signal (Do); writes the values. Nothing is written until this fires.
ports.sessionsRevoked: Value; how many sessions the last write ended. Non-zero only when a password was supplied.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the account has been written.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the write could not happen — blank or unknown id, a refused property, or a username collision. There is no `unchanged`: nothing diffs the row first, and an update aimed at a user that does not exist is a mistake rather than a goal already met.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every attempt.
ports.error: Value; why the last write failed. It never contains a password or a hash.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Every name listed in the `properties` parameter mints one input port called `prop-<name>`, in the Properties group, typed `*`. The set comes from that parameter alone — nothing is read from the backend's `_User` schema and no editor connection is involved — so an authoring tool can derive the port list from the project file. Names are de-duplicated and blanks dropped; a refused name still mints a port and fails at run time with the key named.
patterns: Request `receive` → Update User `store`, with the target's id arriving as a request parameter: the shape of every 'admin acts on account X' function.
Wire `sessionsRevoked` into the response when the function resets a password, so the caller knows the user was signed out everywhere.
antiPatterns: Leaving `userId` unwired and expecting it to mean 'the current user'. It does not, and it never will — that node is Set User Properties, in the browser.
Putting this node in a function with no `call` rule. A function that can change any account's password is a function that must name who may call it (CWF-017).

inputs.name: token
inputs.description: The session token to check, as it arrived in the request body. Not the caller's own — that is already resolved on the Request node's Authenticated and User Id. Connection-only, because a token in a project file is a credential in a project file

inputs.name: treatUnchangedAs
inputs.description: What this node reports when the action was valid and there was nothing to do. Unchanged (the default) keeps it a third outcome of its own. Done suits a project whose chains should carry on either way; Failure suits one whose idiom is that a no-op is a bug. Completed fires whatever this is set to.

inputs.name: verify
inputs.description: Checks the token. Nothing is checked, and nothing is written, until this fires

outputs.name: completed
outputs.description: Fires after every invocation, whatever the outcome — wire this to carry on regardless. Failure still fires and still carries its reason, so this cannot hide an error

outputs.name: done
outputs.description: Fires when the token is a live session — Valid is true and User Id holds whose it is

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Why the last operation could not be performed. It never contains a password, a hash or a token

outputs.name: failure
outputs.description: Fires when the check could not be made at all, such as a blank Token

outputs.name: unchanged
outputs.description: Fires when the token is not a live session on this backend. Nothing failed and nothing changed; the answer is simply no, and this is the branch to wire to your 401

outputs.name: userId
outputs.description: Whose session it is, after Done. Blank on every other branch

outputs.name: username
outputs.description: That user's username, after Done. Blank on every other branch

outputs.name: valid
outputs.description: Whether the token is a live session. The value form of the Done / Unchanged branch

enrichment.summary: Asks this backend whether a session token is one of its own live sessions, and whose. Cloud-only.
enrichment.description: Verify Session Token looks a token up in this backend's `_Session` table and answers who holds it. It is for a token that arrived in the request BODY — from a mobile client, a partner integration, a callback — not the caller's own, which the Request node has already resolved onto `auth` (Authenticated) and `userId` (User Id). ⚠️ This is not CWF-010's JWT Verify: that node verifies somebody else's JWT against a key you hold, while this one asks our own backend about our own session. Only a session matches — an admin credential is not a session and an API key is not a session, so neither can be probed through this node. There is no expiry to report: this backend's session rows carry a token and a user id and nothing else, and a session lives until a password change or a delete revokes it.
enrichment.whenToUse: When a cloud function receives a token it did not get as its own caller's credential and has to decide whether to trust it — a mobile client posting a token in a body, a partner passing a user's token through, a webhook that carries one. Reach for JWT Verify instead when the token was minted somewhere else and is signed with a key. Do not reach for either to check the caller's own session; that is already done.

ports.token: Value, connection-only; the token to check. It cannot be set as a parameter, because a session token in a project file is a live credential in a project file.
ports.verify: Signal (Do); performs the lookup. Nothing is checked, and nothing is ever written, until this fires.
ports.valid: Value; whether the token is a live session. The value form of the `done` / `unchanged` branch.
ports.userId: Value; whose session it is, after `done`. Blank on every other branch — it is cleared before each check, so a stale identity cannot sit on the port while the next answer is in flight.
ports.username: Value; that user's username, after `done`. Blank on every other branch.
ports.done: Signal; fires when the token is a live session.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when the token is not a live session. Nothing failed and nothing changed — the answer is simply no, and this is the branch to wire to your 401.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the check could not be made at all, such as a blank token.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after every check.
ports.error: Value; why a check could not be made. It never contains a token.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum; set it to Failure if an invalid token should take the same path as a broken check.

patterns: Request `receive` → Verify Session Token `verify`, with the body's token wired into `token`; `done` → the work, `unchanged` → a Response with Status set to Failure. That is the whole shape of a token-checked endpoint.
antiPatterns: Putting this in a `public` function. It is an oracle for session tokens by design, so an unauthenticated caller behind an open rule can test tokens at whatever rate the limiter allows. Give the function a `call` rule and a per-function `rateLimit` (CWF-017).
Using it to re-check the caller's own token. The Request node has already resolved it; a second lookup is a database round trip that answers a question already answered.
Confusing it with JWT Verify. Verifying our own session token as if it were a JWT will never succeed, and verifying somebody else's JWT here will always answer `unchanged`.

compatibility.$comment: Connection-compatibility semantics (SUB-005). The permitted-cast TABLE lives in the structural catalog (node-catalog.json#/typecasts) and is exported by the runtime itself (packages/noodl-runtime/src/nodelibraryexport.js); this file documents what the rules and each cast MEAN. scripts/node-catalog/merge.js fails if castSemantics ever drifts from the catalog table, and asserts every verifiedPairs entry against the rule implementation.

rules.gate: The editor permits a connection from output type F to input type T iff: F === T, or F === '*', or T === '*', or the typecast table has an entry {from: F, to: [... T ...]}. This is NodeLibrary.canCastPortTypes (packages/noodl-editor/src/editor/src/models/nodelibrary/nodelibrary.ts).
rules.wildcard: The type '*' (untyped) connects to and from anything. Many dynamic ports (Function/Expression outputs, Object properties) are untyped; the editor will accept any wiring to them, so correctness is the author's responsibility.
rules.delivery: The runtime performs no central value conversion on delivery: the raw output value is handed to the receiving input, whose setter coerces it (usually with plain JavaScript semantics). A permitted cast means 'the receiver knows what to do with this', not 'a converter runs on the wire'.
rules.allowConnectionsOnly: Ports typed with allowConnectionsOnly can only be driven by a connection, never set statically via parameters.
rules.allowEditOnly: Ports typed with allowEditOnly can only be set via parameters, never connected.

signalSemantics.firing: A signal output fires by sending the value true immediately followed by false (Node.prototype.sendSignalOnOutput, packages/noodl-runtime/src/node.js). A signal is a momentary event with no payload.
signalSemantics.receiving: A signal input triggers when its incoming value transitions to true (valueChangedToTrue) — it is edge-triggered, not level-sensitive. Holding a value at true does not re-trigger.
signalSemantics.suppression: A signal output that already fired in the current update cycle is suppressed from firing again until the cycle completes, preventing infinite loops within one frame.
signalSemantics.authoring: Wire signals to signals ('On Click' → 'Do'). Wiring a boolean to a signal input is legal and means 'trigger once on the rising edge'. Wiring a signal to a boolean input is legal and delivers a true-then-false pulse — useful for momentary states, wrong for latching ones.

castSemantics.string→number: Receiver coerces with JavaScript numeric conversion; non-numeric strings become NaN. Prefer a Number value if the source is numeric to begin with.
castSemantics.string→boolean: JavaScript truthiness: empty string is false, any other string (including 'false') is true.
castSemantics.string→image: The string is used as an image source: a project asset path or a URL.
castSemantics.string→color: The string is used as a color value: a project style-color name or any CSS color string ('#ff0000', 'rgba(0,0,0,0.5)').
castSemantics.string→enum: The string must equal one of the input's enum values (the value, not the label); anything else leaves the input unchanged or misconfigured.
castSemantics.string→textStyle: The string names a project text style.
castSemantics.string→dimension: Parsed as a CSS dimension: a bare number is treated as px; '50%' selects percent units.
castSemantics.string→array: The string is passed through unchanged. This cast exists for inputs that accept a named/shared collection id in place of an actual array (legacy Collection semantics). Do not expect JSON parsing.
castSemantics.string→object: The string is passed through unchanged. This cast exists for inputs that accept a Model/Object id in place of the object itself; the receiver resolves the id to the shared object.
castSemantics.boolean→number: true → 1, false → 0 by JavaScript coercion in the receiver.
castSemantics.boolean→signal: Edge trigger: the signal input fires once each time the boolean transitions from false to true. A boolean that is already true when connected does not fire it retroactively.
castSemantics.number→boolean: JavaScript truthiness: 0 and NaN are false, everything else true.
castSemantics.number→string: Decimal string form of the number.
castSemantics.number→dimension: The number is used as a pixel value.
castSemantics.date→string: The receiver converts the Date with JavaScript string coercion.
castSemantics.signal→boolean: The boolean input receives a true-then-false pulse each time the signal fires. Use for momentary behaviour only; the value does not stay true.
castSemantics.signal→number: The number input receives 1 then 0 each firing (boolean pulse coerced numerically). Rarely what you want; prefer States or a Counter.
castSemantics.cloudfile→string: The cloud file's URL as a string.
castSemantics.cloudfile→image: The cloud file is used as an image source (its URL).
castSemantics.textStyle→string: The text style's name as a string.
castSemantics.collection→array: Collection (legacy shared-list type) and array are interchangeable: the same underlying list object flows through unchanged.
castSemantics.array→collection: Array and collection (legacy shared-list type) are interchangeable: the same underlying list object flows through unchanged.
castSemantics.object→string: The runtime serialises with JSON.stringify before the receiver's cast runs (NDA-014, PORT-TYPE-CONTRACT.md). Values with their own toString (e.g. Date) keep that rendering; circular structures deliver '' and raise a warning.
castSemantics.array→string: The runtime serialises with JSON.stringify before the receiver's cast runs (NDA-014, PORT-TYPE-CONTRACT.md). Circular structures deliver '' and raise a warning.
castSemantics.color→string: The resolved color string — a style name resolves to its value (context.styles.resolveColor) before crossing the wire.

verifiedPairs.$comment: Sampled pairs asserted by scripts/node-catalog/merge.js against the gate rule + the catalog typecast table on every merge/check. 'permitted' must pass canCastPortTypes; 'rejected' must fail it.

permitted.note: rising-edge trigger — the idiomatic 'run when this becomes true'
must match an enum value exactly

rejected.note: numbers do not edge-trigger; go via boolean
date only casts to string; use an Expression for timestamps
strings never trigger signals; go via boolean

examples.title: Show a change immediately, then let the server confirm or reject it
examples.description: Optimistic Update writes the new value into the store the moment the user acts, so the UI never waits for a round trip, and keeps what the key held before so a failure can put it back. `Apply` opens the update and hands you a `transactionId`; carry that id through the request and hand it back to `Commit` or `Rollback` so an out-of-order response resolves the right update — several can be in flight, which is what `pendingCount` reports. Wire the server's message into `errorMessage` so a rollback can explain itself instead of being generically 'failed'. Two behaviours worth knowing before you rely on this: `timeout` (30 s by default, `0` to disable) rolls the update back on its own if no answer arrives, firing `rolledBack` and then `timedOut`; and if something else wrote the key after the update was applied, a rollback **keeps the newer value** rather than reverting on top of it — the transaction still resolves as rolled back, and `error` says the value was left alone. `value` is the live store key, not a remembered copy, which is exactly why that check is possible. Note that the request has **three** outcomes, not two: `done` commits and `failure` rolls back, but a request that was cancelled reports `unchanged`, and without a wire for it the update would sit open until its own deadline expired. It rolls back too, because the write never reached the server.

parameters.errorMessage: The server would not accept that name.

examples.title: Agent actions: let a backend drive the UI, but only where you allowed it
examples.description: The idiomatic shape for a backend that sends commands rather than data. Server-Sent Events delivers action objects; Action Dispatcher decides whether each one may run. The vocabulary is closed: `OPEN_SESSION` runs because the Action Handler registered it, `SET_STORE` runs because it is named in `builtIns` and its key is in `allowedKeys`, and anything else is refused with a reason on `refusalReason` — which is wired to a Text node, because a refusal nobody can see is the failure mode this whole design exists to avoid. The handler has `autoComplete` off and completes only once its Set Global Store finished, so an array of actions runs as an ordered flow rather than all at once.

examples.title: Agent chat: stream an AI answer token by token
examples.description: The core agentic-UI wiring. Server-Sent Events POSTs the prompt with an Authorization header — which needs the Fetch transport, since EventSource can neither POST nor set headers — and each streamed token lands on `text`. `text` and not `data`: `data` is JSON-parsed, so for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint it is an object, and `textPath` here (`choices.0.delta.content`) is what turns that envelope into the token. For an endpoint that streams bare text, leave `textPath` blank and `text` is the payload as sent. Text Accumulator collects the tokens with an empty delimiter, so `accumulated` is the answer as it is being written, and `changed` repaints the Text node. `connectionState` drives a status label, so a reconnection is visible rather than looking like a stalled answer, and `onOpen` clears the accumulator when a new response starts.

examples.title: Long-running task monitor: progress, batched log lines, and a visible connection
examples.description: A backend job streams two kinds of frame on one connection. Pattern Extractor pulls the percentage out of human-readable status text, so a progress bar tracks it without a Function node. JSON Stream Parser turns NDJSON log payloads into values — several may complete in one frame, so `values` rather than `parsed` is what feeds downstream. Stream Buffer batches those into a flush every 250 ms, which keeps a busy log from repainting the list hundreds of times a second, and the stream's `onClose` flushes the tail that never reached a full batch.

examples.title: Undo, redo and a named checkpoint over a global store key
examples.description: State History watches one key of a store and records an entry per commit; `coalesceMs` folds a burst of keystrokes into a single undo step, so typing is one step rather than one per character. Undo / Redo drives that history by store name — it owns nothing itself, which is why a store nothing is tracking is reported on `error` instead of being a button that silently does nothing. `canUndo` / `canRedo` are how a graph asks in advance, because undo at the beginning and redo at the end are no-ops rather than errors. An undo is an ordinary store commit, so Subscribe to Store repaints from it exactly as it would from any other write. State Snapshot is the separate idea: saving a checkpoint does not touch the undo stack, but restoring one is an ordinary write and is therefore itself undoable. `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` are on both nodes because a snapshot keeps live objects (a Model, an Array/Collection, a class instance) by reference, so those keys are only partly restorable and the app should be able to say so.

examples.title: Shared state: one store read by two unrelated components
examples.description: Two components that are not parent and child, sharing state through a named store instead of prop drilling or a Send/Receive Event pair. Sign In writes `user` with Set Global Store; Header declares the same store by name and renders `state` — no wiring runs between the two components, because naming the store is what connects them. Header also subscribes to just the `user` key, so a write to any other key does not wake it, and uses `previousValue` against `value` to fire only on the signed-out → signed-in transition rather than on every change. Initial State fills gaps without overwriting live state, so Header remounting cannot reset a store Sign In is already using.

examples.title: Hover highlight: Animate To Value driving a Color Blend
examples.description: The smooth-hover idiom: the card's `hoverStart`/`hoverEnd` signals flip a Switch, whose boolean (cast to 0/1) becomes the `targetValue` of Animate To Value — the node tweens `currentValue` toward the target whenever it changes. That animated 0→1 feeds Color Blend's `blendValue`, interpolating between its configured colors, and the result drives the card background. State, easing and color are three separate concerns in three small nodes.

examples.title: States: a collapsible panel with transitioned values
examples.description: States is the interaction state machine: the `states` parameter names the states ('collapsed,expanded'), the `values` parameter names the outputs each state assigns ('panelHeight'), and with `useTransitions` on, changing state tweens each value. `toggle` flips between two states; the per-value output drives the layout input (number→dimension cast gives pixels). Signal outputs per state and `stateChanged` are registered from the same configuration — this is the current replacement for the deprecated Animation node.

examples.title: Create a record with an uploaded file attachment
examples.description: The create-with-attachment flow: Open File Picker hands the picked browser file to Upload File, which stores it in cloud storage and outputs a `cloudFile`. Cloud File exposes that file's `url`, previewed in an Image (the cloudfile→image cast). When the upload succeeds, Create Record (NewDbModelProperties) writes a new 'Attachment' record whose properties — including the file — are set on the node's schema-generated inputs.

examples.title: Load, edit and save a single record
examples.description: The record-detail flow: a Record node (DbModel2) binds to one database object by `modelId` and exposes its properties as schema-generated outputs. The edit field is initialised from the record, and Save (SetDbModelProperties) writes the changed property back on click, targeting the same id. `done` confirms the round trip, and `completed` fires after it whatever the outcome. Property ports on both nodes come from the database schema — they are runtime-determined, wired here exactly as the editor would write them.

examples.title: One query, two tabs: client-side Filter Records views
examples.description: One Query Records fetch fans out into two Filter Records nodes — 'open' and 'done' — each feeding its own Repeater. The filtering happens client-side against the already-fetched array, so switching tabs costs nothing and both views stay live as the underlying query updates. Filter in the query itself only when the excluded data shouldn't reach the client at all.

examples.title: Records on a REST backend: query, create, update, delete
examples.description: One Record family serves every backend. Query Records fetches on demand into `items` (re-trigger `storageFetch` to refresh — a query with realtime off does not re-query itself), Create/Update/Delete Record each act on a `store` signal and answer `done` (or `failure`) followed by `completed`, and Update and Delete take the record's `modelId`. After any write the query's `storageFetch` is re-triggered to refresh the list. No node here names a backend, so all five resolve the project's selected one; set the `Backend` input to point a single node somewhere else.

examples.title: A list that keeps itself current, with Subscribe To Changes
examples.description: A query is a snapshot — it only refreshes when `Do` fires. Turning on **Subscribe To Changes** closes that gap on the Query Records node itself: it holds a live subscription on the collection and fires `Changed` whenever any client creates, updates or deletes a record, so wiring `Changed` → `Do` keeps the list current without polling. `Subscribed` drives a small 'live' indicator so people can see when realtime updates are actually running, and `Realtime Status` says which of connecting/subscribed/interrupted it is in. Works on every backend that can push — SSE on the built-in backend and PocketBase, a WebSocket on Directus.

examples.title: Add and remove a relation between records; delete a record
examples.description: Relations link records without embedding them: Add Record Relation points `modelId` (the owner) at `targetId` (the related record) on a named relation field, Remove Record Relation severs the same pair, and Delete Record removes a record entirely. All three act on ids delivered by wires — here from the enclosing component's inputs — and fire `done` on success or `failure` with `error`, with `completed` after either.

examples.title: Upload a private file and preview it with a signed URL
examples.description: Open File Picker hands the picked file to Upload File with its `private` input set, so the backend ACLs the upload to its uploader instead of leaving it public. A private file's plain URL is not directly usable in an `` — it 403s for anyone else, including an unauthenticated preview — so on the picker's `done` the resulting `cloudFile` is wired into Sign File URL, whose `sign` signal is fired from the same `done`. Sign File URL mints a short-TTL signed URL (the row-ACL check that gates it is the same one the file's own GET route uses), and THAT url — not the cloudFile's own plain url — feeds the Image's `src`. Re-signing before every render (rather than persisting the signed URL) is the idiomatic use: a stored, expired signature just 403s later.

examples.title: Reacting to what another user changed, without owning the query
examples.description: **Subscribe To Changes** watches one class on the selected backend and fires signals when anything in it changes — no query, no list, no configuration beyond the class. Here it does the two things it is for at once: `changed` re-runs a Query Records node so the list on screen stays current, and `created` drives a 'new order' notice off `changedRecord`, which the subscription already carries so nothing has to be fetched to show it. `subscribed` drives a live indicator, so a dropped connection is visible rather than a screen that has quietly stopped updating. Against the built-in backend this needs no Backend setting at all: the picker defaults to the project's active backend and is not even shown when there is only one.

examples.title: CSS Definition: project stylesheet applied via class names
examples.description: CSS Definition injects the stylesheet in its `style` parameter into the page — it has no output ports; its presence is its effect. Visual nodes opt in through their `cssClassName` input. Use it for what node parameters cannot express (pseudo-selectors, keyframe animations, media queries); prefer node style parameters for everything they can express, since the editor cannot inspect CSS effects.

parameters.style:
.pulse-banner { animation: pulse 2s infinite; }
@keyframes pulse { 0% { opacity: 1; } 50% { opacity: 0.6; } 100% { opacity: 1; } }

examples.title: HTTP Request with scripted post-processing and error display
examples.description: HTTP Request (net.noodl.HTTP) fetches the `url` when `fetch` fires and delivers `response` (parsed body), `statusCode`, and either `done` or `failure` with `error` — plus `completed` after either, to carry on regardless. The response is post-processed by a Script node (Javascript2), whose input/output ports are declared by its own code — here it reads `Inputs.response` and produces a `headline` output. Errors surface as a level: `failure` evaluates a Condition whose `result` shows the error text.

examples.title: Logic Builder: block-built logic with generated ports
examples.description: Logic Builder holds a visual block workspace (`workspace`) from which the editor generates JavaScript (`generatedCode`); the inputs, outputs and signals the blocks declare or use become the node's ports. Here the block program turns a name into a greeting: the text input feeds the block-declared `name` input, `run` executes the program, and the block-declared `greeting` output lands in a Text. Both parameters are editor-managed — author the blocks, never hand-write either string. Use Logic Builder where non-programmers must be able to read and edit the logic; use Function for anything a programmer maintains.

examples.title: REST node feeding a repeater
examples.description: The REST node wraps a request/response pair in two scripts: the request script assembles the call from the node's script-declared inputs, and the response script maps the payload onto script-declared outputs — here an `items` array. Ports come from those scripts (that is its dynamism). `fetch` on mount loads the list; `success`/`failure` sequence what follows. For a one-off GET without mapping scripts, HTTP Request is the lighter tool.

examples.title: Create a client-side object and bind to it by id
examples.description: Create New Object (NewModel) makes a fresh client-side object with the property values on its schema-declared inputs and outputs the new `id`. An Object node (Model2) bound to that id then exposes the object's properties reactively — the create node acts, the Object node observes. This id-handoff is the core client-data shape: writers and readers connect through ids, not direct wires.

examples.title: Repeater item writes back to its own record object
examples.description: Inside a Repeater item component, Repeater Item (For Each Actions) exposes `itemId` — the id of this row's object. Wiring it into Set Object Properties (SetModelProperties) `modelId` makes the write target exactly this row: toggling the checkbox stores `done` on the row's object, and every other node bound to that object updates. The row never needs to know which list it belongs to. The title rides the checkbox's own `label` port (`useLabel` on) rather than a sibling Text, so the words are a real click target that toggles the box.

examples.title: Wizard step state shared via Component Object
examples.description: Component Object is per-component-instance shared state: every node in the same component instance — and, via the Parent variants, in its child components — reads and writes the same object without wires between them. The wizard holds `step` in its Component Object; the embedded controls component advances it with Set Parent Component Object Properties and reads it with Parent Component Object. Two wizard instances on one page would each have their own independent `step`, which is exactly what plain shared Objects would not give you.

examples.title: Settings form: the standard input controls bound to values
examples.description: One of each core control: Text Input's live string comes out of `onTextChanged`, Checkbox exposes `checked` (level) plus `onChange` (edge), Dropdown (net.noodl.controls.options) takes an items list and emits the selected `value`, Slider (net.noodl.controls.range) emits a numeric `value` between `min`/`max`, and a Radio Button Group reports the `value` of whichever child Radio Button is selected. Values flow into a live summary — no submit step needed for value binding.

examples.title: Run Tasks: batch-process an array with a worker component
examples.description: Run Tasks executes its `taskTemplate` component once per element of `items`, up to `maxRunningTasks` at a time, and fires `completed` when the whole batch has finished, whatever the outcome — `done` is the narrower signal that the run finished having done its work. The worker is a plain component: it receives the item's properties through Component Inputs and reports completion through Component Outputs signals (success/failure), which Run Tasks consumes to schedule the next task. Here a fresh array is assembled with New Array and processed on click.

examples.title: Named shared array with insert, remove and clear
examples.description: A client-side list without a backend: an Array node (Collection2) binds to the named shared array 'todos' and feeds a Repeater. Add Item (CollectionInsert), Remove Item (CollectionRemove) and Clear (CollectionClear) mutate the same array by its `collectionId`; every node bound to that id — including the Array feeding the list — sees the change immediately. Ids on wires tie the writers to the store.

examples.title: Static array filtered and mapped into a list
examples.description: Local data without a backend: Static Array holds inline JSON, Array Filter narrows it with a per-item filter script, Array Map reshapes each element with a map script, and the result drives a Repeater. Filter and Map are non-destructive — they emit new arrays and leave the source untouched, so several differently-filtered views can share one source.

parameters.mapScript: map({ name: object.name, label: object.name + ' — $' + object.price })

examples.title: Agent chat over a WebSocket, with the connection visible
examples.description: A minimal two-way agent surface: the WebSocket node connects on load, the prompt field feeds `message`, the Send button fires `send`, and each reply arrives on `receivedRaw`. The two status texts are the point of the example rather than decoration — `connectionState` reads idle/connecting/open/reconnecting/closed/error, and `lastError` says why whenever it lands on the last of those, so an outage is something the user can see instead of a screen that has quietly stopped answering. `whenDisconnected` is left on Queue, so a message typed during a reconnect is held in order and sent once the socket is back rather than lost.

examples.title: Server-side aggregation exposed as a cloud function
examples.description: Aggregate Records runs count/sum/min/max/average over a database class without transferring the records — it exists only in the cloud runtime, so the idiomatic shape is a small cloud function around it: Request triggers the aggregate's fetch, `fetched` sends the Response, and the aggregate results (outputs generated from the `aggregates` configuration) are returned as response params. The browser calls it like any cloud function and renders the statistic.

examples.title: Cloud function round trip: browser call → request → response
examples.description: A cloud function is a component that runs server-side: Request is its entry (its `params` become outputs carrying the caller's inputs; `receive` fires per invocation) and Response is its exit (its `params` become inputs; `send` returns them). In the browser, Call Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) names the function; the function's request params appear as inputs and its response params as outputs. Here two numbers are summed server-side: the browser sends a and b, the function computes with an Expression, and `sum` comes back on `success`.

examples.title: Cloud function that sends an email notification
examples.description: A cloud function that receives a recipient/subject/message from its caller and emails it through the backend's configured SMTP server. Request's `params` become this function's inputs; Send Email fires on `receive` and reports success/failure back to Response, which the caller reads as usual. This is the general-purpose shape for any application email (signup confirmations, receipts, alerts) — distinct from the backend's own automatic password-reset/verify-email flows (BAK-002), which never need a Send Email node.

examples.title: Function node: custom JavaScript with discovered ports
examples.description: The Function node (JavaScriptFunction) runs the JavaScript in `functionScript`. Its data ports do not exist until the script mentions them, and they are named with a prefix the script does not use: reading `Inputs.amount` creates the port `in-amount`, assigning `Outputs.formatted = …` creates the port `out-formatted`, and calling `Outputs.done()` creates the signal output `out-done` — this is why the catalog marks them runtime-determined. Note the connections below: they use `in-amount` and `out-formatted`, not the bare names in the script, which are display labels only. The node's own `run` signal is a declared port and stays unprefixed. The script runs when `run` is triggered (or when connected inputs change, if `run` is unconnected). Here a button converts a text amount to a formatted price.

examples.title: Debounced autosave with timestamped status
examples.description: The debounce idiom: every keystroke fires Value Changed, whose signal restarts a 1.5-second Timer — the save only runs when the user pauses. The save Function stamps the moment; Date To String formats it, Unique Id issues a save id shortened by Substring, and String Format assembles the status line. Signals sequence the flow; values shape the display.

examples.title: Gate a button on all required checks, reveal a note on any optional one
examples.description: And and Or as pure boolean-value combiners over numbered inputs. Two required checkboxes feed an And node's "input 0" and "input 1"; its `result` drives the submit button's `enabled` as a level, so the button enables the instant both are ticked and disables again if either is cleared. Two optional email checkboxes feed an Or the same way; its `result` shows an explanatory note while at least one is ticked. No signals are involved — everything here is level logic.

parameters.label: I accept the terms of service

parameters.text: We will only email you what you asked for. Unsubscribe anytime.

examples.title: Quantity stepper: Counter with remapped and formatted readouts
examples.description: Two buttons drive a Counter up and down within limits. The count feeds three displays: a String Format caption ('{count} items'), a String Mapper that maps special values to words (0 → 'empty'), and a Number Remapper converting the 0–10 range into 0.2–1 opacity for a fill indicator. Counter holds the state; the display nodes are pure value-shaping between it and the UI.

examples.title: Toggle a details panel with a self-labelling button
examples.description: The standard show/hide toggle: one button flips a Switch, and everything else derives from the Switch's boolean `state` as levels — the details Group's visibility directly, the summary text's visibility through an Inverter (visible only while collapsed), and the button's own label through Boolean To String so the button always names what it will do next. Note the split of flow kinds: `onClick` → `flip` is a signal (momentary), while every `state`-derived wire is a value that holds its level.

parameters.text: 3 items — tap the button for a full breakdown.
2 × Coffee beans, 1 × Filter papers. Free shipping.

examples.title: Push and pop a Component Stack (wizard flow)
examples.description: Stack-style navigation: a Page Stack (Component Stack) named 'Checkout' hosts two components, defined in its `pages` parameter with `pageComp-<id>` entries mapping each page to a component in this file. Inside /Cart, a Push Component To Stack node (PageStackNavigate) pushes /Confirm with a transition when the Continue button is clicked. Inside /Confirm, a Pop Component Stack node (PageStackNavigateBack) pops back: the Back button triggers its plain `navigate` signal, while the Place-order button triggers the `backAction-confirmed` signal input declared via the `backActions` parameter — that same action surfaces as the `backAction-confirmed` signal output on the Push node in /Cart, where it fires an Event Sender. This is the round-trip: back actions are declared on the Pop node inside the pushed component and consumed on the Push node that pushed it.

examples.title: Show a popup and close it from inside with a close action
examples.description: The popup pair: a Show Popup node (NavigationShowPopup) opens the /Confirm Delete Dialog component as an overlay when the Delete-account button is clicked. The Close Popup node (NavigationClosePopup) lives INSIDE the popup component — it is the only way the popup ends itself. Its `closeActions` parameter declares 'confirm,cancel', which registers `closeAction-confirm` and `closeAction-cancel` signal inputs on Close Popup and matching signal outputs on the Show Popup node that opened it: the host reacts to `closeAction-confirm` without knowing anything about the dialog's internals. A close action both closes the popup and routes the outcome; plain `close` (not used here) would fire Show Popup's generic `Closed` output instead.

parameters.text: Delete your account? This cannot be undone.

examples.title: URL-driven detail page: Router, Page Inputs, Navigate To Path and External Link
examples.description: URL-style navigation end to end. A Router named 'Main' hosts /Home and /Product (its `pages` parameter is `{ routes, startPage }`); each page component is rooted by a Page node whose `urlPath` defines its URL pattern — /Product uses 'product/{productId}', so the id lives in the URL. On /Home, a Navigate To Path node (PageStackNavigateToPath) builds the URL from its `path` parameter: the '{productId}' placeholder becomes the `p-productId` input, set here as a parameter, and clicking the button pushes the compiled path into browser history, which the Router picks up. On /Product, a Page Inputs node declares `pathParams: "productId"` so the value parsed from the URL is exposed as its `pm-productId` output, wired into a Text. An External Link node (net.noodl.externallink) opens an outside URL in a new tab — external URLs never go through the Router.

examples.title: Router page navigation from a button
examples.description: URL-style navigation: a Router hosts the app's pages (each page is a component, configured in the Router's `pages` parameter), and a Navigate node (RouterNavigate) switches it. The Button's `onClick` signal triggers `navigate`; which page to go to, and any path parameters, are set on the Navigate node's parameters — those ports are created from the Router's page configuration at edit time, which is why they are runtime-determined in the catalog.

examples.title: List page: Repeater fed by Query Records
examples.description: The canonical data-list shape. Query Records (DbCollection2) fetches a database class and exposes the result on its `items` array output; the Repeater (For Each) consumes that array and instantiates its `template` component once per record. Each record's properties are delivered to the item component through Component Inputs whose names match the record's property names — the item component reads them like any other input. The Repeater and its item template component are separate components by design.

examples.title: Decoupled communication with Send Event / Receive Event
examples.description: Events carry a signal (and optional payload values) between components with no wire between them: every Receive Event listening on the same `channelName` fires when a Send Event on that channel sends. Here a toolbar button broadcasts 'RefreshRequested', and a separate component re-runs its data fetch when it receives the event. Use events when the sender must not know who reacts; for parent↔child data flow prefer Component Inputs/Outputs.

examples.title: Card grid: Query Records into a Repeater, in a Columns node that reflows on its own
examples.description: The canonical data grid, and the layout decision most often got wrong. Use a Columns node with sizing "autoFit" and a minWidth of 260-320px: it fits as many columns as the CONTAINER holds and reflows by itself, with no breakpoints to maintain. Columns handles a Repeater child correctly — the Repeater draws nothing and adds its items as siblings, so Columns skips it and gives each real item a column box. The card component is width 100% and lets the column size it, which is what makes the SAME card work in this grid, in a 2-up related row, and in a sidebar. Do NOT reach for a Group with flexWrap: a wrapped flex row does not shrink its children, so each item needs a hardcoded percentage track, and — the part that matters — no Group anywhere in the runtime has a breakpoint, so that layout can never collapse on a narrow screen. Record fields reach the item through Component Inputs whose names match the record properties, and wiring a field straight into a Group's visible port is conditional rendering with no logic node.

examples.title: Closing CTA band: a designed ground, a badge, one measure centred inside it
examples.description: The band a landing page ends on, and the one section that is allowed to shout. Three things make it a section rather than a paragraph on a colour: a gradient ground (--gradient-brand) so it reads as a different surface from the bands above it; a pill badge above the headline, which is the smallest designed object a page can carry; and a measure that is CENTRED rather than left-anchored. That last one is a ruling, not a preference — on a wide window a headline with its own maxWidth inside a full-width band leaves all the empty space on one side, which reads as a mistake. Here the SHELL carries the measure (maxWidth 720) and the band centres it, so the white space is equal left and right at every width. Copy the ground onto any band you want to change the mood of; the layout does not change. Light text only: --primary-foreground throughout, and the secondary button borders on --border-glass rather than --border, which would vanish.

parameters.text: Start with the kiln already warm.
Everything on this page is a starter asset. Nothing was downloaded, nothing phones home, and the whole kit works with the network off.

examples.title: Data table: a header row, and a Repeater over ONE row component
examples.description: The admin half of every app, and the shape most often written as duplicated rows. A table IS a Repeater over a row component: there is exactly one MemberRow in the project, a For Each instantiates it once per record, and nothing about the table grows when the data does. If you find yourself authoring a second row by hand you have already left this recipe. THE COLUMN CONTRACT — the hard part, because there is no `<table>` and a flex row will not line itself up. One rule, stated once and obeyed in two places: every cell is a Group with an explicit percentage width, the percentages sum to exactly 100, and the header Group and the row component's root Group declare the SAME list. Here it is 34 / 30 / 18 / 18. Three things keep it honest. (1) NO horizontal padding on the header, on the row root, or on the table — all of it lives inside the cells (--space-4 each side), so the header's content box and every row's content box are the same box and the columns cannot drift apart. (2) NO columnGap on either row: a gap is subtracted from the 100% and would shift the header and the rows by different amounts the moment one of them acquires a gap the other lacks. (3) Groups default to boxSizing border-box, so a cell's own padding is inside its 34%, not added to it. Vertical padding goes on the header and the row root, never on a cell, so every cell in a row shares one baseline. AT 390px the percentages would give a 44px Role column, so the table does not squeeze: it sits in a Group with flexDirection row, scrollEnabled and nativeScroll true, and carries minWidth 720px. Below 720 the whole table scrolls sideways as one object, which is what keeps the header nailed to its columns — a header that scrolls independently of its rows is the classic version of this bug. Static Array holds the rows so the recipe stands alone; swap it for Query Records (DbCollection2) on a real collection and nothing else changes. Record fields reach the row through Component Inputs, whose ports are plugged "output" — that is what makes them the component's INPUTS, and getting it backwards silently drops every connection drawn out of them.

nodes.label: Sideways scroller — keeps header and rows together under 720px
Body — the Repeater draws nothing, its items land here
Row — vertical padding here, horizontal padding never
Status pill — sizeMode contentSize, so it shrink-wraps its label

examples.title: Empty state: what a list shows when it has no rows
examples.description: A list with nothing in it should say what it is and what to do, not render nothing. The designed version is small and centred inside a dashed card: an icon in a muted disc, one heading, one line of explanation capped at ~380px, and exactly one action. The switch is one wire: the query's `isEmpty` boolean into the empty state's `mounted` input. Use `mounted`, not `visible` — `mounted` takes the element out of the layout, while `visible` only hides it and keeps the space it occupies, which leaves a page-height hole above your empty state. The list needs no gate at all: a `For Each` over an empty array renders no rows and occupies no height, so nothing has to be inverted and no logic node is involved. Skipping the empty state is the difference between an app that looks unfinished on first run and one that does not, and first run is when it is always seen.

examples.title: Site footer: the three link columns are one component over a data array, not three hand-written subtrees
examples.description: The corrected version of a footer that shipped wrong, so lift the fix and not the artefact. The reference build wrote Shop, Company and Help as three structurally identical Group(Text x5) subtrees: 27 nodes, one `repeated-sibling-subtree` warning, and a fourth column costs another six nodes. Here the whole nav is one Static Array of {title, links} driving a For Each over a FooterColumn, and the link list inside each column is a second For Each — repetition is data at BOTH levels, so 17 nodes total and a fourth column is one line of JSON and no nodes at all. ⚠️ Every object in an inline array carries an `id`. A plain array reaching a Repeater's Items is wrapped with Model.create, which mints a fresh anonymous id per element, so a second delivery of the same array matches nothing in the id diff and the list renders TWICE — measured at 31 texts where 19 were authored, forward then reversed. Ids make the diff idempotent. The row is a Columns node with layoutString "1.6 1 1 1" and smallLayout "1" below 760px, because no Group in the runtime has a breakpoint — the original crammed four tracks into 390px and broke words mid-syllable. Two more that are easy to miss: marginY is what gives the collapsed stack its vertical rhythm, and the legal row's two Texts need sizeMode contentSize, or they are each width 100%, justifyContent has nothing to distribute and flexWrap has nothing to wrap.

examples.title: Form field: label, control, error and hint as one reusable component
examples.description: The unit every form is made of, built once as a component and instantiated. A column Group at --space-2 rhythm holds a label Text, the Text Input control, an error line and a hint line. ⚠️ THE TRAP: net.noodl.controls.textinput ships sizeMode "contentSize", and in that mode the width port is INERT — measured inside a 592px card, a field left at the default renders 196px wide (the browser's intrinsic 170px input plus its padding) at 1280px AND at 390px, never once responding to its container. Set sizeMode to "contentHeight" and the same width 100% measures 526px on desktop and 276px on phone. sizeMode "explicit" also frees the width but takes the height port with it, so a field that should grow with its own padding and font wants "contentHeight". ⚠️ THE SECOND TRAP, and the reason the error line is wired to `mounted` and NOT to `visible`: `visible` sets visibility:hidden and KEEPS the space it occupies (see its own port description), so an error line hidden that way leaves a permanent hole under the control. `mounted` removes the element from the page entirely. Measured: the no-error field is 71px with `mounted` and 87px with `visible` — 16px of dead row under every clean control. Both are still falsiness with no logic node: the same string drives the Text's `text` and its `mounted`, so "" both empties the line and takes it out of the layout. ⚠️ It only fires if something DRIVES the port — an instance that simply omits `error` never sends anything, `mounted` keeps its default true, and the line renders as an empty box; that is why every instance here passes error and hint explicitly, empty string included. ⚠️ The error line is --red-700, not --destructive: --destructive is a FILL colour, sized for white text on top of it rather than for being read as text. Measured as 14px text on the --surface a form card sits on, across all six shipped palettes: --destructive is 4.62:1 in the defaults but 4.38:1 under Playful and 4.49:1 under Soft, both under AA's 4.5:1, while --red-700 never drops below 6.03:1. The trade is deliberate and it is the reverse of the usual one: --red-700 is a raw palette token no preset re-themes, and a legible error line in every palette is worth more than one that moves. (An earlier note here read 3.60:1 and fails AA; that was measured 2026-08-11, when --destructive was #ef4444. DEF-001 moved it to #dc2626 on 2026-08-29 and the default now passes -- the conclusion outlived its evidence, and the presets are what still carry it.) The control's ring is --border-control (3.62:1 on --background), the token that exists because --border does not clear 3:1. The interface is the point — every port on Component Inputs is plugged "output", which is what makes it a component INPUT, and the typed value leaves through a Component Outputs port plugged "input". This is the LAYOUT recipe: for validating a value before acting on it see validate-before-submit, and for the whole control set see ctl-settings-form.

examples.title: Hero on a designed ground: a gradient band, fluid display type, glass panel
examples.description: The band a landing page opens with, and the thing a flat-colour page is missing. Three capabilities, all on ONE Group: `backgroundGradient` takes a gradient token ("var(--gradient-spotlight)") as the band's ground, so the section reads as a decision rather than a default; the headline uses `--display-lg`, a FLUID token whose value is a clamp() — 44px on a phone and 96px on a wide desktop, from one parameter and with no responsive port anywhere; and the stat strip is a translucent panel (`--surface-glass` fill, `--border-glass` hairline, `backdropBlur` 14px) which is how depth is expressed here — `opacity` on a Group would fade its own children, so translucency has to come from an alpha fill. Text on a dark ground is `--primary-foreground`, and the secondary button borders in `--border-glass` rather than `--border-control`, which is invisible on ink. Note what is NOT here: no absolutely-positioned overlay stack. A gradient ground plus a scrim is one node.

examples.title: A photograph as the ground, with a scrim that keeps the words readable
examples.description: The other half of `backgroundGradient`, and the reason it is a separate port from `backgroundColor`. `backgroundImage` and `backgroundGradient` compose into ONE css background-image declaration with the gradient FIRST — so "var(--gradient-scrim)" paints over the picture and text laid on top stays legible whatever the photograph happens to be. That is the whole hero-over-an-image problem solved on one node, instead of an Image with an absolutely-positioned Group on top of it that an authoring model gets subtly wrong. `backgroundSize` cover crops the picture to the box; `backgroundPosition` decides what survives the crop; height is explicit because a band whose only content is a heading would otherwise collapse to the heading. `justifyContent` flex-end puts the copy at the foot of the frame, where the scrim is darkest — the scrim is a vertical gradient for exactly that reason. ⚠️ The shell inside it MUST carry `sizeMode: "contentHeight"`. Without it the shell is the runtime's 100%×100% default, becomes `flexGrow:100` in a column, fills the whole 520px band, and the band's `justifyContent` has nothing left to justify — the copy silently sits at the TOP with the scrim's dark end below it, empty. That is register V1, and it bit this recipe on its first render. `backgroundImage` here is `noodl_modules/starter-imagery/ground-city-dusk.webp`, one of the 44 CC0 photographs every project is created with — pick another by SUBJECT from `get_style_vocabulary`'s `imagery` block, or point it at your own asset or an https URL. Leaving it empty is not broken: the gradient alone is still a designed ground.

examples.title: A complete landing page: eight bands, seven photographs, five item components
examples.description: THE WORKED PAGE. Every other UI recipe in this corpus is one band; this is what they look like assembled, and it is the thing to copy when the brief is "a landing page". Read it for the SHAPE, then replace every word and every picture — the copy here is a Somerset veg-box scheme because a page written in a real voice about a real thing is the only kind that shows what the voice is for. Eight bands, and the grounds ALTERNATE: a photograph under a scrim, --surface with hairlines, the page background, --surface again, --gradient-deep, --gradient-surface, --gradient-brand, --muted. That sequence is the point. A page with one background colour end to end is the first thing that reads as a template, and no amount of spacing rescues it. Each band is exactly ONE shell (maxWidth 1200, --space-6 either side), so all eight gutters agree; a band that disagrees reads as a bug rather than a choice. THE HERO is the one departure worth studying: `imageGround` with a real photograph, a --gradient-scrim over it, and a shell that is EXPLICIT 100% height with justifyContent space-between — so the nav sits at the top of the picture and the copy at its foot, with no absolutely-positioned node anywhere. Everywhere else on this page a shell carries sizeMode contentHeight, because a shell that fills its band by accident leaves the band nothing to justify. Filling one on purpose and justifying inside it is a different thing. THE MEASURE lives on the shell and on the copy GROUP, never on the headline. A maxWidth on the type strands the white space on one side of a wide viewport, which is the thing that reads as broken at 1900. THE PICTURES are seven different photographs from the bundled starter imagery, each chosen by SUBJECT: turned soil as the hero ground because the page is about growing; a market stall beside the copy that explains the boxes; three different vegetables on three cards; three different faces in three testimonials. Nothing here is decoration — a page whose every image is the same abstract is decorated, not designed. THE REPEATED THINGS are components (FeatureItem, BoxCard, StatTile, QuoteCard, FooterColumn), each with a Component Inputs node whose ports are explicitly declared and plugged "output". An undeclared port is a parameter silently discarded at the instance, and writing the subtree out three times is a repeated-sibling-subtree warning.

Three levels: a BAND is full width and owns a background (sections alternate --background and --surface so the page reads as parts, not a scroll); inside it exactly one SHELL, width 100% with maxWidth 1200px and --space-6 side padding, centred by alignItems "center" on the band; content lives in the shell. examples.title: Slide-over: an overlay panel that is a real width on desktop and full-bleed on a phone
examples.description: A slide-over is an ARRANGEMENT, and this recipe is only the arrangement — `logic-toggle-details-panel` owns the wiring that flips it (a Switch, `onClick` -> `flip`, `state` -> the panel's `open`), and the two are meant to be read together rather than merged. A real overlay IS authorable on this canvas, and this is how. (1) THE OVERLAY LAYER is a Group with `position: "fixed"`, width and height 100%, laid out `row` with `justifyContent: "flex-end"`. Measured at 1280x900 it is 1280x900 — the viewport — while the page canvas that contains it is only 1280x278. `"absolute"` also overlays, but its box is the nearest positioned ancestor (every Group is `position: relative` by default), so on a short page an absolute slide-over is a short slide-over; `"fixed"` is the one that does not depend on how tall the page happens to be. (2) THE SCRIM is a second box, `position: "absolute"` at 100%x100%, painted `var(--foreground)` with `opacity` 0.5 — no colour token carries an alpha channel, so `opacity` is how a scrim gets its tint. It is the FIRST child, because child order is paint order, and it carries the click that closes. (3) ONE WIDTH, NOT TWO: the panel is `width: 100%` with `maxWidth: 420px`. Measured, that is 420px at 1280 and 390px full-bleed at 390 with no breakpoint anywhere — there are no media queries on this canvas, and a panel pinned at 420px is 30px wider than a phone. Full-bleed also means no scrim is left to tap, which is why the header's close button is not optional. (4) THE BODY carries `scrollEnabled: true` and `height: 100%`, so a long panel scrolls inside itself: measured in a 1280x300 window the body reports scrollHeight 284 against clientHeight 231 while the page height stays 300 — the panel scrolled and the page did not grow. (5) STATE WITH NO LOGIC NODE: `open` goes straight to the overlay's `mounted`. ⚠️ Use `mounted`, not `visible` — `visible: false` only sets `visibility: hidden`, so the panel keeps its box and its whole subtree (measured: 30 boxes closed with `visible`, 16 with `mounted`, against 30 open). ⚠️ Both ports on the Component Inputs node are plugged "output", because a component INPUT is a port whose own plug is "output"; plugged "input" it becomes an output, and every connection drawn out of it is dropped as unhealthy.

The copy column carries the page's one display headline (--display-lg — a fluid clamp() that is 44px on a phone and 96px on a wide desktop — with --font-bold, --leading-none and --tracking-tighter; tight tracking is what makes a large heading look set), an eyebrow above it, a lead paragraph capped at ~520px, and two buttons whose concrete parameters are copied from the style vocabulary because `variant` is a connection-only port. The image gets sizeMode "explicit" plus a width, a height and objectFit "cover" — without explicit sizing those three ports are inert and the photo renders at its natural size.

examples.title: Stat tile row: one tile component, four instances, collapsing to two then one
examples.description: The top of an admin screen. The tile is its own component — four hand-written copies is a `repeated-sibling-subtree` warning — and the row is a Columns node that folds 4 -> 2 -> 1 as the container narrows. Inside a tile the VALUE is the only large thing: a muted uppercase label, one --text-3xl semibold number, and a small delta line. A tile whose label competes with its number reads as a form, not a dashboard. Wire each value from a Query Records count or a Cloud Function output.

examples.title: Sticky nav: a header band that stays put while the page scrolls, on a canvas with no position offsets
examples.description: Position and stacking without top/left/right/bottom ports — and it IS authorable. Every visual node carries a `position` port; set the header band to "sticky" and it holds the top edge while the page scrolls under it (measured: the band's viewport top stays 0 at scrollTop 305 of 1205 at 1280px, and 811 of 1655 at 390px). Four things decide whether it works. (1) THE INSET COMES FROM `alignY`, because no `top` port exists: for any non-relative position `alignY` already defaults to "top" and that is what writes `top: 0` — declare it so the intent is visible, and never set it to "center", which writes `top: 450px` on a 900px viewport and parks the band 422px down the screen where it never reaches the edge at all. A margin shifts the band's RESTING place (`marginTop` put it 16px lower) and not its stuck place, which stayed 0, so a sticky band floating below the top edge is not expressible: put the gap inside the band. (2) It sticks inside ITS PARENT's box, so the band must be a direct child of the tall page column; wrapped in a Group only as tall as itself it scrolls straight off, measured at top -305. (3) Any ancestor with Clip Content on kills it — the same -305, silently, with no error anywhere. (4) `zIndex` is structural here, not decoration: leave it off and the band's geometry is still right, top 0, while the section text paints straight through it, illegible, and takes the clicks — the sibling bands are position relative too, so DOM order wins without it. Prefer sticky to "fixed" for a header: fixed takes no space, so the page measured 1148px instead of 1205px — exactly one band shorter — with the first section starting underneath it. Unwrapped, the nav row is 463px wide and forces the layout viewport open at 390px, so the shell sets `flexWrap: "wrap"` and the band grows from 57px to 85px instead of overflowing.
